file: 2002/2002-05-15_powerpoint slides_ceos visit_needs to fix.gif
title: Honest Slides for the CEO

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you finished your "PowerPoint" slides for the CEO's visit?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes. I'm focusing on all the things we do wrong, because that's what he needs to fix.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Just kidding. There's no useful information.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't joke!

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, asks Alice whether her PowerPoint slides for the CEO's visit are done. Alice says she is highlighting everything the company does wrong so the CEO can fix it, which alarms him. She then says she was kidding and that the slides contain no useful information, and he scolds her for joking.
punchline: The Boss is far more upset by the idea of a joke than by the admission that the presentation contains nothing useful, and he would have been fine with that had she not joked about the honest version.
summary: An employee's candid plan to expose company failures to the CEO is swapped for the admission that her slides are empty, and her manager only objects to the humor.

file: 2002/2002-11-20_lab accident_sheep_soft and warm_form opinions_want wool_start shaving.gif
title: Dogbert the Sheep Offers Wool

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A lab accident turned me into a sheep.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's not all bad. In addition to being soft and warm, I never need to form opinions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you want some wool, just grab me and start shaving. I'll barely struggle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Cool!

situation: Dogbert, dressed in a sheep costume, tells The Boss that a lab accident turned him into a sheep. He lists the perks, including never having to form opinions, and invites The Boss to shave his wool. The Boss, holding a coffee mug, happily plugs in an electric shaver.
punchline: Dogbert's sheep-like lack of opinions is a swipe at conformist, passive employees, and The Boss eagerly takes advantage of someone offering no resistance.
summary: A sheepified Dogbert cheerfully explains the advantages of mindless conformity and offers his wool to a delighted boss.

file: 2002/2002-07-26_beginning to feel_daily_defective_hreatened_vendor comparison.gif
title: Threaten Me Daily Or Nothing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you finish the vendor comparison that you promised you'd give me today?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm one of those people that needs to be threatened every day or I won't do anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're very defective.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Good start. I'm beginning to feel something.

situation: Dilbert asks a seated coworker whether he finished a vendor comparison he promised for today. The coworker says no and explains that he only works when threatened daily. When Dilbert insults him by calling him defective, the coworker treats it as a good start at motivation.
punchline: The slacker coworker interprets Dilbert's insult as the threat he needs, so Dilbert's attempt to shame him accidentally becomes the very motivation he asked for.
summary: A procrastinating employee admits he only works under daily threats, and then happily takes an insult as a promising first step.

file: 2002/2002-04-09_bragging_hours per week_made up_reorganized pattern_seventy hours_sixty hours_complaining.gif
title: One-Upping Overwork Brag Pattern

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I worked sixty hours last week.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's nothing. I worked seventy hours.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's nothing...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh, wait... I just recognized the pattern.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting, with snacks and coffee cups
situation: Dilbert, Wally and Alice sit around a meeting table eating. Dilbert says he worked sixty hours last week, Wally claims seventy, and Alice begins to top them with a dismissive 'That's nothing' before catching herself.
punchline: Alice realizes that she was about to join a pointless contest of exaggerated overwork, recognizing the competitive one-upmanship pattern and stopping herself.
summary: Three coworkers start competing over who suffered the longest work week until one of them realizes how silly the game is.

file: 2002/2002-04-23_engineering anaysis_unnecessary assignment_non existent software_sweet smell.gif
title: Sweet Smell of Pointless Assignment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's critical that you finish this engineering analysis by Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aahh... it has the sweet smell of an unnecessary assignment.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes, I can smell it from here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop being you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Feasibility of using non-existent software.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hee hee!

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert an engineering analysis and says it is critical to finish by Tuesday. Dilbert and Wally both sniff out that it is a pointless assignment. When the Boss tells Dilbert to stop being so cynical, Dilbert reveals the topic is the feasibility of using non-existent software, which Wally finds hilarious.
punchline: The supposedly critical analysis is about whether to use software that doesn't exist, confirming it really is an unnecessary assignment.
summary: A manager insists on an urgent technical study, but the employees correctly sense it is busywork about a nonexistent product.

file: 2002/2002-07-22_bankrupt_401k money gone_investing_competitors stock_wally rich_investing in competition.gif
title: Wally Profits From Competitor's Stock

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, what are we going to do now that we're bankrupt and our 401k money is gone?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No problem. I've been investing all of my money in our competitor's stock. Now I'm rich.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why do you still come to work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't know how to make coffee.

situation: Alice asks Wally what they will do now that the company has gone bankrupt and their 401k savings are wiped out. Wally calmly explains that he put all his money into the competitor's stock and is now rich. When Alice asks why he still shows up for work, he admits he doesn't know how to make coffee.
punchline: Wally, though newly wealthy, keeps coming to work only because he lacks the basic skill of making his own coffee, which pokes fun at his laziness and dependence on the office.
summary: While the company collapses around everyone else, Wally secretly bet on the rival firm and got rich, yet still turns up daily for a very petty reason.

file: 2002/2002-05-31_choose attitudes_dopey_gullible_book.gif
title: Alice Turns Boss's Book Against Him

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, according to this book, people can choose their attitudes!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So you decided to go with a dopey and gullible theme?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And that's another interesting choice. Now I see how this works.

situation: The Boss approaches Alice holding a self-help book and tells her that people can choose their attitudes. Alice calmly replies that he must have chosen a dopey and gullible theme for himself. She points at him as he grimaces and fumes, and says she now understands how the book's idea works.
punchline: Alice takes the book's premise that attitudes are a choice and uses it to insult the Boss, implying his dopiness is deliberate, which leaves him angry and speechless.
summary: A manager quotes a self-help book about choosing your attitude, and Alice uses that very idea to mock him for choosing to be gullible.

file: 2002/2002-01-24_transfer to engineering_pay cut_work for free_work in sales_apreciative.gif
title: Begging to Return to Engineering

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please, I beg you, transfer me back to engineering.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll take a pay cut. No, I'll work for free. No, I'll pay you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I should make all of my engineers work in sales for a while. You come back more appreciative.

situation: Dilbert, now working in sales, desperately pleads with the Boss to be transferred back to engineering, offering a pay cut, free labor, and finally to pay the Boss himself. The Boss, reclining with his feet up while Dilbert tends to his shoes, concludes that sending all engineers to sales would make them more appreciative.
punchline: Instead of recognizing Dilbert's misery as a sign of a bad reassignment, the Boss takes it as proof that making employees suffer in another job is a great management technique.
summary: A miserable salesman offers anything to get his old job back, and his manager decides his desperation is a feature worth repeating.

file: 2002/2002-09-24_chronic mahjobbis_puke_doctor_exam_diagnosis_user interfaces_designed by engineers_interface poisoning_dead in a week_medical.gif
title: Interface Poisoning Is Fatal

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You have chronic mahjobbis crappus but that's not why you puked.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Have you been exposed to any user interfaces designed by engineers?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: You have interface poisoning. You'll be dead in a week.

situation: A doctor reviews a patient's results and announces a made-up chronic ailment, saying it isn't what made her vomit. He asks whether she has used any user interfaces designed by engineers, and when she says yes, he diagnoses her with fatal 'interface poisoning' with a week to live.
punchline: Software interfaces designed by engineers are so awful that they are treated as a literal, deadly poison.
summary: A physician traces his patient's sudden illness to the terrible software screens she has been forced to use and delivers a grim prognosis.

file: 2002/2002-10-20_unwritten rule_talked to boss's boss_rule against_interesting_wonder why_transmitting_rules of esp_outgoing signals_silent_not supposed to_unwritten_boss_alice.gif
title: Unwritten Rule, Unblocked Signals

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I did what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You talked to my boss without my permission.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't remember reading a rule against that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's because it's an unwritten rule.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Unwritten you say? Hmm... Isn't that interesting? I wonder why it's unwritten.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I would think you'd be proud to write down an excellent rule such as that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But if you prefer to keep transmitting rules by ESP, your skull seems to be blocking the outgoing signals.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If you're sending a new rule now, turn your head so it can come out your ear hole.

situation: The Boss scolds Alice for talking to his boss without his permission. Alice points out she never read any rule against that, and he says it is an unwritten rule. She mocks the idea of unwritten rules, suggesting he is transmitting them by ESP and that his skull is blocking the signals.
punchline: Alice sarcastically exposes the absurdity of unwritten rules by claiming the Boss must be sending them telepathically, with his head blocking the transmission.
summary: When her manager punishes her for breaking a rule nobody ever wrote down, Alice answers with a barrage of sarcasm about mind-reading and blocked signals.

file: 2002/2002-09-15_feasibility analysis_two years_obsolete_project can't succeed_credible in market_stupid things_complete waste_behind schedule.gif
title: Doomed Project Started for Credibility

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I completed the feasibility analysis.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It would take us two years to build a product that will be obsolete one year from now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, let's get started.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... no, the point is that the project can't succeed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We want people to think we're developing this sort of product, so we'll be credible in the market.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So our plan is to do stupid things until we appear credible?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!! My life is a complete waste!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll ask him why he's behind schedule.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Very evil. Nicely done.

setting: The Boss's office, with a final panel at a desk or coffee area
situation: Dilbert presents a feasibility analysis showing the project would take two years to build a product that will be obsolete in one. The Boss ignores the conclusion and says to start anyway, then explains the goal is merely to look credible in the market. Dilbert despairs, while the Boss plans to blame him later for being behind schedule, to the approval of Dogbert.
punchline: The project is intentionally pointless and doomed, and the Boss will additionally torment Dilbert by demanding to know why he's behind schedule on a task that was never meant to succeed.
summary: A doomed product is greenlit purely for appearances, leaving the engineer despairing while his manager schemes to scold him over deadlines.

file: 2002/2002-01-14_dilbert as waiter_hots on customer_insults customer_specials_rude_age.gif
title: Waiter Dilbert Hits On Customer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be your server tonight... Whoa, you're beautiful.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would your grandfather mind if I asked you out?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: He's my husband.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Moving right along, would you like to hear about our specials?

situation: Dilbert, working as a waiter, flirts with a young woman dining with an older man. He asks whether her grandfather would mind if he asked her out, and she says the man is her husband. Dilbert awkwardly changes the subject to the daily specials.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to flirt backfires when he insults the couple by assuming the older man is her grandfather, and he tries to brush past the embarrassment by pitching the specials.
summary: A flirtatious waiter mistakes a diner's husband for her grandfather and then hurriedly pivots to reciting the menu.

file: 2002/2002-09-30_integrate_inventroy_finance systems_nitiwt_ogre_fired_thirty years.gif
title: Integration Project With Doomed Stakeholders

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I want you to integrate our sales database with our inventory and finance systems.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The managers of those systems are a nitwit, an ogre, and a $#!%, respectively.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And they know that two of them will be fired when it's complete.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can get that done in thirty years.

situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert a project to integrate the sales database with the inventory and finance systems. He warns that the managers of those systems are difficult people, and that two of them will lose their jobs once the integration is finished. Dilbert responds that he can complete it in thirty years.
punchline: Because the system managers will resist a project that gets them fired, Dilbert sarcastically estimates an absurdly long timeline, implying the integration will never realistically happen.
summary: A manager hands over a system integration job whose success would cost two stakeholders their positions, and the engineer quotes a decades-long schedule.

file: 2002/2002-04-24_new reality_leave reality_don't like leave.gif
title: Leaving Reality Is Not Possible

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a new reality. If you don't like it, you can leave!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: How can we leave reality? Aren't we always in it by definition?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Never mind... Apparently everyone else knew what you meant.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces to his staff that there is a new reality and anyone who dislikes it can leave. Dilbert literally questions how anyone could leave reality, since we are always in it by definition. After noticing that his coworkers are all asleep, he realizes everyone else understood the boss's meaning and that he was the only one paying attention.
punchline: Dilbert pedantically parses the boss's cliche, only to discover everyone else is asleep, which implies they tuned out the boss's empty rhetoric entirely.
summary: A manager's tough-love slogan gets taken literally by one attentive employee while the rest of the room dozes off.
keywords: if you don't like it you can leave

file: 2002/2002-11-24_performance review_objectives_play computer_solitaire_drink coffee_valuable lesson_reading documents_signing_games of solitaire_something new_employee of month.gif
title: Wally's Slacker Performance Review Objectives

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hate today... I hate today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally's annual performance review.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's compare your objectives with...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What the...?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Apparently your objectives are "play computer solitaire and drink coffee."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope you're learning a valuable lesson about reading documents before signing them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, we'll use what we have. How many games of solitaire did you win?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Win? I didn't know you could win. Is that something new?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He made you the employee of the month?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He thinks he signed a warning for my file.

setting: The Boss's office and a cubicle area
situation: The Boss dreads conducting Wally's annual performance review. He discovers that the objectives on file, which he signed himself, are to play computer solitaire and drink coffee. When he tries to salvage the review by counting solitaire wins, Wally claims he didn't even know you could win, and afterward Wally tells Dilbert the boss thinks he signed a warning.
punchline: Wally, the master slacker, exploited the boss's habit of signing documents without reading them, so he can't be criticized for doing exactly what his own objectives said, and the boss doesn't even realize he approved an employee-of-the-month award.
summary: A manager reviewing his laziest employee finds that he himself signed off on goals that amount to doing nothing, and the employee turns the situation entirely in his favor.

file: 2002/2002-08-10_telecommuted for 4 years_fired_unemployment_empowerment_sixth sense.gif
title: Telecommuter Realizes He Was Fired

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I telecommuted for four years without knowing until today that I'd been fired.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Apparently unemployment feels exactly like empowerment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is just like that movie, "The Sixth Sense." Did you like that movie, Wally? ...Wally?

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Three coworkers sit around a table with snacks. One man explains that he worked from home for four years before discovering he had actually been fired. Another notes that unemployment feels just like empowerment, and the first compares it to The Sixth Sense and asks Wally if he liked the movie, but Wally does not respond.
punchline: Wally has been fired too, and like the ghost in The Sixth Sense, he may not have realized it, so his silence suggests he is no longer really there.
summary: A man who just learned he lost his job years ago is joined by a coworker who calls it liberating, and a movie reference hints that the silent colleague may be in the same oblivious state.

file: 2002/2002-04-15_cleaned tool shed_running tally_time waster_frozen snake_shovel_five years one day.gif
title: Alice Tallies Boss's Wasted Time

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This weekend I cleaned out my tool shed.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's that for?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I keep a running tally of how much of my time you waste.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...and I thought it was a frozen snake but it was actually a shovel!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Five years, one day.

situation: The Boss stops by Alice's desk to tell her a pointless story about cleaning his tool shed. Alice clicks a stopwatch, and when he asks why, she explains she tracks how much of her time he wastes. As he finishes his rambling snake-versus-shovel anecdote, she announces the running total: five years and one day.
punchline: Alice's running tally of time wasted by the boss's pointless chatter has reached five years and one day, showing how much of her working life he has consumed with trivia.
summary: A worker quietly times her manager's pointless stories and reveals the accumulated total of lost time has become staggering.

file: 2002/2002-12-30_power point presentation_ceo slip trance_subliminal suggestions_increase budget_more budget_kill boss_pointy haired monster.gif
title: Hypnotizing the CEO With PowerPoint

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make your "PowerPoint" presentation so boring that our CEO will slip into a trance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I'll whisper to him subliminal suggestions to increase our budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: More budget.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Kill the Pointy-Haired Monster.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to make his PowerPoint presentation deliberately boring so the CEO falls into a trance. The Boss plans to whisper subliminal suggestions to get a bigger budget. In the meeting, the CEO slumps in a trance while the Boss murmurs his request, and the CEO mumbles back a very different command.
punchline: The entranced CEO responds to the Boss's budget suggestion by ordering that the Boss himself be killed, revealing the CEO's true opinion of him.
summary: A manager tries to hypnotize his executive with a dull slideshow, but the dazed executive blurts out his real feelings about the manager instead.

file: 2002/2002-10-07_tv ad eeffectivesness_heard of company_boring commercial_viewers drift off_ad money_special hole.gif
title: Throw Your Ad Money Into a Hole

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A survey of your TV ad effectiveness shows that no one has heard of your company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your ad only says your name once, at the end of a boring commercial when viewers have drifted off.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend throwing your ad money into a special kind of hole.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When can we start?

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells company executives that a survey shows nobody has heard of their company because their TV ad is boring and mentions the company name only once at the end. He recommends throwing their ad money into a special kind of hole, and the Boss eagerly asks when they can start.
punchline: Dogbert's sarcastic advice to waste the ad budget in a hole is eagerly embraced by the clueless Boss, showing management will happily pay for a useless recommendation.
summary: A consultant dog mockingly tells a company to dump its advertising budget into a hole, and the eager boss wants to begin immediately.

file: 2002/2002-06-20_accounting system_less transparent_investors_bad people_corrupt corporate culture.gif
title: Corrupt Culture Excuses Hiding Accounting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our assignment is to make our accounting system less transparent.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We don't want investors to know what we're doing.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Are we bad people?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're good people who have been influenced by a corrupt corporate culture.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Oh, okay. Carry on.

situation: Dilbert tells the team, including Asok, that their assignment is to make the company's accounting system less transparent so investors can't see what is going on. Asok asks whether this makes them bad people, and Dilbert reassures him that they are good people corrupted by company culture. Asok accepts this excuse and goes along with it.
punchline: Asok is satisfied by the flimsy rationalization that blaming corporate culture makes participating in accounting fraud acceptable.
summary: A team is ordered to obscure the company's books from investors, and one worker's conscience is quickly soothed by a convenient excuse.

file: 2002/2002-08-08_empty cubicles_frightens customres_adopt cubicle_decorate_appear occupied_phil de cube_imaginary employee.gif
title: Imaginary Employees Fill Empty Cubicles

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have too many empty cubicles. It frightens our customers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Each of you will adopt an empty cubicle and decorate it to appear occupied.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: My imaginary employee will be a Frenchman named Phil de Cube.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nice.

situation: In a meeting, the Boss complains that too many empty cubicles scare customers and orders each employee to adopt an empty cubicle and decorate it so it looks occupied. Afterward, Phil proudly announces the fake employee he has invented, and Dilbert politely approves.
punchline: Phil's imaginary employee is a Frenchman named Phil de Cube, a pun on 'file de cube' / 'fill the cube' that turns the absurd management order into wordplay.
summary: Management responds to a half-empty office by having staff stage fake occupants, and one worker invents a punny French persona.

file: 2002/2002-11-03_coproaret social responsibilty_cut salary_poor people_extra money_hose stock holders_hurt stock options_pollute less_bucket_river_sludge out_coffee_zesty.gif
title: Bucket Brigade Corporate Social Responsibility

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: We need to show more corporate social responsibility.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, I'll cut your salary and give the extra money to poor people.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I was hoping we could hose the stockholders, not me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That would hurt my stock options.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if we pollute less?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Yes, yes! That's what I'm talking about. We could pollute less!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, take a bucket to the river and see how much of our sludge you can get out.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Where would I put it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it just me or has the coffee improved?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Zesty!

setting: Boss's office, with a final panel in the office coffee area
situation: Carol suggests the company show more corporate social responsibility, and the Boss first offers to cut her salary to give to the poor. When she asks to protect neither herself nor his stock options, he proposes polluting less, then assigns her to scoop sludge out of the river with a bucket. In the last panel Dilbert and Wally remark on the coffee tasting better.
punchline: The Boss's idea of reducing pollution is to have Carol bucket sludge out of the river by hand with nowhere to put it, while the coffee in the last panel is implied to be made with that polluted river water.
summary: A manager turns a request for social responsibility into a pointless manual cleanup chore, while two coworkers unknowingly enjoy coffee that seems suspiciously improved.

file: 2002/2002-03-19_consciousness_ability to predict_results of actions_fully conscious_array of sensors_collect data.gif
title: Dilbert Lectures Sleeping Date About Consciousness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My theory is that consciousness is the ability to predict and then observe the results of actions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I think you could build a computer that would be fully conscious.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Zzzzz

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Obviously you'd need an array of sensors to collect the data.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Zzzzz

setting: Outdoors on a grassy lawn with hedges, during a walk or date
situation: Dilbert enthusiastically explains his theory of consciousness and how to build a conscious computer to a woman walking with him. She falls asleep standing up and drifts off, and by the last panel he is carrying her slumped over his shoulder while he keeps lecturing, unaware.
punchline: Dilbert is so absorbed in his technical monologue that he fails to notice his date has fallen asleep and is being carried, ironically showing a lack of awareness himself.
summary: A geeky man drones on about artificial consciousness so thoroughly that his companion nods off and he ends up hauling her around without noticing.

file: 2002/2002-01-12_server job_abusive customer_kindness_tablecloth.gif
title: Server Job Interview With Violence

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi. I came to apply for a server job.

transcript.speaker: Restaurant Manager
transcript.text: Okay. Tell me how you would handle an abusive drunken customer like this guy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... with kindness?

transcript.speaker: Restaurant Manager
transcript.text: You might want to shield yourself with a tablecloth.

situation: Dilbert arrives at a restaurant to apply for a server job. The manager, who is gripping a drunken customer by his necktie while he slumps in his chair, asks how Dilbert would handle such a patron. Dilbert suggests kindness, and she advises him to shield himself with a tablecloth instead.
punchline: The interviewer's dark answer reveals that customers at this restaurant are so abusive that physical self-defense, not kindness, is the real job skill.
summary: A job candidate offers a gentle approach to a rowdy patron and learns the restaurant expects him to take cover.

file: 2002/2002-11-13_short timer_retiring_honest feedback_doing nothing_create the illusion_fanatsize_good enough.gif
title: Retiring Employee Fakes Listening, Fantasizes Fishing

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Short-Timer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're retiring soon, so you can give me honest feedback.

transcript.speaker: Short-Timer
transcript.text: Wouldn't that be harder than doing absolutely nothing?

transcript.speaker: Short-Timer
transcript.text: How about if I create the illusion of listening while I fantasize about fishing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good enough.

situation: The Boss tells an older employee who is about to retire that he can now give honest feedback. The employee points out that this would take more effort than doing nothing, and instead offers to pretend to listen while daydreaming about fishing. The Boss readily accepts this arrangement.
punchline: The boss is so indifferent to real input that he happily accepts a retiring employee faking attention while mentally checked out, showing that the appearance of engagement is all he cares about.
summary: A manager asks a soon-to-retire worker for candid input, but the worker offers a lazy pretense of attention that the manager gladly accepts.

file: 2002/2002-10-26_drop lawsuit_fight dirty_dispatch goons_billy blanks on ur butt_mother_dilmom_suing company_family.gif
title: Mom Threatens Goon With Tae Bo

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mom, you have to drop your lawsuit against my company. They fight dirty.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Bring 'em on! I've been watching my "Tae Bo" videos! I'll dispatch their goons to hell!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They sent me. I'm their goon.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: After dinner, I'm going Billy Blanks on your butt!

situation: Dilbert visits his mother in her kitchen and asks her to drop a lawsuit she has filed against his company, warning that the company fights dirty. She boasts that her Tae Bo workout videos have prepared her to beat up any goons the company sends. Dilbert admits he is the goon they sent, and she promises to give him a Tae Bo beating after dinner.
punchline: The company's feared dirty-fighting goon is just Dilbert, and his own mother is ready to beat him up with her newly learned Tae Bo moves.
summary: A man sent by his employer to pressure his mother into dropping a lawsuit learns she is eager to pummel the company's enforcer, who turns out to be him.

file: 2002/2002-10-13_communication_integrity_teamwork_pyramid pillars_team memeber idiots_honest opinion_team player_agree bad ideas_two legged stool.gif
title: Pillars of a Pyramid Team

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The three pillars of our pyramid are communication, integrity, and teamwork.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Since when do pyramids have pillars?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Answer: Shut up.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Problem: All of my team members are idiots.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If I communicate my honest opinion of their ideas, I won't be a team player.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But if I pretend to agree with their bad ideas, I won't have integrity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So instead of being a pyramid, can I be a two-legged stool like you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! That was much better than my pillar question.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Aren't I on your team?

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss presents a pyramid diagram with three pillars: communication, integrity, and teamwork. Dilbert questions the logic of pyramids having pillars and is told to shut up, then Alice describes her dilemma that being honest about her team's idiocy violates teamwork, while faking agreement violates integrity.
punchline: Alice's reply shows that the pillars contradict each other, leaving her with only two legs to stand on, and the exchange makes Dilbert's question look tame by comparison.
summary: A manager's slogan-filled diagram falls apart when an employee points out that the core values cannot all be honored at once when your colleagues are fools.

file: 2002/2002-08-02_budget cuts_customer service_pranks calls to elderly_neighbor_treasure buried_under lawn.gif
title: Budget Cuts Turn Support Into Pranksters

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our budget cuts are affecting customer service.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How much?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our customer service center spends all day making prank calls to the elderly.

transcript.speaker: Customer Service Rep
transcript.text: According to our records, your neighbor has treasure buried under his lawn.

setting: Boss's office and a customer service call center
situation: Dilbert reports to the Boss that budget cuts are hurting customer service. When the Boss asks how badly, Dilbert explains the call center now spends its days making prank calls to the elderly. A headset-wearing rep is shown mid-call, feeding an elderly person a fake story about buried treasure next door.
punchline: The 'impact' of the budget cuts is that the demoralized, underfunded support staff have stopped helping customers and now amuse themselves by tormenting old people.
summary: Cost-cutting leaves a support department so neglected that its staff pass the time pranking senior citizens by phone.

file: 2002/2002-01-10_grow beard_while unemployed_message_who you are_shopping cart_filthy rags.gif
title: Unemployed Dilbert Considers Growing Beard

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think I should grow a beard while I'm unemployed?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's a great idea. A beard sends a message about who you are.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I assume you already have a shopping cart and filthy rags.

situation: Dilbert, standing in his undershirt and boxer shorts, asks Dogbert whether he should grow a beard while he is out of work. Dogbert enthusiastically agrees, saying a beard sends a message about who you are. When Dilbert hesitantly accepts, Dogbert adds that he must already own a shopping cart and filthy rags.
punchline: Dogbert implies that an unemployed man with a beard looks like a homeless person, so Dilbert's beard would signal that he is destitute.
summary: Dogbert cheerfully endorses his jobless owner's beard plan, then reveals that the look he has in mind is that of a vagrant.

file: 2002/2002-07-15_30 thousand employees_emails jokes per week_file bankruptcy_lost prodcutivity_ten million_holding employee responsible.gif
title: Blaming Tina for Company Bankruptcy

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Tina, our records show that you forward an average of nineteen e-mail jokes per week.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Each joke goes to 30,000 employees, costing us ten million per year in lost productivity.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We plan to blame you when we file for bankruptcy next week.

setting: Tina's office, with Catbert standing on her desk
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, confronts Tina about the e-mail jokes she forwards every week. He calculates that the jokes reach 30,000 employees and cost the company ten million a year in lost productivity. He then announces that the company will blame her when it files for bankruptcy next week.
punchline: Management makes an employee the scapegoat for a bankruptcy that is obviously caused by far bigger problems than forwarded e-mail jokes.
summary: The HR cat tallies up the cost of one employee's chain-letter humor and informs her she will take the fall for the company's imminent collapse.

file: 2002/2002-05-20_senior vice presdient_cyrus_virus_infection_managers_old cronmies_pointy haired pete.gif
title: Cyrus the Virus Infects Management

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like you to meet our new Senior Vice President, Cyrus the Virus.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Like an infection, he will soon attack the managers in this company and replace us with his old cronies.

transcript.speaker: Cyrus
transcript.text: Tell Pointy-Haired Pete to get over here right away.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss introduces the company's new Senior Vice President, whose nickname is Cyrus the Virus. He cheerfully admits the newcomer will attack the existing managers and replace them with his own cronies. The new executive then immediately phones to summon a replacement manager, Pointy-Haired Pete.
punchline: The Boss calmly and cheerfully announces that the new executive will wipe out the current managers, including himself, without seeming to grasp that he is the one about to be replaced.
summary: A manager happily introduces a corporate hatchet man who is about to purge the very managers he is addressing.

file: 2002/2002-12-24_anti itch lotion_might cause itching_customer list_bear_mean dogbert_evil thinking_hates people.gif
title: Honey Lotion Scam Sold to Bears

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I plan to sell an anti-itch lotion that's really just honey.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll put a tiny disclaimer on the bottle that says, "Might cause itching."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not nice.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And then I'll sell my customer list to bears.

setting: Outdoor dirt path in a grassy field
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert walk along a path while Dogbert lays out a business plan to sell honey as anti-itch lotion with a tiny disclaimer saying it might cause itching. Dilbert objects that this is not nice. Dogbert escalates by revealing he will sell his customer list to bears.
punchline: Dogbert's scheme is not just deceptive but dangerous, since honey-slathered customers sold to bears as a mailing list will be hunted by them.
summary: A scheming dog plans to dupe customers with honey lotion and then hand their contact details to hungry bears.

file: 2002/2002-04-02_buzzwords_strung together_same status reprt_every week_eleven years_mission statement.gif
title: Wally's Status Report Became Mission Statement

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, your status report is just a bunch of buzzwords strung together.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've been giving you that same status report every week for eleven years.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Five years ago you adopted it as our mission statement.

situation: The Boss complains to Wally, who is holding his coffee mug, that his status report is nothing but strung-together buzzwords. Wally calmly points out that he has submitted the identical report weekly for eleven years. He adds that the company adopted it as its mission statement five years ago.
punchline: The company's official mission statement is the same meaningless buzzword filler Wally has been recycling as a status report, exposing corporate mission statements as empty jargon.
summary: A manager criticizes an employee's vague report, only to learn that the company already uses that very text as its guiding mission.

file: 2002/2002-04-25_key card_tailgate_network password_voicemail_stop working.gif
title: Everything Stops Working, Including Him

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What a day I'm having. First my key card doesn't work, so I have to tailgate into the building.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Then my network password doesn't work. Now my voicemail doesn't work!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Is it possible for anything else to stop working today?!

setting: Office, in front of the boss's desk
situation: An employee in a white shirt and tie complains to the boss about his terrible day. His key card failed, then his network password, then his voicemail. In the last panel the boss sits grinning in his chair, saying nothing.
punchline: The employee's access has been shut off one system at a time, and the boss's smug grin suggests the employee has been fired and nobody has told him yet.
summary: A man rants about his accounts failing one after another while his smiling boss silently watches, hinting at why everything is going wrong.

file: 2002/2002-01-20_new house_next week_heavy objects_help_cares about career_professional companies exist_move things_wonderful system_mobile home_trailer.gif
title: Boss Wants Free Moving Help

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm moving to a new house next week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have lots of heavy objects that need to be moved.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder who will help me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe it will be someone who cares about his career.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you know that professional moving companies exist?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's true. You give them money and they move your heavy things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a wonderful system. You should look into it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And maybe you can bring your trailer.

transcript.speaker: Female coworker
transcript.text: It's a mobile home!

situation: The Boss hints repeatedly that he expects an employee to help him move to a new house, implying it would be good for the employee's career. Dilbert sarcastically points out that professional moving companies exist and that you simply pay them. The Boss ignores this and asks Dilbert to bring his trailer, while a coworker nearby protests that hers is a mobile home.
punchline: The Boss shrugs off the obvious solution of hiring movers and keeps trying to get free labor and equipment from his employees by implying career consequences.
summary: A manager angles to get an underling to haul his furniture for free, brushing aside the suggestion of simply paying professionals.

file: 2002/2002-02-26_attacking me_number accurate_too late to apologize_hate your guys.gif
title: Questioning A Number Triggers Hatred

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this number accurate? It seems low.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why are you attacking me? Stop attacking me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think the number is low.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's too late to apologize. Now I hate your guts.

setting: Office desk during a one-on-one conversation
situation: Dilbert holds a report and politely asks a coworker whether a figure is accurate because it looks low. She reacts as if he is attacking her and demands that he stop. When he simply repeats his concern, she declares it is too late to apologize and says she now hates him.
punchline: A neutral question about data accuracy is treated as a personal attack, and the coworker invents an apology that never happened to justify her hostility.
summary: A routine question about a suspicious figure sends an oversensitive colleague into a defensive rage, ending in grudge-holding over an apology nobody offered.

file: 2002/2002-02-05_all natural_cd drive_holistic tech support_natural and holistic_tree bark_meditate.gif
title: Dogbert's Holistic Tech Support Hotline

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hello, this is Dogbert's all-natural and holistic tech support.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try stuffing tree bark in the CD drive and meditating.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, of course it won't damage anything; it's all natural!

setting: Dogbert's tech support call desk and the caller's office
situation: Dogbert runs a tech support line and answers the phone wearing a headset. He tells a worried-looking caller to stuff tree bark into the computer's CD drive and meditate. When the caller objects, Dogbert insists it can't cause damage because it's natural.
punchline: Dogbert applies the fallacy that 'natural' means harmless to give absurd, destructive advice, showing that tech support can be both useless and confidently wrong.
summary: A tech support hotline offers New Age advice that has a customer shoving tree bark into his computer, defended by the claim that anything natural is safe.

file: 2002/2002-10-15_computer_recycled paper_doomed to fail_find joy_misery_technology.gif
title: Wally's Joy in Project Failure

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I asked Dilbert to lead the team in making a computer entirely from recycled paper.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Ha ha ha!! You are totally doomed to fail!!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally is teaching me to find joy in the misery of others.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're on my project team.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss announces that Dilbert will lead a team to build a computer entirely from recycled paper. Asok, a team member, bursts into laughter and gleefully declares the project doomed. He explains that Wally has been teaching him to enjoy other people's misery, and Dilbert points out that Asok is on his own project team.
punchline: Asok is delighting in the failure of a project he is himself assigned to, so the misery he is gloating over is partly his own.
summary: A new hire cheerfully mocks an impossible assignment, forgetting that he has been drafted onto the doomed team too.

file: 2002/2002-12-29_last three times_thought stolen_parked it_forgot_magic powers_car stolen_parking lot_car will appear.gif
title: Carol's Magic Reappearing Car Trick

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, call the police. My car has been stolen.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Is it like the last three times that you thought it had been stolen?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: And later you realized that you just forgot where you parked it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. This time is different. My car is totally gone.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Watch me use my magic powers to make your car reappear in the parking lot.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Presto auto reappearo!!!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: After all the other cars leave the parking lot, your car will appear.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Freaky.

setting: Office cubicle area and the company parking lot
situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to call the police because his car has been stolen. Carol points out he has made the same claim three times before and always just forgot where he parked. When he insists this time is different, she mockingly performs a magic spell, and at the end he finds his car in the lot.
punchline: Carol's fake magic spell is really just the obvious fact that his car will turn up once the other cars leave, and the boss is foolishly amazed that it worked.
summary: A forgetful executive reports another supposedly stolen car, and his assistant sarcastically 'conjures' it back, which the gullible man finds eerie.

file: 2002/2002-02-02_man hating supervisor_men are oblvious_i quit_vials_storage room_self respect_no fun.gif
title: Boss Bottles Employees' Self-Respect

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Man-hating supervisor

transcript.speaker: Man-Hating Supervisor
transcript.text: The men here are oblivious to my abuse. What did you do to them?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I siphoned off their self-respect and keep it in vials in a storage room.

transcript.speaker: Man-Hating Supervisor
transcript.text: This is no fun. I quit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you want to yell at the vials with me?

situation: A new supervisor who enjoys abusing male employees complains that the men don't even notice her mistreatment. The Boss reveals he has drained their self-respect and stored it in vials in a storage room. She quits in frustration, and he cheerfully invites her to yell at the vials with him.
punchline: The Boss has literally bottled his employees' self-respect, which is why they can't be offended, and he sees nothing wrong with continuing to abuse the vials instead.
summary: A bullying supervisor learns her staff are immune to her cruelty because her boss has stored their dignity in jars.

file: 2002/2002-04-20_boss booked_highest ratio_unavailabilty_usefulness_sound insulting_do math_human resources_business.gif
title: Unavailable Boss's Insulting Usefulness Ratio

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: How about any Tuesday this year?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I'm booked.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You have the highest ratio of unavailability to usefulness I've ever seen.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does that sound like an insult?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If I could do math I wouldn't be working in human resources.

situation: Carol, holding a notepad, tries to schedule a meeting with the Boss, who claims to be booked every Tuesday this year. She then tells him he has the highest ratio of unavailability to usefulness she's ever seen. The Boss asks whether that was an insult and Catbert, sitting on the desk, admits he can't do math.
punchline: Catbert dodges the question by joking that HR people can't do math, which implies the ratio-based insult went over everyone's head while also taking a swipe at HR competence.
summary: A scheduling request turns into a mathematical put-down that the boss can't parse, and the HR cat declines to do the arithmetic for him.

file: 2002/2002-10-16_eat lunch_few typos_launch prodcut_new prodcut_other thing_marketing_business.gif
title: Wally's Sleepy Email Launches Product

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click click send

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: ZZZZZ

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Marketing

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: Someone named Wally is telling us to launch the new product.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: Or it might say to eat lunch with a penguin. It has a few typos.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Woman
transcript.text: I already ate, so let's do the other thing.

setting: Wally's cubicle and the Marketing department office
situation: Wally falls asleep at his keyboard and an email gets sent while he is dozing. In Marketing, two employees read the garbled message and conclude it either orders a product launch or tells them to eat lunch with a penguin. Since one of them has already eaten, they decide to go with the product launch.
punchline: A major product launch is decided by a typo-filled email sent by a sleeping employee, and the tie-breaker is that one person has already had lunch.
summary: A garbled message from a napping engineer ends up steering a company's biggest decision because the readers pick whichever interpretation suits their lunch plans.

file: 2002/2002-06-06_desk feels better_fluorescent lights_close door_teach him_new office.gif
title: Dilbert Enjoys Office, Gets Caught

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aah...even the desk feels better when you have your own office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The fluorescent lights are warmer and brighter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remind me to teach him when to close the door.

situation: Dilbert sits in his newly assigned private office, blissfully admiring how nice the desk and lighting feel. In the last panel, Alice and the Boss stand in the doorway and see Dilbert stretched out on the desk in only his boxer shorts, his clothes in hand. The Boss says Dilbert still needs to learn when to close the door.
punchline: Dilbert's glee over having a private office led him to strip down and lounge on the desk, and he forgot to close the door so his colleagues caught him in his underwear.
summary: A man thrilled by his first private workspace gets so comfortable that he is spotted half-undressed by passersby who didn't expect the show.

file: 2002/2002-04-13_manager_individual contributor_job description_wear huge glasses.gif
title: Dilbert Defends Individual Contributor Status

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Are you a manager?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I'm an individual contributor.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: So, basically, you have the same job description as an ant?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to see an ant try to wear huge glasses like these!

setting: Social gathering or party, both holding wine glasses
situation: A woman at a party asks Dilbert whether he is a manager, and he says he is an individual contributor. She replies that this makes his job description the same as an ant's. Dilbert indignantly responds by pointing to his large glasses as proof that he is different.
punchline: Dilbert, stung by the comparison of his role to an ant's, defensively offers his huge glasses as his only distinguishing feature, which undercuts his own case.
summary: At a party, a woman likens a non-managerial worker's role to an insect's, and he can only protest by boasting about his oversized eyewear.

file: 2002/2002-10-30_client_to dumb_embezzle_dogbert the lawyer_calling jury dumb.gif
title: Dogbert Insults the Jury Lawyer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will prove that my client is too dumb to embezzle.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Or, failing in that, I'll prove that you're too dumb to know he did it.

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: Mister Dogbert...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't get me started about you.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a defense lawyer, addresses a jury and argues that his client is too dumb to have embezzled money. He then adds that if that fails, he'll prove the jurors are too dumb to realize the client did it. The judge begins to reprimand him, and Dogbert retorts by insulting the judge as well.
punchline: Dogbert insults everyone in the courtroom, jury and judge alike, treating the legal system itself as full of fools.
summary: A canine attorney defends his embezzling client by calling the jury idiots and then mocking the judge who tries to scold him.

file: 2002/2002-03-23_boss_errors_flatter yourself_forward to friends_idiot boss_spelling_mass email.gif
title: Forwarding the Boss's Misspelled Email

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Trie to be moor prophesional in your commudicashuns.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's forward it to all our friends so they can see what an idiot we work for.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But you're my only friend.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't flatter yourself.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's desk
situation: The Boss types an email that is full of spelling mistakes while telling his staff to be more professional in their communications. Wally suggests forwarding it to all their friends so they can see what an idiot they work for, and Dilbert laughs. Dilbert then points out that Wally is his only friend, and Wally brushes him off.
punchline: Wally's reply to Dilbert's admission that he has only one friend turns what sounds like a compliment into an insult, implying Wally doesn't even count Dilbert as a friend.
summary: A boss berates his staff for sloppy writing in an email riddled with typos, and a coworker's plan to share the blunder ends with a deflating remark about friendship.

file: 2002/2002-02-18_chosen to design_worlds safest nuclear plant_great assignment_safe_not near my house.gif
title: Safest Nuclear Plant, Far From Home

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, you have been chosen to design the world's safest nuclear power plant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the greatest assignment that any engineer could hope for. I'm flattered by the trust you have in me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: By "safe" I mean "not near my house."

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has been chosen to design the world's safest nuclear power plant. Dilbert earnestly thanks him for the trust and calls it the greatest engineering assignment possible. The Boss then clarifies that his definition of "safe" simply means the plant won't be located near his own home.
punchline: The Boss's idea of a safe nuclear plant has nothing to do with engineering safety and everything to do with keeping the risk away from himself.
summary: A manager hands an engineer a prestigious safety-focused project, then reveals his notion of safety is purely about his own property.

file: 2002/2002-06-02_daring commando raid_internet provider_cancel_phone or email_service agreement_stun gun_overused joke.gif
title: Commando Raid to Cancel Internet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you like to join me on a daring commando raid?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want to know why?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Not really.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My Internet provider won't let me cancel by phone or by e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The service agreement says I have to stage a daring commando raid on their headquarters.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Does this mask make me look fat?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That joke is overused, Bob.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: ZAP

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The stun gun is in good working order.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I should carry the stun gun.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't worry; I'll do you last.

setting: Outdoors at night and near a building, with the team dressed as commandos
situation: Dilbert recruits Dogbert and Bob for a commando raid because his internet provider's service agreement requires one to cancel his account. Bob jokes about his mask making him look fat, Dilbert says the joke is overused, and Dogbert zaps Bob with a stun gun. Dilbert then wonders whether he should carry the stun gun.
punchline: Dogbert's reassurance that he'll stun Dilbert last confirms he plans to zap everyone, including his friend, which is hardly comforting.
summary: A man drafts his friends into a masked assault on his internet company, only for the team's stun gun to be turned on its own members.

file: 2002/2002-03-24_bad management_company dying_customer centric_four small groups_participation_skits_electricity.gif
title: Customer Centric Skits for Four People

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our company is dying... but not because of bad management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's because we're not...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, I for one feel better knowing we have correctly identified the problem.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That was a little thing I call participation; you should try it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now let's break into four small working groups...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And develop skits based on our new focus of customer centricity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... there are only four of us.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... never mind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll call my skit "The Electricity of Customer Centricity."

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team the company is dying but insists bad management isn't the cause, pointing to a slide saying the company isn't 'customer centric.' He then orders the four attendees to split into four small working groups to develop skits, until Dilbert realizes the absurdity and gives in, resigning himself to performing a solo skit.
punchline: The Boss's cluelessness about basic arithmetic forces each of the four employees into a one-person working group, so Dilbert sarcastically resigns himself to writing a ridiculous solo skit with a silly title.
summary: A manager blames a failing company on everything except himself, then demands skits from employees split into groups that turn out to contain just one person each.

file: 2002/2002-09-26_3 projects_cucbicle_double wide_elevator_scarbble_night_counterfeit vowles.gif
title: Mom Compares Dilbert to Norma's Son

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Norma's son finished three projects last year. You only did one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: His cubicle is a double-wide. And his CEO once said hi to him in the elevator.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Thanks to you, my "Scrabble" night is a living hell.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you still use counterfeit vowels?

situation: Dilbert's mother stirs a pot while comparing her son's career unfavorably to Norma's son, citing project counts, cubicle size and an elevator greeting from the CEO. She complains that his underachievement makes her weekly Scrabble night miserable. Dilbert calmly replies by asking if she still cheats at the game.
punchline: Dilbert deflects his mother's nagging about career bragging rights by pointing out she cheats at Scrabble with counterfeit vowels, implying her competitive pettiness is the real problem.
summary: A mother measures her son's worth against a neighbor's child using absurdly petty workplace status symbols, and he retorts by accusing her of cheating at board games.

file: 2002/2002-12-27_performance review_two jobs_well_attaboy_no budget for raise_cheapen.gif
title: Attaboy Too Valuable To Cheapen

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Performance review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You did two jobs for a year and did them well.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have no budget for raises, so all I can offer is an attaboy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The problem is: I don't want to cheapen the whole attaboy system.

setting: Boss's office during a performance review
situation: During a performance review, the Boss tells Dilbert he did two jobs for a year and did them well. He says there is no budget for a raise, so he can only offer an attaboy. He then adds that he doesn't want to cheapen the attaboy system by giving one.
punchline: The Boss implies that an attaboy is so valuable it would be cheapened by giving it to Dilbert, so he effectively offers him nothing at all for a year of double work.
summary: A manager praises an employee's double workload, pleads poverty on raises, then withholds even the token compliment to protect its prestige.

file: 2002/2002-06-10_conversations banned_talk about work_applies work hours_home_family_sleeping_harsh rules_evil director_human resources_business.gif
title: Work-Only Talk Ban at Dinner

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: To: Employees. From: Catbert.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: All non-work conversations are banned.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: From now on you're only allowed to talk about work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Dinner Companion
transcript.text: I think it only applies during work hours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't take that chance.

setting: Catbert's office, then a dinner table at home
situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, sends a memo banning all non-work conversations and then another extending it to talk only about work. At a dinner table, Dilbert's guests have fallen asleep from boredom as he sticks to work talk. When a companion suggests the rule only applies during work hours, Dilbert refuses to risk it.
punchline: Dilbert is so afraid of violating Catbert's policy that he obeys it even at home, boring his whole dinner party to sleep.
summary: An HR memo forbidding casual chat is taken so literally by an employee that it kills conversation at his family dinner.

file: 2002/2002-07-13_refreshed_vacation for boss_calm and relaxed_burn clothes_wally sat in chair_cooty squad.gif
title: Boss's Vacation Calm Shattered by Cooties

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm refreshed from my vacation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I am calm and relaxed.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Wally sat in your chair.

transcript.speaker: Cooty Squad
transcript.text: We'll have to burn your clothes too.

situation: The Boss returns from vacation thinking happy, relaxed thoughts as he walks in and sits down at his desk. His assistant Carol tells him Wally sat in his chair. In the last panel, workers in yellow hazmat suits from the Cooty Squad are hauling away his chair and tell him his clothes must be burned too.
punchline: Wally's presence is treated as a contamination hazard, so the Boss's brief vacation calm is destroyed by a hazmat team that has to sanitize his chair and burn his clothes.
summary: A freshly rested boss learns that a lowly coworker touched his seat, triggering a hazmat cleanup crew to destroy his belongings.

file: 2002/2002-10-19_impossible assignment_right place_reword_objectives_match_analyzed_feasibility_project_discontinue.gif
title: Rewording Objectives to Match Results

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you help me weasel out of an impossible assignment?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You came to the right place.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Gradually reword the objectives of the project until one day they match what you've already done.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Six months later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I successfully analyzed the feasibility of discontinuing the project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Success!

setting: Dogbert's home, then the office six months later
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert, who is sitting on a couch, how to get out of an impossible project. Dogbert advises him to slowly rewrite the project objectives until they match whatever he has already done. Six months later Dilbert tells the Boss he has successfully analyzed the feasibility of discontinuing the project, and the Boss declares it a success.
punchline: By redefining the goals to fit what was actually accomplished, the failed project is declared a success, and the Boss never notices the goalposts were moved.
summary: Dogbert coaches Dilbert to quietly rewrite a doomed project's goals until his failure counts as an achievement, and the oblivious Boss applauds the result.

file: 2002/2002-08-07_employees_not allowed to eat_work cubicles_gulp_chomp chomp_ignores rules_business.gif
title: Catbert Watches Alice Eat

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Alice, employees are not allowed to eat in cubicles.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Gulp

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Chomp chomp chomp

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm going to see that every time I close my eyes!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You started it.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, walks up to Alice and tells her that eating in cubicles is against the rules. Alice responds by stuffing food into her mouth and chewing loudly, spraying crumbs as Catbert looks on. A traumatized Catbert says he will never unsee it, and Alice replies that he provoked her.
punchline: Alice defies the rule by gorging herself in the most disgusting way possible, so the HR enforcer ends up punished by the sight, and she blames him for starting it.
summary: A cat from HR scolds a coworker for snacking at her desk and gets a revolting, crumb-spraying demonstration of her defiance.

file: 2002/2002-04-18_assignment_job_department_manager_pretend job useful_business.gif
title: Boss Admits Empire-Building Pointless Assignment

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... You gave me an assignment that isn't my job and doesn't need to be done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm trying to take over another department by doing their work. Later I'll say their manager should report to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Could we at least pretend my job is useful?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't I always?

situation: Dilbert holds a paper and complains to the Boss that the assignment he was given is not part of his job and doesn't even need doing. The Boss cheerfully explains he is trying to absorb another department by doing its work, so he can later claim its manager should report to him. Dilbert asks to at least pretend his job is useful, and the Boss insists he always does.
punchline: The Boss's claim that he always pretends Dilbert's job is useful implies Dilbert's work is never actually useful, and the Boss is only using him for his own empire-building.
summary: A manager reveals he is using his employee's pointless busywork as a scheme to seize control of another department.

file: 2002/2002-08-14_analyzed_corporate culture_findings_bunch unmotivated_weasels_knapsack.gif
title: Consultant's Report Insults Employees, Praises Himself

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've analyzed your corporate culture and put my findings in this report.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "The employees are a bunch of unmotivated weasels. I look good in this hat."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I would have mentioned my knapsack but it's only a summary.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant in a yellow hard hat, hands the Boss a report analyzing the company's corporate culture. The Boss reads it aloud and finds it consists of an insult toward the employees and a remark about how good Dogbert looks in his hat. Dogbert then explains that he left out mention of his knapsack because the report is only a summary.
punchline: The consultant's expensive report contains no real analysis, just an insult and vanity about his hat, and he deadpans that the trivial content is only a summary of an even more irrelevant full report.
summary: A hard-hatted dog consultant delivers a culture study that turns out to be little more than name-calling and self-admiration.

file: 2002/2002-06-21_accounting records_congress_erasing memories_impenetrable complications_management_outside firm_project team_hit head_hammer on head_knocked on head_politics.gif
title: Preparing the Boss for Congress

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As requested, my project team has added impenetrable complications to our accounting records.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And an outside firm is erasing all memories from senior management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do they do that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, you're ready to talk to Congress.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you.

situation: Dilbert reports to the Boss that his project team has made the accounting records impossibly complicated, as requested. He adds that an outside firm is erasing the memories of senior management. The Boss asks how they do it, and Dogbert, holding a mallet, has knocked him senseless in his chair.
punchline: The memory erasure is just Dogbert hitting the Boss on the head with a mallet, leaving him dazed and conveniently unable to remember anything when testifying to Congress.
summary: A company covers up its books with obfuscation and then gets its executive's memory wiped by blunt force before a congressional hearing.

file: 2002/2002-08-04_meeting_start with prayer_fear no downsizing_fist of death_job skills_investment protfolio_doing well_higher return_escape clowns_stew in bile_business.gif
title: Alice's Meeting Prayer For Wealth

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If there are no objections, I'd like to start the meeting with a prayer.

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: I'm a...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yea, though I walk through the valley of idiots, I shall fear no downsizing.

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: But I'm...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: For I have a fist of death, and highly marketable job skills.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But my investment portfolio isn't doing as well as I'd hoped.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So, if it's not too much to ask...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I need a higher return so I can escape these clowns...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And live in splendor while they stew in their own bile!

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: Maybe we won't do this again.

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: Whatever you say, heathen.

situation: Alice announces she will open the meeting with a prayer, and a colleague tries to object that he follows a different religion. She ignores him and delivers a prayer that mocks her coworkers as idiots, boasts of her fighting skills and job marketability, and begs for a better investment return so she can escape them. Afterward, the stunned attendees quietly agree to avoid prayers in future meetings.
punchline: Alice uses the cover of a prayer to insult her colleagues and air her selfish wishes with impunity, and her coworkers are too intimidated to do anything but call her a heathen.
summary: Under the guise of a solemn invocation, a woman at a staff gathering lampoons her coworkers and petitions for investment riches so she can leave them behind.

file: 2002/2002-09-03_hate everyone_entire world_weasels_wide eyed_innocent child_unconditionally_tiny wesels.gif
title: Dilbert Hates Everyone, Even Children

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today I realized I hate everyone in the entire world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I used to think I might like some people I hadn't met. But now I think they're weasels too.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How about a wide-eyed and innocent child who loves you unconditionally?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tiny weasels.

situation: Dilbert announces to Dogbert, who sits on the couch, that he has come to hate everyone in the world, including strangers he has not met. Dogbert asks whether he could at least like an innocent child who loves him unconditionally, and Dilbert replies that children are just tiny weasels.
punchline: Dilbert's misanthropy is so complete that it extends even to innocent, adoring children, whom he dismisses as miniature versions of the weasels he thinks everyone else is.
summary: A thoroughly disillusioned engineer tells his dog that humanity is irredeemable, and even the sweetest children fail to make the cut.

file: 2002/2002-12-01_research expense_highly trained engineer_not a clerk_employee_trivial task_project cancelled_assignment_kudos award.gif
title: Boss Assigns Petty Expense Investigation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, research this expense and find out what it's for.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's only $2.37.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It could take all day to track it down!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a highly trained engineer, not a clerk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can you justify wasting a valuable employee like me on a trivial task like this?!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That reminds me: your project got canceled. This is your only assignment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Woo-hoo! In your face!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder if he'll find out I spent $2.37 on his "kudos" award.

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to research a tiny $2.37 expense. Dilbert protests that a highly trained engineer shouldn't do clerical work, so the Boss reveals Dilbert's project was canceled and this is his only assignment.
