The Boss gleefully gloats, then privately worries the expense is the cost of Dilbert's own recognition award.
punchline: The petty expense Dilbert is told to investigate is the $2.37 the Boss himself spent on Dilbert's cheap "kudos" award, and the Boss is gloating at Dilbert's expense while hoping he never finds out.
summary: A manager sends an engineer to hunt down a trivial charge, and after wrecking his plans, nervously realizes the charge is his own cheap gift to the employee.

file: 2002/2002-09-04_mouse training_mandatory_western grip_carpal tunnel_weak muscles_two handed mouse_massage_back.gif
title: Mandatory Mouse Training Class Pain

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: I'm signing up people for the mandatory mouse training class.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: I see you're using a Western grip. That's just begging for carpal tunnel.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Weak muscles... I'll put you in the two-handed mouse class.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ouch.

situation: A woman with a clipboard comes around to sign employees up for a mandatory mouse training class. She critiques how Dilbert holds his mouse, warning of carpal tunnel, then squeezes his arm and declares his muscles weak. She assigns him to the two-handed mouse class, and he winces in pain.
punchline: Even something as trivial as using a mouse becomes a mandatory corporate training program, and Dilbert is judged inadequate and sent to a remedial class for using the mouse with two hands.
summary: A trainer inspects how an employee holds his computer mouse and decides he is so feeble that he needs the special class for people who need both hands.

file: 2002/2002-08-06_three hole punch_waltzing in_borrowing things_whack list_demanding_in exchange for_hole punch.gif
title: Hole Punch Costs You a Hit

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: May I use your three-hole punch?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Whoa whoa whoa!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You can't come waltzing into this department, using our stuff and leaving your holes.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll clean up the holes.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I want you to whack the people on this list.

situation: A coworker holding a sheet of paper politely asks to borrow Carol's three-hole punch. Carol objects angrily to him using her department's supplies and leaving a mess of paper holes. When he offers to clean up the holes, she demands instead that he murder the people on a list she hands him.
punchline: A trivial office-supply request escalates absurdly into Carol demanding a hit job as the price of borrowing a hole punch.
summary: Asking to borrow a hole punch earns a man a territorial lecture and then a request to assassinate people on a list.

file: 2002/2002-04-28_meeting with favorites_management perspective_top priority_price_service_circles are round_flew in_ate up time_stole a day_revenge.gif
title: Boss Hijacks Customer Meeting Rambling

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Hey, it's a meeting with our favorite customers!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's lucky I was passing by.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know what this meeting is about but I'm sure it needs some management perspective.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our top priority is quality. Our other top priority is price...and service...and...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One hour later

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And that's why circles are round.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: We flew here for this meeting and you used up all of our time saying nothing.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: You stole a day of my life! I will hunt you to the end of time! Revenge will be mine!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it just me or is that phrase starting to be overused?

setting: Conference room during a meeting with customers
situation: A coworker welcomes visiting customers to a meeting when the Boss wanders in uninvited, admits he doesn't know the topic, and offers 'management perspective.' He rambles about priorities for an hour, and the customers, who flew in specially, are furious that he wasted all their time saying nothing.
punchline: After wasting the customers' entire meeting and provoking a vengeful threat, the oblivious Boss only worries that the threat phrase is becoming a cliché.
summary: A clueless manager barges into a customer meeting, talks for an hour without saying anything, and shrugs off the visitors' vengeful rage.
keywords: stole a day of my life

file: 2002/2002-07-21_highlight_staff meeting_wally report_hair styled_usual_hair stylist_used nose trimmer_seemed right_salon brawl.gif
title: Wally's Nose-Hair Trimmer Haircut

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now for the highlight of the staff meeting: the Wally report.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yesterday I was getting my hair styled as usual.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But this time I forgot to remove my glasses, and what I saw was disturbing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My stylist was using a nose-hair trimmer to cut my hair!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I protested, but she said she's been doing my hair that way for years.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: She said it just "seemed right."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Tempers flared. I threw some hair gel. A salon brawl broke out!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Don't we use the same stylist?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would explain why she has a plunger.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: Wally gives his weekly staff-meeting report, which turns out to be a story about his haircut. He realized only when he wore his glasses that his stylist had been using a nose-hair trimmer on his hair for years, and a brawl broke out when he complained. A coworker asks whether they share the same stylist, and Dilbert quips that this explains something.
punchline: The coworker's weird grooming habits are explained when Dilbert implies that the stylist also uses a plunger on their hair, suggesting she has no idea what proper tools to use.
summary: A balding employee turns his meeting slot into a rant about a salon disaster, and a colleague's hairdo reveals the same incompetent stylist is at fault.

file: 2002/2002-01-07_downsized_not one of them_project cancelled_wonder_zombie_offer to walk_boos_fired_let go_shock.gif
title: Walking Among the Living Dead

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your project is cancelled. You'll be downsized in ninety days.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Until then, feel free to wander around like a zombie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I walk among them but I am not one of them.

setting: The Boss's office, then an office hallway
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert his project has been cancelled and that he will be laid off in ninety days. He suggests Dilbert wander around like a zombie until then. Dilbert walks down the hallway thinking he is not one of the living, while two coworkers look on with alarm.
punchline: Because Dilbert is doomed to be fired, he sees himself as the walking dead, a zombie among coworkers who still have a future at the company.
summary: A boss gives an employee a ninety-day layoff notice with a zombie joke, and the employee imagines himself drifting among the living as one of the doomed.

file: 2002/2002-05-17_the ceo visit_presentation_requires two people_impressive improvements_efficiency.gif
title: Two Presenters for 0.01% Efficiency

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The CEO visit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And now Dilbert and Alice will give you a presentation.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I'm curious to hear why that requires two people.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Our department made impressive improvements in...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Efficiency!

setting: Conference room during a CEO visit
situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert and Alice to give a presentation to the visiting CEO. The CEO wonders aloud why it takes two people to present. Alice and Dilbert then split a single sentence between them, pointing at a chart showing a mere +.01% improvement in efficiency.
punchline: The department's claimed efficiency gains are a trivial 0.01%, and the presentation itself is wastefully inefficient, with two people needed to deliver one sentence.
summary: A visiting executive questions the need for two presenters, and the pair's tiny, split-up boast about efficiency proves his skepticism right.

file: 2002/2002-03-20_need to know_basis_crawl space_underhouse_news_don't believe news_fake news.gif
title: Dogbert's Suspicious Need-to-Know Policy

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm putting you on a strict "need to know" basis.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And stay out of the crawl space under the house.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And don't believe anything you see in the news for about six months.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch holding a drink and a remote while Dogbert sits beside him issuing instructions. Dogbert says Dilbert will be told only what he needs to know, then warns him to stay out of the crawl space under the house and to disbelieve the news for six months. Dilbert stays silent and passive throughout.
punchline: Dogbert's escalating instructions imply he has done something terrible, like hiding something in the crawl space, and is preparing a cover-up before the news breaks.
summary: Dogbert lays out a series of increasingly ominous house rules that hint at a hidden crime and an incoming scandal.

file: 2002/2002-05-12_lunch_outrage_stealing free time_wind beneath my wings_work during lunch_working lunch.gif
title: Wally Outsmarts the Working Lunch

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This is an outrage!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The so-called "working lunch" tomorrow!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: They're stealing the only free time I have during the day!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: They give us some lousy sandwiches and expect us to work during lunch! Bah!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is nothing sacred?!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why doesn't this bother you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I plan to eat their sandwiches and go to lunch after the meeting.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I... I can actually feel the wind beneath my wings!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sorry.

situation: A coworker storms up to Wally's cubicle, furious that tomorrow's working lunch will eat into his only free time of the day. When he asks why Wally isn't equally upset, Wally calmly explains he will eat the free sandwiches at the meeting and then still take his own lunch afterward. The coworker is overwhelmed by this loophole.
punchline: Wally, the master of laziness, has found a way to turn the working lunch into a free extra meal, and the indignant coworker is moved to near-tears by his brilliance (the wind beneath my wings line is a mock-tribute), while Wally apologizes as if he'd stolen the credit.
summary: A man fumes about a lunchtime meeting until his slacker colleague reveals he will simply eat the free food and then take his real lunch anyway.

file: 2002/2002-05-05_socialize_getting buy in_dialoging for feedback_building consensus_temperature check_straw man_inoculate stakeholders_letter from sa.gif
title: Corporate Buzzword Soup Conversation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to socialize your idea with the rest of the department.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Socialize? Is that the same as getting buy-in?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's one step below buy-in. It's more like dialoging for feedback.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... I thought that building a consensus was one step below buy-in.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just run it up a flagpole and see who salutes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't it be better to do a temperature check using a straw man?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe... but is that going to inoculate the stakeholders?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dear Reader, If you or anyone you love understands the preceding conversation you have my deepest sympathy. S.A.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to socialize his idea with the department, and the two trade increasingly meaningless corporate jargon about buy-in, consensus, flagpoles, temperature checks, straw men and stakeholders. Neither can pin down what the terms mean or how they differ. A final panel contains a note from the cartoonist to the reader.
punchline: The conversation is pure strings of management buzzwords with no real meaning, and the author wryly offers sympathy to anyone who actually understands it.
summary: A manager and an employee volley empty business jargon back and forth until the cartoonist pities anyone who can follow along.

file: 2002/2002-06-19_accounting system_accounting troll_groupies_worse place_finance troll_project.gif
title: Accounting Troll Joins For Groupies

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need you to be a subject matter expert on my accounting system project.

transcript.speaker: Accounting Troll
transcript.text: Will it make the world a worse place to live?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think so.

transcript.speaker: Accounting Troll
transcript.text: I'm in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's it like to be an accounting troll?

transcript.speaker: Accounting Troll
transcript.text: To be honest, I'm only in it for the groupies.

situation: Dilbert asks the accounting troll to serve as a subject matter expert on his accounting system project. The troll's only condition is that the project make the world a worse place, and Dilbert assures him it will. Dilbert then asks what it's like being an accounting troll, and the troll admits he does it for the groupies.
punchline: The troll's only job requirement is making the world worse, and his real motivation is the absurd idea that accounting trolls attract groupies like rock stars.
summary: A grumpy troll agrees to consult on an accounting project once he's promised it will worsen the world, then reveals he's really in it for the fans.

file: 2002/2002-05-22_cubicle_loser cruiser_perfectly respectable_get used to it_demotion_loser_cry_no reason to cry.gif
title: Demoted Boss Meets Loser Cruiser

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Demoted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A cubicle isn't so bad. I can get used to it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's perfectly respectable. There's no reason to cry.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: How do you like your new "Loser Cruiser"?

situation: The Boss, newly demoted, has been moved from his office into a cubicle. He thinks to himself that the cubicle is acceptable and that he has no reason to cry, though he is visibly sweating and anxious. Catbert then appears and mockingly asks how he likes his "Loser Cruiser."
punchline: The Boss's attempt to reassure himself that his demotion is no big deal is undercut by Catbert gleefully mocking the cubicle as a "Loser Cruiser," confirming it is indeed a humiliating downgrade.
summary: A demoted manager tries to talk himself into accepting his new cubicle until a sadistic HR cat rubs it in with a cruel nickname.

file: 2002/2002-02-14_outsourcing_project_huge hourly rate_specified.gif
title: Outsourcing Contract Hidden Hourly Rate

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've reduced our development costs by outsourcing the project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does the proposal have a huge hourly rate for any work not specified in the contract?

transcript.speaker: Man at table
transcript.text: Stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why do you ask?

situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that he has cut development costs by outsourcing the project. Dilbert asks whether the proposal charges a huge hourly rate for any work not specified in the contract. A colleague silently thinks 'Stay out of it' while the Boss asks why Dilbert wants to know.
punchline: Dilbert knows outsourcing vendors recoup low bids through expensive change-order rates, and the Boss's suspicious 'why do you ask?' reveals he hasn't noticed the catch or doesn't want it pointed out.
summary: A manager brags about slashing costs through outsourcing until an employee probes for the usual fine-print trap in the vendor's contract.

file: 2002/2002-11-06_temp requested_afraid of commitment_stand like this_no chair needed.gif
title: Temp Worker Fears Commitment

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Here's the temp you requested.

transcript.speaker: Temp
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! No handshake! I'm afraid of commitment!!

transcript.speaker: Temp
transcript.text: I won't need a chair. I like to stand in this position.

situation: Carol brings in a temporary worker that Dilbert requested. When Dilbert reaches out to shake hands, the temp panics and refuses, saying he is afraid of commitment. He then declines a chair, insisting he prefers to stand, keeping everything temporary.
punchline: The temp worker is so wary of permanence that he avoids even a handshake or sitting down, taking the idea of being a temporary employee to an absurd extreme.
summary: A skittish temp refuses even the smallest gestures of settling in, treating a handshake and a chair as binding obligations.

file: 2002/2002-02-08_good meeting_reveal incompetence_attendees_bad meeting.gif
title: Good Meetings Are Just Short Ones

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just had a good meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe it just didn't last long enough to reveal the incompetence of the attendees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's what I call a good meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm having a bad meeting.

setting: Dilbert's home or office, with Dogbert lounging on a couch
situation: Dilbert announces that he just had a good meeting. Dogbert suggests it was only good because it ended before the attendees' incompetence became obvious. Dilbert agrees that this is exactly his definition of a good meeting, and Dogbert remarks that his own conversation with Dilbert is a bad meeting.
punchline: A good meeting is simply one that ends before the participants' incompetence shows, and Dogbert sarcastically implies that his talk with Dilbert has gone on long enough to reveal Dilbert's incompetence.
summary: A man defines a successful meeting as one that wraps up before anyone's ineptitude comes to light, prompting his dog to quietly judge their own chat a failure.

file: 2002/2002-12-20_i was grim reaper until_antidepressants_still reap_not grim_over limit_catch and release.gif
title: Antidepressant Grim Reaper Catch-and-Release

transcript.speaker: Grim Reaper
transcript.text: I was a Grim Reaper until I started taking antidepressants.

transcript.speaker: Grim Reaper
transcript.text: I still reap, because I like the work, but I'm not grim.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Am I dead?

transcript.speaker: Grim Reaper
transcript.text: No, I'm over my limit today, so I'm doing catch-and-release.

setting: A dark, cave-like area marked 'Death', with a doorway into the afterlife
situation: A cheerful Grim Reaper escorts Dilbert toward a dark opening labeled 'Death' while explaining that antidepressants made him less grim but he still enjoys reaping. Dilbert, unsure of his fate, asks if he is dead. The Reaper explains he has already hit his daily quota, so he is letting Dilbert go.
punchline: The Reaper, made upbeat by medication, treats collecting souls like a sport with a daily limit and casually releases Dilbert like a catch-and-release fish.
summary: A pleasantly medicated Grim Reaper marches Dilbert toward the afterlife, then spares him because he has reached his daily limit, like an angler throwing back a fish.

file: 2002/2002-10-14_man on moon_recycled paper_flawed analogy_good analogies.gif
title: Moon Landing Analogy Gets Shot Down

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we can put a man on the moon, we can build a computer made entirely of recycled paper.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your flawed analogy only shows that other people can do other things.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you should call other people and ask how they do it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe they use good analogies.

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk and demands a computer built entirely from recycled paper, justifying it by pointing to the moon landing. Dilbert dismisses the comparison as a flawed analogy, and the Boss responds by telling him to phone the people who did the other impressive things. Dilbert fires back that those people probably use better analogies.
punchline: The Boss misses the point of Dilbert's criticism and sarcastically suggests asking others how they do it, while Dilbert retorts that the real difference is that they reason with good analogies.
summary: A boss defends an absurd paper-computer demand by comparing it to space travel, and his engineer mocks the logic twice over.

file: 2002/2002-11-19_mostly cosmetic change_unplug_invention_people into sheep_cosmetic change.gif
title: Sheep Machine Already Worked on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My invention will turn people into mindless sheep.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm curious how you'll know it works. I assume it's mostly a cosmetic change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, did you unplug it as I asked you?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Couldn't be bothered.

situation: Dilbert works on a green robotic machine and announces it will turn people into mindless sheep. Dogbert, sitting on a stool, remarks that it would only be a cosmetic change. In the last panel Dilbert has been turned into a sheep, and Dogbert admits he didn't bother to unplug the machine as asked.
punchline: Dilbert, who is already a mindless follower, is turned into a literal sheep by his own invention, and Dogbert's laziness in not unplugging it lets the joke land at Dilbert's expense.
summary: An inventor's sheep-making device turns on its creator because his dog couldn't be bothered to switch it off.

file: 2002/2002-01-03_padded cost estimates_co workers_cost etsimates_inaccurate data_half full glass.gif
title: Ignoring Estimates, Bidding to Win

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I gathered all the padded cost estimates from the liars and scoundrels I'm ashamed to call co-workers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's okay. I usually ignore our cost estimates and make bid proposals that I think will win.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I gather inaccurate data for a living. Luckily no one uses it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your glass is half full.

situation: Dilbert hands the Boss a stack of cost estimates he collected from his dishonest co-workers, which he knows are padded. The Boss says he ignores the estimates anyway and just writes bids he thinks will win. Dilbert laments that his job is gathering inaccurate data that nobody uses, and Dogbert cheerfully calls that an optimistic outlook.
punchline: Dilbert's data-gathering work is completely pointless because management ignores it, and Dogbert sarcastically frames this uselessness as a positive.
summary: A worker's painstaking collection of inflated numbers turns out to be irrelevant because his boss simply guesses what bid will win.

file: 2002/2002-04-30_perfromance evaluation_seven layers_sign_boss sign evaluation_manage myself.gif
title: Boss Delegates His Own Evaluation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, write a performance evaluation of yourself for me to sign.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What will our seven layers of management be doing while I manage myself?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sorry. I'll ding myself for that on my evaluation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you can't find me, have Carol sign my name.

situation: The Boss tells Alice to write her own performance evaluation so he can simply sign it. Alice asks what the seven layers of management will be doing if she has to manage herself. The Boss says he will penalize himself on his own evaluation, then tells her to have Carol forge his signature if he is absent.
punchline: The Boss's self-penalty is meaningless since he is dodging his managerial duties anyway, and he casually tells Alice to have his assistant forge his signature, showing that management does no real work.
summary: A manager hands off his review duties to his subordinate and shrugs off the criticism by promising to mark himself down.

file: 2002/2002-11-27_computer screen_defective_ignoring_knock yourself out_over rated_vigorusly.gif
title: Ignore the Broken Screen Corner

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: The lower left part of my computer screen is defective. May I order a replacement?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That part of the screen is overrated. Try ignoring it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: May I vigorously bang my head on your desk?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure. Knock yourself out.

situation: Asok asks the Boss for a replacement computer monitor because part of the screen is defective. The Boss dismisses the request and tells him to just ignore the broken area. Frustrated, Asok asks if he can bang his head on the Boss's desk, and the Boss cheerfully allows it.
punchline: The Boss is so dismissive of a reasonable equipment request that he not only refuses it but also casually approves his employee's self-harm out of frustration, with 'knock yourself out' serving as a pun on both permission and unconsciousness.
summary: A worker with a faulty monitor is told by his boss to simply disregard the broken part, driving him to ask permission to pummel his own head against the desk.

file: 2002/2002-12-28_employee meail_monitor_recently estranged lovers_curse words_job title.gif
title: Catbert Promotes Estranged Lover Over Rival

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I can monitor all employee e-mail from here.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm looking for recently estranged lovers so I can promote one of them over the other.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why is my new job title a long string of curse words?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I win.

setting: Office, Catbert's desk and a workplace hallway
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, sits at his computer boasting that he can read all employee e-mail, then reveals he is hunting for recently broken-up couples. He plans to promote one ex over the other. A coworker then holds up a paper complaining his new job title is a string of curse words, while a smug colleague declares victory.
punchline: Catbert uses his e-mail snooping to stir up personal revenge, so the promoted ex gets to humiliate the other with an insulting official job title.
summary: Catbert eavesdrops on staff messages to pit ex-partners against each other, rewarding one and letting her gleefully insult the loser through a company title.

file: 2002/2002-03-28_answers_code language_engineers_justified_no understanding_questions_roi_policy.gif
title: ROI Policy Lacks Its Own ROI

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, everything we do must be justified by R.O.I.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the R.O.I. for this new policy about calculating the R.O.I.?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I said, "From now on."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What about your answer? No R.O.I.

situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that every action must be justified by return on investment. Dilbert asks what the ROI is for the new policy of calculating ROI. The Boss dodges by claiming the rule only applies from now on, and Dilbert points out that this answer itself has no ROI.
punchline: The Boss exempts his own policy from the rule he just created, and his evasive answer shows he has no real justification and is applying the standard only to others.
summary: A manager imposes a new rule of justifying everything by return on investment, then wriggles out when asked to justify the rule itself.

file: 2002/2002-06-14_engineering decison_project_need to act_fiber capacity_serial input_meeting_communication problems_table_business.gif
title: Boss Makes Dilbert Back Nonsense Decision

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I needed to make an engineering decision about your project this morning.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll need to act like you agree with it so I don't look stupid.

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: Explain to us how fiber capacity can be increased by serial input at breakfast.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, then a conference room
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he made an engineering decision about Dilbert's project without consulting him. He then instructs Dilbert to pretend to agree so the Boss won't look stupid. In the meeting, a colleague asks Dilbert to explain the absurd decision, leaving him to justify it.
punchline: The Boss's nonsensical technical decision is now Dilbert's burden to defend, and the question posed in the meeting is meaningless gibberish that Dilbert must somehow explain to protect his boss's ego.
summary: After making an uninformed technical call, a manager forces his engineer to publicly defend the gibberish so the manager can save face.

file: 2002/2002-05-11_fix interface_million dollars_close eyes_wish hard_saving.gif
title: Wishing Away the Terrible Interface

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can fix our incomprehensible user interface for a million dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or we can close our eyes and wish real hard that our users won't care.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's saving a million dollars. What did you do today?

situation: Dilbert presents to a meeting, pointing at a slide showing a computer and a dollar sign, and offers two options: spend a million dollars to fix the unusable interface, or just hope users won't care. The second option is shown with a slide of a nervous, sweating man. The Boss then praises Dilbert for saving a million dollars and asks a coworker what he accomplished.
punchline: The Boss rewards the cheap, wishful non-solution as cost savings, ignoring that it leaves the product unusable and implicitly shames those who actually do work.
summary: A presenter sarcastically proposes hoping customers won't notice a baffling interface instead of paying to fix it, and management treats the dodge as a triumph of thrift.

file: 2002/2002-01-29_man hater_angry women_pantsuits_turned on_decisive_supervisor.gif
title: Boss Hires Angry Supervisor, Admires Her

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a man-hater to be your supervisor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Frankly, I'm kinda turned on by angry women in pantsuits.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She's decisive. I like that.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has hired a man-hating woman to be Dilbert's new supervisor. When Dilbert asks why, the Boss admits he is attracted to angry women in pantsuits. In the last panel the supervisor has apparently roughed him up, leaving him bent over and rumpled, yet he still praises her decisiveness.
punchline: The Boss's creepy attraction to an angry, man-hating supervisor ends with her physically manhandling him while he cheerfully insists he likes her decisiveness.
summary: A manager picks a hostile new boss for his employee for inappropriate personal reasons, then gets pummeled by her and still praises her.

file: 2002/2002-07-27_worthless_incompetent bug_two phone calls and a meeting.gif
tags: two phone calls and a meeting
title: Boss Yells, Gets Almost Nothing Done

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need your help yelling at a guy to make him do his job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yay!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You worthless, incompetent bug!!! I'll have your head!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much work did that buy?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Two phone calls and a meeting.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss to help him yell at a coworker who isn't doing his job, and the Boss gleefully agrees. The Boss screams insults and threats at the coworker. Dilbert then asks how much work that bought, and the coworker answers with a trivial amount.
punchline: All that furious shouting produced only a pathetically small amount of actual work, showing that intimidation is an inefficient way to motivate people.
summary: A manager's enthusiastic tirade at a slacking employee turns out to yield almost nothing useful.

file: 2002/2002-08-26_five year plan_compared to plan_dust heap_history_education.gif
title: Old Five-Year Plan Targets Microsoft

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's this? It's our old five-year plan!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder how we did compared to plan.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have we relegated Microsoft to the dust heap of history?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shhh! They might hear!

situation: The Boss discovers an old five-year plan in his desk and wonders how the company performed against it. He asks Dilbert whether they have succeeded in relegating Microsoft to the dust heap of history, which was apparently one of the plan's goals. Dilbert nervously hushes him, afraid Microsoft might overhear.
punchline: The company's old plan absurdly aimed to destroy Microsoft, a goal wildly out of reach, and Dilbert's fearful whisper implies Microsoft is still enormously powerful and dangerous to cross.
summary: Digging up a forgotten long-range plan, the boss cheerfully checks whether his firm managed to bury a software giant, while his employee panics about being overheard.

file: 2002/2002-08-24_software_week_ordering system_honeymoon_two weeks_parole board_outside system_engineering.gif
title: CFO Approval Depends on Parole Board

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I need the software in a week.

transcript.speaker: Procurement Clerk
transcript.text: Cheryl is the only one who knows the ordering system.

transcript.speaker: Procurement Clerk
transcript.text: She's on her honeymoon for two weeks. You need CFO approval to buy software outside the system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine. I'll talk to the CFO. When will he be available?

transcript.speaker: Procurement Clerk
transcript.text: Depends on the parole board.

setting: Office, phone call between Dilbert's cubicle and a procurement clerk's desk
situation: Dilbert phones the procurement department because he needs software within a week. The clerk explains that the only person who knows the ordering system is on her honeymoon, and that buying software outside the system requires the CFO's approval. When Dilbert asks when the CFO will be available, the clerk says it depends on the parole board.
punchline: The CFO is a convicted criminal awaiting parole, implying corporate financial misconduct and making the required approval effectively unobtainable.
summary: A purchasing roadblock ends with the revelation that the one executive who could authorize a workaround is stuck in prison.

file: 2002/2002-03-13_loud personal calls_medical mel_squishy sound_cubicle neighbor_patch eye_sling_wounded_office.gif
title: Medical Mel's Squishy Phone Calls

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Meet your new cubicle neighbor. His name is Medical Mel.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mel will be making loud personal phone calls all day.

transcript.speaker: Medical Mel
transcript.text: Is it supposed to make a squishy sound? Listen to this...

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to his new cubicle neighbor, Medical Mel, who has an eye patch and an arm in a sling. The Boss warns that Mel will make loud personal phone calls all day. In the last panel, Mel is heard from the next cubicle asking someone on the phone about a squishy sound, and Dilbert is left listening.
punchline: The loud personal calls from Medical Mel are graphic discussions of his own injuries, which are far more unpleasant to overhear than ordinary phone chatter.
summary: A banged-up new coworker moves in next door and Dilbert gets to eavesdrop on his cringe-inducing medical conversations.

file: 2002/2002-12-04_project summaries_summarize summary_doomed.gif
title: Summarizing the Summary of Summaries

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, take these project summaries and summarize them into one summary.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And when you're done, take that summary and summarize it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What is a shorter word for doomed?

setting: The Boss's office and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The Boss hands Asok a stack of project summaries and orders him to condense them into one summary. He then adds that Asok should summarize that summary as well. Asok walks back to the cubicle area, where Dilbert sits at his desk, and asks for a shorter word for 'doomed'.
punchline: Asok recognizes that an endless chain of summarizing is a pointless task, and he wryly asks for a shorter word for 'doomed', which is itself a request for a summary of his own situation.
summary: A manager piles ever more condensing work onto a young employee, who responds by looking for a more concise way to describe his fate.

file: 2002/2002-10-08_ratbert_rat hole_share money_stop digging_smell feet.gif
title: Dogbert's Money Pit Digging Scheme

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ratbert, I need you to dig a huge rat hole, so companies can throw money in it.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yes!!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I might share some of the money with you.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You had me at "hole."

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: When should I stop digging?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When you smell feet.

setting: Dogbert's home, then a wooded outdoor area
situation: Dogbert asks Ratbert to dig a huge rat hole so companies can throw money into it, and Ratbert eagerly agrees after a vague promise of shared profits. Later Ratbert is digging in the woods and asks when to stop, while Dogbert relaxes on a cushion.
punchline: Dogbert tells Ratbert to dig until he smells feet, implying the hole will go all the way to China, a joke about a pointless, bottomless money pit that Dogbert exploits.
summary: Dogbert enlists an eager Ratbert to excavate a bottomless pit meant to swallow corporate cash, and tells him to keep going until he reaches the other side of the world.

file: 2002/2002-12-17_work to death_six months_mentally incompetent_remove name_beneficiaries.gif
title: Lawyer Questions Dilbert's Mental Competence

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Estate planning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I expect to work myself to death in six months, so I need a will.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Are you mentally incompetent?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think so.

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Okay then, I'll remove my name from the list of beneficiaries.

setting: A lawyer's office, at his desk
situation: Dilbert visits an estate-planning lawyer and explains that he expects to work himself to death within six months, so he needs a will. The lawyer asks whether Dilbert is mentally incompetent, and when Dilbert says he doesn't think so, the lawyer says he will remove his own name from the list of beneficiaries.
punchline: The lawyer's assumption is that only a mentally incompetent person would work himself to death, and since Dilbert is not, the lawyer drops his own plan to be named a beneficiary of the will.
summary: A man planning his will because his job will kill him is quizzed about his sanity by a lawyer who seems to have been counting on inheriting from him.

file: 2002/2002-09-02_code_projects expenses_assigns codes_breaking hard.gif
title: Code Clerk Hates Your Project

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I need a code for charging my project's expenses.

transcript.speaker: Code Clerk
transcript.text: No. I hate your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It doesn't matter if you hate it. You're just the guy who assigns codes.

transcript.speaker: Code Clerk
transcript.text: Get out of here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why is everything in this company so freakin' hard?

transcript.speaker: Code Clerk
transcript.text: Because of people like you.

setting: A clerk's desk in the office
situation: Dilbert asks a clerk who assigns accounting codes for an expense code for his project. The clerk refuses simply because he hates the project, and when Dilbert points out it isn't his call, the clerk throws him out. Dilbert then complains that everything at the company is difficult, and the clerk blames people like him.
punchline: The petty bureaucrat who obstructs everyone claims the company is hard to work with because of the very people he is obstructing.
summary: A grudge-holding administrator blocks a simple request and then blames the requester for the company's dysfunction.

file: 2002/2002-08-05_employees_called resources_too complimentray_human capital_demanding hay_business.gif
title: Employees Are Human Capital, Not Livestock

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm tired of calling the employees "resources." It's too complimentary.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm thinking of something along the lines of livestock or human capital.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I don't want them demanding hay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good point. We'll go with human capital.

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, tells the Boss he is tired of calling employees "resources" because it sounds too flattering. He suggests calling them livestock, then rejects that because livestock might demand hay. The Boss agrees and they settle on "human capital."
punchline: Management picks a label for employees by weighing which one gives workers the fewest expectations, showing how little regard they have for them as people.
summary: An HR villain shops for a more demeaning name for staff and picks the one that sounds least likely to lead to demands for feed.

file: 2002/2002-08-18_pet peeve_cellphones_restaurants_public_talk louder_just rude_decides whats rude_commitee_common sense_drive through_using microphone.gif
title: Dilbert Mocks Cell Phone Etiquette Rules

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: My pet peeve is when people use cell phones in restaurants.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why? Do they talk louder than the other people in the restaurant?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: No. It's just rude.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who decides what is rude? Is there a committee?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: It's common sense. You're not supposed to talk into electronic gadgets at a restaurant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What about a drive-through place? Is it okay to order your food using the microphone?

transcript.speaker: Drive-through speaker
transcript.text: Yello.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hi, Ratbert... Yeah, he made the mistake of talking... The goodnight kiss is a definite no-go.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: No, it's not awkward, but thanks for asking.

setting: Outdoor path on a date, with hills in the background
situation: Dilbert is on a walk with a date who complains that cell phone use in restaurants is rude. Dilbert keeps challenging her reasoning, asking who decides what is rude and whether drive-through microphones count. Meanwhile Dogbert is on a phone call, apparently coaching Ratbert about how Dilbert's date is going.
punchline: Dilbert's pedantic arguing over etiquette has ruined the date, and Dogbert is on the phone reporting that the goodnight kiss is out of the question.
summary: A man's habit of nitpicking his date's complaint about phone manners sinks the evening, as his dog gleefully reports the failure by phone.

file: 2002/2002-03-04_staff meetings_late for meetings_ten minutes_stupid stuff_fine work_noticing.gif
title: Why Everyone Is Late To Meetings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can anyone tell me why everyone is always late for my staff meetings?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Because the first ten minutes are always stupid stuff like "Why are people late?"

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, that was some of your finest work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Thank you for noticing.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss asks his staff why they are always late to his meetings. Alice answers that the first ten minutes are always wasted on pointless topics like asking why people are late. The Boss praises her answer as her finest work, apparently missing that it was a criticism of him.
punchline: Alice's sarcastic answer is an insult aimed at the boss, but he takes it as a compliment, and she sarcastically thanks him for noticing.
summary: A manager wonders why his staff arrives late, and the answer he gets is a barbed explanation that he cheerfully mistakes for praise-worthy work.

file: 2002/2002-09-20_woman_peeved questions_hostile_personality disorder_critical_mean_nasty.gif
title: Woman Offended By Simple Greeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet a woman who acts peeved at any sort of question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How are you?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Poink

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: How am I???

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. I gotta show this to Wally.

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to a coworker, warning that she gets irritated by any question at all. Dilbert politely asks how she is, and she reacts with exaggerated outrage. Dilbert is so amused by the display that he wants to bring Wally over to see it.
punchline: Even the most innocuous small-talk question sets her off, making her a fascinating curiosity for Dilbert and Wally rather than a real problem.
summary: A new acquaintance flies into a rage at the most ordinary pleasantry, leaving Dilbert eager to share the spectacle with a friend.

file: 2002/2002-07-11_sitting in_boss_walk around_avoid decisons_grossly underpaid_did before_more money.gif
title: Boss's Job: Being Loathed, Avoiding Decisions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you like sitting in for the boss?

transcript.speaker: Substitute Boss
transcript.text: It's easy.

transcript.speaker: Substitute Boss
transcript.text: All I do is walk around and make people loathe me while I avoid making decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's all you ever did before.

transcript.speaker: Substitute Boss
transcript.text: Apparently I was grossly underpaid.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker, who is temporarily filling in as the boss and holding a coffee mug, how he likes the job. The coworker describes the role as simply wandering around, being disliked, and dodging decisions. Dilbert points out that this is exactly what he did in his old job, and the coworker concludes he must have been underpaid.
punchline: The stand-in realizes his old job was identical to a management role in its useless duties, so the real problem is that he wasn't paid a manager's salary for it.
summary: A coworker covering for the boss finds the role laughably simple and decides his earlier pay must have been far too low.

file: 2002/2002-12-25_award_family haters_association_anti family practice.gif
title: Boss Hangs Embarrassing Anti-Family Award

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I got an award!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "The 'Family-Haters Association' is proud to give you this award for your anti-family practices."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope no one reads it.

situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss excitedly opens an envelope and announces he has won an award. He reads it aloud and discovers it is from the 'Family-Haters Association' for his anti-family practices. He still hangs the certificate on his wall, hoping nobody will read what it says.
punchline: The Boss is happy to display any award for its prestige, even though it publicly labels him as hostile to families, and he naively hopes no one will notice.
summary: A manager proudly hangs a plaque from a group that honors him for being bad to families, while privately wishing nobody looks closely.

file: 2002/2002-12-12_moneybags magazine_ask employees_claims are true_cover story.gif
title: Lazy Reporter Swallows Foot Massage Story

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur Secretary
transcript.text: The reporter from Moneybags Magazine is here.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Send him in.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you planning to ask my employees if my claims are true?

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Nah, too lazy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I credit my success to the foot massages I personally give to each employee.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Cover story!

situation: Dogbert, acting as a company head, is told a reporter from Moneybags Magazine has arrived. The reporter admits he is too lazy to check Dogbert's claims with employees. Dogbert then credits his success to giving personal foot massages to every employee, and the reporter excitedly decides it is a cover story.
punchline: Business magazines publish glowing profiles of executives without verifying any claims, so even an absurd boast gets printed as a cover story.
summary: A lazy journalist skips fact-checking and happily turns a CEO's ridiculous self-promotion into the magazine's headline feature.

file: 2002/2002-07-30_expansive projects_failed_drink coffee_economic basis_watch and learn.gif
title: Coffee Drinker Claims Top Performer Status

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Over the past year, most of my co-workers have managed expensive projects that failed.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've done nothing but drink coffee. So on an economic basis, that makes me your top performer.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Watch and learn.

setting: Office meeting room or boss's desk
situation: Wally sits across a table from the Pointy-Haired Boss and argues that, because his coworkers' expensive projects all failed while he only drank coffee, he has cost the company the least. He therefore declares himself the top performer. He then sips his coffee and tells the boss to watch and learn.
punchline: Wally twists a cost-based performance metric so that doing nothing at all looks better than costly failures, and he smugly presents his laziness as a model to follow.
summary: A slacker employee argues that idly sipping coffee all year makes him the most valuable worker since everyone else burned money on failed projects.

file: 2002/2002-09-23_user interface_colors_puke_flu_interface design.gif
title: Ugly Interface Makes Coworker Vomit

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I designed the user interface myself. How do you like the colors?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: PUKE

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Flu?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Interface design.

situation: Dilbert proudly shows Alice the user interface he designed and asks what she thinks of the colors. Alice looks horrified, rushes to a cubicle wall and vomits. When someone asks if she has the flu, she clutches her stomach and says it was the interface design.
punchline: Alice's physical illness is caused not by a virus but by the sheer ugliness of Dilbert's interface design, a brutal wordless critique of his color choices.
summary: A proud engineer's homemade software colors are so repulsive that a coworker gets violently sick and blames the design rather than the flu.

file: 2002/2002-03-31_superior perfromance_not effective_budget increase approved_retroactive_be happy_some no raises_10% raise_future raise.gif
title: Raise That Never Actually Arrives

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, your performance this year was superior. I'm giving you a 10% raise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But it's not effective right away.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It kicks in as soon as my budget increase gets approved.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When will that be?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As soon as the economy improves and profits go up!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But my raise will be retroactive to today, right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You should be happy. Some people aren't getting any raises at all.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must... control fist... of... death.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I got a 14% future raise just for showing up.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway
situation: The Boss tells Alice her superior performance earns her a 10% raise, then keeps adding conditions: it only starts when his budget increase is approved, which depends on the economy and profits improving, and it won't be retroactive. Alice struggles to contain her anger, and a coworker walks by boasting about a 14% future raise he got just for showing up.
punchline: A raise that is contingent on indefinite future conditions is effectively no raise at all, and the final insult is that a coworker who did nothing got a bigger one.
summary: A manager praises his best employee with a raise so heavily qualified that it may never materialize, while a slacker down the hall gets a bigger promise.

file: 2002/2002-03-10_hands free phone_insulting comments_boss directed_pointy haired_face transplant_baboon_personal calls_company time.gif
title: Insulting The Boss Via Hands-Free Phone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're an ignorant maggot. You disgust me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You should get a face transplant from a baboon.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not talking to you. I'm using my hands-free phone.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh...for a minute I thought...well, never mind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha! You might be the most gullible moron in the galaxy!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You pointy-haired, gray-suited pile of crud!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mom, can you hold? My excellent boss wants to talk to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No personal phone calls on company time!

situation: Dilbert stands in his cubicle hurling insults while the Boss overhears and thinks they are aimed at him. Dilbert claims he is on a hands-free phone, and the Boss believes him. Dilbert then openly insults the Boss to his face, and when the Boss finally appears, Dilbert pretends to be talking to his mother, so the Boss scolds him only for making a personal call.
punchline: Dilbert gets away with insulting his gullible boss by claiming he is on a hands-free phone, and the Boss ends up objecting only to the personal call on company time, not the abuse.
summary: An employee abuses his boss to his face under the cover of a phantom phone call, and the oblivious manager only complains about time wasted on a private conversation.

file: 2002/2002-04-03_next speaker_athlete_drugs_booze_inspirational.gif
title: Substance-Ruined Athlete Not Inspirational Yet

transcript.speaker: Emcee
transcript.text: Our next speaker was a famous athlete until drugs and booze ruined his life.

transcript.speaker: Guest Speaker
transcript.text: Shank hew vewy mush.

transcript.speaker: Woman in audience
transcript.text: It's not inspirational until he stops doing those things.

transcript.speaker: Emcee
transcript.text: What?

setting: A motivational speaking event at a company, with the audience seated in rows
situation: An emcee with spiky hair introduces a guest speaker as a former famous athlete whose life was ruined by drugs and booze. The speaker staggers up, slurring his words and clearly still intoxicated. A woman in the audience points out that his story isn't inspirational until he actually quits.
punchline: The motivational speaker is still visibly drunk or high, so his cautionary tale of redemption has not actually reached the inspiring part yet.
summary: A booked speaker with a tragic substance-abuse story shows up still impaired, undermining the whole point of the talk.

file: 2002/2002-06-03_need me_page me_soar flares_low tide_humidity_equinoxes_high tide.gif
title: Pager Excuses From Unreliable Wally

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you need me, just page me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll call you right back unless solar flares stop your page from getting through.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And of course you'll have some blockage during high tide, low tide, humidity, and most of your equinoxes.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, stands in front of the Boss's desk and tells him to page him if he needs anything. He then lists increasingly absurd natural phenomena that might prevent the page from reaching him. The Boss sits behind his desk listening.
punchline: Wally dresses up his plan to ignore his boss's pages as a technical limitation by blaming solar flares, tides, humidity, and equinoxes, which together cover nearly every possible moment.
summary: A lazy employee promises to answer pages but lists so many far-fetched atmospheric interruptions that he can effectively never be reached.

file: 2002/2002-06-28_battle of wills_leave message_call me_ignores calls_cubicles_same office_one cubicle over.gif
title: Voicemail Standoff With Cubicle Neighbor

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm in a battle of wills with a guy who lets all of his calls roll over to voicemail.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I do that too, so all day long we trade messages saying "Call me," and then we ignore the incoming calls.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe he's out of the office.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, I can hear him. He's one cube over from me.

situation: At a meeting, Wally complains about a coworker who sends every call to voicemail, and a bald colleague admits he does the same thing, trading 'call me' messages all day. The Boss suggests the man may be out of the office, but Wally says he can hear him in the next cubicle.
punchline: Two coworkers sitting a few feet apart waste the whole day leaving voicemails for each other instead of simply walking over and talking.
summary: A pair of neighbouring employees refuse to pick up their phones and keep trading voicemails while sitting almost within earshot of each other.

file: 2002/2002-08-11_technically impossible_costs less_much cheaper_plan one or two_engineers.gif
title: Cheapest Impossible Plan Gets Approved

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Both plans are technically impossible.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which one costs less?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... I don't see how that matters, but plan one is much cheaper.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Plan one is the best.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll take it to our VP.

transcript.speaker: Vice President
transcript.text: I like plan two.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Great minds think alike!

transcript.speaker: Vice President
transcript.text: Excellent. Ask one of our engineers to present plan two to the board.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Guess what.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every day I make the world a little bit worse.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's it like to make a difference?

setting: Dilbert's office, the Boss's office and a VP's office
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that both proposed plans are technically impossible. The Boss only cares which is cheaper and picks plan one, then takes it to the VP, who prefers plan two, so the Boss instantly agrees. The impossible plan two is then dumped on Dilbert to present to the board.
punchline: Management picks plans based on cost and on agreeing with the VP rather than feasibility, and the engineer is left to take the fall, with a sarcastic remark about 'making a difference' as the jab.
summary: A manager ignores a warning that both options are unworkable, flips his preference to match his superior, and hands the doomed one to an engineer to present.

file: 2002/2002-12-07_blame insurance carrier_give reason_master plan_parking lot_reason_remove all joy_tell kids_universe_no skateboarding.gif
title: Banning Skateboarders, Blaming the Insurer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, tell those kids they can't skateboard in our parking lot.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Should I give them a reason, or is this part of your master plan to remove all joy from the universe?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They know about the plan.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Fool! I told you to blame our insurance carrier!

setting: Boss's office overlooking the company parking lot
situation: The Boss looks out his window at kids skateboarding in the parking lot and orders his assistant Carol to tell them to stop. Carol asks whether he wants her to give a reason or if this is part of a plan to destroy all joy. The Boss admits the kids already know about the plan, and Catbert, standing by a globe, scolds him for not blaming the insurance carrier.
punchline: The Boss and Catbert really are conspiring to remove all joy from the world, and the Boss blew their cover by failing to use the standard excuse of blaming the insurance company.
summary: A manager shoos skateboarders from the lot and his assistant sarcastically suspects a plot against happiness, which his evil feline adviser confirms by scolding him for skipping the usual excuse.

file: 2002/2002-02-10_extra funding_extra network traffic_hard data_infinte capacity_logic_opinions_science works_weasel misrepresnting_science.gif
title: Weasel Misinterpreting Network Data

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think our network can handle the extra network traffic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Opinions don't matter to me. I base my decisions on hard data.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about logic? Our network is already too slow and we plan to quadruple usage.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bah! Watch how science works and maybe you'll learn something.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Doug, come here for a minute.

transcript.speaker: Doug
transcript.text: The data proves that our network has infinite capacity, so your budget should be diverted to my project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not science! That's a weasel misinterpreting data to get extra funding!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There are days when you really hate to hear the phrase "po-tay-to, po-tah-to."

situation: Dilbert warns his boss that the network can't handle a planned quadrupling of traffic. The boss claims to base decisions on hard data and brings in Doug, who presents data supposedly showing infinite network capacity and asks for Dilbert's budget. Dilbert objects that this is a weasel misusing data for funding.
punchline: Dilbert tries to separate real science from a self-serving misreading of data, but the closing remark suggests that dismissing it as a matter of differing interpretations is just as infuriating.
summary: A boss who prizes hard data ignores an engineer's capacity concerns and rewards a colleague who twists numbers to claim limitless bandwidth and grab the budget.

file: 2002/2002-02-21_dont judge_elbonia_electricity_huge barges_ideas_toasters_trained porpoises_brainstorm.gif
title: Brainstorming Porpoises Tests Coworker's Restraint

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do we get the electricity from our nuclear plant in Elbonia to the toasters over here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's brainstorm, and remember not to judge any ideas at this stage.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm thinking huge barges and trained porpoises — lots of them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: Must... not... judge.

setting: Conference room during a brainstorming meeting
situation: Dilbert stands at a whiteboard diagram showing a nuclear plant and a toaster and asks the group how to deliver electricity from Elbonia. He sets the brainstorming ground rule of no judging, then a coworker suggests huge barges and trained porpoises. A tense, sweating attendee in the corner thinks to himself that he must not judge the absurd idea.
punchline: The brainstorming rule against judging is immediately tested by a ridiculous suggestion, leaving a participant straining to hold back his criticism.
summary: A no-criticism brainstorm collides with an absurd proposal involving barges and porpoises, and one attendee silently struggles to keep quiet.

file: 2002/2002-07-19_accounting firm_headed for bankruptcy_conflict of interest_t shirt design business.gif
title: Accounting Firm's T-Shirt Side Business

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How could our accounting firm not notice that we were heading for bankruptcy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe there was a conflict of interest with their T-shirt design business.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This one says, "I'm with Bankrupt" and it has an arrow.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hee hee!

setting: Boss's office and a back room where the T-shirts are examined
situation: Dilbert asks The Boss how the company's accounting firm failed to warn them about heading toward bankruptcy. The Boss suggests the firm may have had a conflict of interest with its T-shirt design business. Dogbert and Ratbert then examine a novelty shirt that reads "I'm with Bankrupt" with an arrow.
punchline: The accounting firm was apparently more interested in selling novelty T-shirts mocking the company's bankruptcy than in warning the company about it, which is the conflict of interest.
summary: An auditor that missed its client's financial collapse turns out to have been busy printing gag shirts about the very bankruptcy it failed to flag.

file: 2002/2002-07-28_frequent grocery club_memebership_card_engineer spittle_carry card_inconvienced_junk mail list_charge me same.gif
title: Grocery Club Card Rant

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: Are you a member of our frequent grocery club?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. What is it?

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: You get a membership card that entitles you to discounts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's see if I have this straight...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be inconvenienced by having to fill out a form and carry your stupid card around...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And in return, you'll put me on a junk mail list, and charge me the same as the grocery store across the street?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you'll expect me to be happy about it?!!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: But it's free!

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: Cleanup on register two... it's engineer spittle.

situation: A cashier asks Dilbert if he wants to join the store's frequent grocery club. Dilbert, standing in line with other shoppers, breaks down the deal and realizes it only inconveniences him with forms, cards and junk mail while offering no real price advantage. He rants so heatedly that he spits, and the cashier calls for a cleanup.
punchline: Dilbert's furious, logical takedown of the loyalty card program is so intense that he sprays spit, requiring a cleanup announcement for 'engineer spittle.'
summary: A shopper offered a store loyalty card dissects the deal so angrily that his ranting leaves a mess at the register.

file: 2002/2002-07-31_new baby_lack of sleep_taking toll_i am mother_no sleep_working with no sleep.gif
title: Sleep-Deprived Dad Mistaken for Baby

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's your new baby?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Wonderful, but the lack of sleep is taking a toll on my body.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's Becky doing?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I am Becky. Bob looks worse.

setting: Office, in front of a coworker's workspace
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker how his new baby is doing. The coworker, visibly exhausted and unshaven, says the baby is wonderful but the lack of sleep is wearing him down. When Dilbert asks how Becky is doing, the man reveals that he is Becky and that Bob looks even worse.
punchline: The man is so sleep-deprived that he has lost track of his own identity, believing he is the baby Becky and that the parent, Bob, is in even worse shape.
summary: A new father's exhaustion becomes so extreme that a casual chat about his infant ends with him claiming to be the baby.

file: 2002/2002-11-21_turned into sheep_problems are interesting_fricken sheep.gif
title: Nobody Cares About Your Sheep Story

transcript.speaker: Sheep Coworker
transcript.text: Before we start the meeting, I should explain how I turned into a sheep.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Why do people think their problems are interesting to other people?

transcript.speaker: Sheep Coworker
transcript.text: I stepped in a puddle.

transcript.speaker: Sheep Coworker
transcript.text: I'm a fricken sheep!!!

situation: At a meeting table, a coworker who has somehow turned into a sheep offers to explain how it happened before the meeting starts. A bald, bespectacled colleague sarcastically asks why people assume their problems interest others. The sheep then gives his minimal explanation, stepping in a puddle, and angrily insists on how bad his situation is.
punchline: The colleague's cynical complaint about people oversharing their problems is delivered right after a man has literally been transformed into a sheep, making his dismissiveness absurd and the sheep's outburst justified.
summary: A man who has been turned into livestock tries to share his story, only to be brushed off by a coworker who finds personal troubles tedious.

file: 2002/2002-05-10_training cd_brainwashed_cuborg_insurance_cosmetic surgery_jump off roof_game system.gif
title: Doctor Suggests Jumping Off Roof

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My training CD went bad and brainwashed me to become a cyborg.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Your insurance doesn't cover cosmetic surgery but you can game the system by jumping off the roof.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: I hear that the follow-up visits don't get any easier.

setting: Doctor's examination room, then a rooftop
situation: A man who has been partly turned into a cyborg by a corrupted training CD visits a doctor. The doctor explains that insurance won't pay for cosmetic surgery to fix him, but would cover treatment for injuries from a fall, so he suggests jumping off the roof. In the last panel the two stand on the roof, and the doctor makes a casual remark about follow-up visits.
punchline: The doctor cheerfully advises the patient to injure himself deliberately to exploit an insurance loophole, then jokes about how unpleasant the recovery visits will be.
summary: A cyborg-afflicted patient gets medical advice to defraud his insurer by leaping from a building.

file: 2002/2002-02-27_first week_never do work_non work_tasks_thinking_wally period_wally week_want week.gif
title: The Wally Period Explained

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The first week after getting an assignment is called "the Wally period."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Never do work during the Wally period because most tasks become unnecessary within seven days.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I want a period named after me!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Whoa, Asok. That takes many years of non-work.

setting: Office, with both characters holding coffee mugs
situation: Wally explains to Asok that the first week after receiving an assignment is the 'Wally period,' during which you should do no work because most tasks get cancelled or become unnecessary. Asok eagerly says he wants a period named after himself, and Wally tells him that honor requires years of not working.
punchline: Wally's lazy philosophy is treated as a prestigious achievement, implying that having a named period requires a long, dedicated career of avoiding work.
summary: A veteran slacker coaches a young engineer on dodging assignments, then deflates the newcomer's ambition to earn similar fame.

file: 2002/2002-12-11_boost revenues_offshore_subsidary_lie to media_criminal activity_gag a rat_corruption.gif
title: Dogbert's Fraud Plan Gags Ratbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll artificially boost revenues by selling to our own offshore subsidiary.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then we'll book our expenses as capital, lie to the media about our prospects, bribe an industry analyst, and cash out!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I know I'm doing something right when my business practices gag a rat.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Aak aak aak

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant or executive, lays out a scheme of accounting fraud and corruption: selling to his own offshore subsidiary, capitalizing expenses, lying to the media, and bribing an analyst. Ratbert listens at the table and ends up gagging in disgust while Dogbert takes it as a sign of success.
punchline: Dogbert is proud of his corrupt business practices, treating it as validation that they are so unethical they make even a rat retch.
summary: A scheming dog presents a catalogue of corporate fraud tactics and boasts when his tiny rodent colleague is physically sickened by them.

file: 2002/2002-09-11_new ceo_robbed us_breaking law_written opinion_tax lawyer_board of directors_loading van.gif
title: CEO Robs Company, Board Helps

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then our new CEO backed up a moving van to the building and robbed us.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At first we thought he was breaking the law, but he had a written opinion from his tax lawyer saying it was probably okay.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What did the board of directors do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: After loading the van?

setting: Dilbert's home living room, with Dogbert on the couch
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that the company's new CEO drove a moving van up to the building and emptied it out. The CEO justified it with a written opinion from his tax lawyer saying it was probably legal. When Dogbert asks what the board did, Dilbert reveals they helped load the van.
punchline: The board of directors, supposed to oversee the CEO, instead took part in the looting, satirizing corporate governance failures and executive pillaging.
summary: A company's new chief executive empties the building into a moving van with a lawyer's blessing, and the directors who should have stopped him pitched in.

file: 2002/2002-07-12_temporary boss_revamp_project staus_color codes_confess_only one idea_emabrrassing.gif
title: Temporary Boss's Only Idea: Beige Status Codes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My first act as temporary boss is revamping our project status color codes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Red, yellow and green will be replaced by white, off-white and eggshell.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have to confess, it was embarrassing to realize I only have one idea.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: A temporary boss addresses his team and announces that his first act in charge is to overhaul the project status color codes. He points to a whiteboard where red, yellow and green are swapped for white, off-white and eggshell, which are nearly indistinguishable. He then admits that coming up with this was embarrassing because he only has one idea.
punchline: The new color scheme is useless because the shades are practically identical, and the boss's admission that it's his only idea shows how hollow and unproductive his leadership is.
summary: A stand-in manager proudly replaces meaningful traffic-light status colors with near-identical pale shades, then sheepishly admits he has nothing else to offer.
themes: change for the sake of change

file: 2002/2002-05-13_ceo visit_discontinue work_five days_illusion of productivity_diversity_few open slots.gif
title: Faking Productivity for the CEO Visit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO is visiting next week. Discontinue all real work immediately.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have five days to create the illusion of productivity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's the diversity sign-up sheet. We still have a few open slots that only require a hat.

setting: Office, in front of Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the CEO is coming to visit and that all real work must stop so the team can look busy for five days. He then hands over a diversity sign-up sheet, explaining that the remaining slots can be filled by anyone wearing a hat.
punchline: The company stages its diversity as a costume, so the CEO will see a diverse team without anyone actually being diverse, just as the team fakes productivity.
summary: Ahead of an executive visit, a manager orders his staff to stop working and put on a show of busyness and diversity.

file: 2002/2002-02-01_man hating supervisor_fired_being a man_happy to be man_dances_asok happy.gif
title: Fired for Being a Man

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Man-hating supervisor
