transcript.speaker: Man-Hating Supervisor
transcript.text: You're fired for being a man.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No one has ever called me a man before! This is the happiest day of my life!

transcript.speaker: Man-Hating Supervisor
transcript.text: Stop enjoying life!!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm a man!

situation: A female supervisor, labeled as man-hating, fires young intern Asok for being a man. Asok is thrilled to be called a man for the first time and celebrates joyfully. The supervisor, angered by his happiness, orders him to stop enjoying life while he dances around gleefully.
punchline: The supervisor's insult backfires because Asok, who is never treated as an adult, is delighted to be called a man, and being fired barely registers.
summary: A hostile boss dismisses a young employee for his gender, but he is overjoyed at finally being seen as a grown man.

file: 2002/2002-05-04_too much supervision_review_insanity_time wasting_lard filled suit_supervising.gif
title: Reviewed for Too Much Supervision

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My review says I "need too much supervision." Are you insane?!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Most days I can't get your time-wasting, lard-filled suit out of my cubicle with a freakin' crane!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: GAAA!! It's a trap! You're supervising me too much right now!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I win.

situation: Alice storms into the Boss's office waving her performance review, which says she needs too much supervision. She rants that she can barely get him out of her cubicle even with a crane, then realizes that by standing in his office complaining she is being supervised right now. The Boss calmly declares victory.
punchline: Alice's furious complaint about the review ends up proving the Boss's point, since she herself notes how much he hovers over her and his supervision is unavoidable.
summary: A fuming employee protests a review criticizing her for needing constant oversight, then realizes her own tirade confirms it.

file: 2002/2002-08-17_dilberts moother_making conversation_massively incompetent_ashamed_dilmom.gif
title: Mom Critiques Dilbert's Commercial

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mom, here's our new commercial.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: It gives no information about your products. Are you ashamed or just massively incompetent?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why can't we be both?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I was just making conversation.

setting: Mom's living room, sitting on couches with coffee and a donut
situation: Dilbert shows his mother the company's new commercial. She bluntly criticizes it for providing no product information and asks whether the company is ashamed or just incompetent. Dilbert replies that it could be both, and she says she was only making conversation.
punchline: Dilbert cheerfully admits his company could be both ashamed and massively incompetent, while his mom treats her harsh critique as casual small talk.
summary: A mother's brutal feedback on her son's company advert is met with deadpan acceptance of both insults, as she insists it was merely chitchat.

file: 2002/2002-01-08_downsized_info_last day_projects_right away_soon enough_90 days.gif
title: Downsized Employee Needs Information Sooner

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here are some projects to finish before your last day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But...I'll have to interact with people who know I've been downsized.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll get this information to you right away. Is ninety days soon enough?

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a stack of projects to finish before his last day, since he has been downsized. Dilbert points out he will have to ask for help from colleagues who know he is leaving, and the Boss chuckles. In a meeting, a coworker cheerfully offers to deliver the information Dilbert needs in ninety days.
punchline: Once coworkers know Dilbert is being laid off, they have no incentive to help him, so they stall far beyond his remaining time.
summary: A doomed employee is handed more work, only to find that colleagues who know he is leaving will happily drag their feet.

file: 2002/2002-03-12_daily prayer services_blood_bain washing_ambitious plans.gif
title: Cult Prayer Room Request

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd like permission to hold daily prayer services in a conference room.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll do it before work and of course I'll clean up any blood.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So far I'm the only member of my religion but I have ambitious plans for brain-washing.

situation: A robed figure in a tall pointed hood, carrying a staff topped with a stuffed animal head, asks the Boss for permission to hold daily prayer services in a conference room. He casually mentions cleaning up blood afterward and admits he is the only member of his religion so far, with plans to brainwash others. The Boss listens with a wary, uneasy expression.
punchline: An employee requests religious accommodation for what is obviously a blood-sacrificing, brainwashing cult, and the dread on the Boss's face suggests he may be unable to refuse.
summary: A hooded worshipper politely requests office space for his sinister new religion and cheerfully discloses its gory rituals and recruitment ambitions.

file: 2002/2002-07-01_procurement_special cable_rope_exclusive contract_rope distributer_monkey_cheaper_desk_animals.gif
title: Procurement Monkey Offers Rope Instead

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Procurement

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to order a special cable for my computer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, that's a piece of rope. Yes, I know it's cheaper.

transcript.speaker: Procurement Monkey
transcript.text: Ooh hoo hoo hoo!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, maybe it was a mistake to sign an exclusive contract with a rope distributor.

transcript.speaker: Procurement Monkey
transcript.text: Ooh hoo hoo jerk.

setting: Procurement department office, at the monkey's desk
situation: Dilbert asks the procurement department for a special cable for his computer. The procurement clerk, a monkey, hands him a piece of rope instead because it is cheaper. Dilbert grumbles that signing an exclusive contract with a rope distributor was a mistake, and the monkey calls him a jerk.
punchline: The procurement department's exclusive supplier deal means every purchase request gets filled with rope, showing how cost-driven purchasing ignores what employees actually need.
summary: A purchasing monkey substitutes cheap rope for a requested computer cable, exposing the folly of a locked-in supplier agreement.

file: 2002/2002-12-03_weasel of layoffs_experience_histiate_defects_list of defects.gif
title: Weasel of Layoffs Humiliates Ted

transcript.speaker: Weasel of Layoffs
transcript.text: Hell-o-o-o, Ted. I'm the Weasel of Layoffs.

transcript.speaker: Weasel of Layoffs
transcript.text: If there's any way I can make this experience more humiliating, don't hesitate to ask.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Why, why me??!!

transcript.speaker: Weasel of Layoffs
transcript.text: I'll tape a list of your defects to your old chair.

situation: A hooded, scythe-carrying weasel dressed like the Grim Reaper arrives at Ted's desk to announce he is being laid off. He cheerfully offers to make the experience more humiliating, and when Ted cries out in despair, the weasel responds by promising to tape a list of Ted's defects to his old chair.
punchline: The layoff messenger treats humiliation as a customer service feature and, instead of offering sympathy, answers Ted's anguished plea by planning to publicly shame him further.
summary: A grim-reaper-style weasel tells a worker he's being fired and then eagerly proposes extra ways to embarrass him on his way out.

file: 2002/2002-01-09_unemployed_drive electric car_abs_not romantic_turn on_socialize_mingle_party_drinks.gif
title: Dilbert's Disastrous Party Pickup Pitch

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm unemployed and I drive an electric car.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: These are my abs. I talk too much about myself and I'm not romantic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I realize it's a long shot but does any of that turn you on?

situation: Dilbert holds a cocktail glass at a party and introduces himself to a woman by listing his unappealing traits: he's unemployed, drives an electric car, has soft abs, talks too much about himself and isn't romantic. She listens with an increasingly unimpressed expression while he awkwardly shows off his belly. He then asks hopefully whether any of it turns her on.
punchline: Dilbert sabotages his own chances by honestly listing every unattractive trait, then hopefully asks if any of them might be appealing.
summary: At a mixer, an awkward engineer confesses a litany of his own flaws to a woman and optimistically wonders if any might attract her.

file: 2002/2002-12-15_new ustomer_sign it_write it_valable time_trapped in endless loop_criticized_start over_write letter yourslef.gif
title: Dilbert Drafts His Own Instructions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I want you to write a letter to our new customer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll tell you what to say, then you'll go write it and I'll sign it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This way I won't waste my valuable executive time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's efficient.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, that's one possible outcome.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's another.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'll keep forgetting to mention important things that should be in the letter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be trapped in an endless loop of writing, tracking you down, getting criticized and starting over.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or you could simply write the letter yourself and save us both a huge hassle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In paragraph one, say something like "Hi."

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to write a customer letter based on the Boss's instructions, claiming this saves executive time. Dilbert predicts the process will become an endless cycle of revisions and criticism, and suggests the Boss just write it himself. The Boss ignores the advice and begins dictating the letter's content to Dilbert anyway.
punchline: Dilbert's logical argument is completely ignored, as the Boss simply starts dictating instructions, proving Dilbert's predicted inefficient loop is about to begin.
summary: A manager insists on dictating a letter for his employee to write, brushing off a sensible warning about the hassle ahead.

file: 2002/2002-09-12_reduce expenses_new dress barrles_casual barrel day_barrel rides up.gif
title: Barrels Become the Company Dress Code

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To remind us all of our need to reduce expenses, the new dress code is barrels.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Except for Friday, which will be casual barrel day.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Has anyone else noticed that the barrel rides up on you when you sit?

setting: Office conference room and cubicle area
situation: The Boss, standing in a barrel, announces a new dress code of barrels as a cost-cutting measure. He then adds that Fridays will be casual barrel day. In the final panel, employees seated at a table in barrels with their arms sticking out complain that the barrel rides up when they sit.
punchline: The expense-cutting dress code is absurd, and the 'casual barrel day' exception mimics casual Friday, while employees are left dealing with the impractical consequences of wearing barrels.
summary: A manager imposes barrel-wearing on staff to save money, complete with a relaxed Friday policy, and the employees discover the practical downside while seated.

file: 2002/2002-03-02_criticize employees_recreational criticising_read email_alice needs to talk.gif
title: Recreational Criticizing Over Email

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm in a bad mood. Maybe I'll feel better if I criticize some employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm doing some recreational criticizing. What do you have for me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: E-mail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You read e-mail like a chimp!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice said she needs to talk to you.

situation: The Boss, in a bad mood, decides to cheer himself up by criticizing his employees. He asks Dilbert what he has for him, and Dilbert's only answer is 'E-mail.' The Boss immediately insults how Dilbert reads email, and Dilbert calmly passes along that Alice wants to talk to him.
punchline: The Boss's criticism is baseless and invented purely for his own amusement, since Dilbert has done nothing except mention email, and Dilbert's deadpan reply reveals he is unfazed by the pointless abuse.
summary: A grumpy manager goes looking for someone to berate for fun and picks an arbitrary insult about how his employee reads messages.

file: 2002/2002-08-30_punctuated equilibrium_third eye_natural advantage_dinosaurs_enemies_ziteye.gif
title: Dinosaur Plans Zit Evolution, Meets Bully

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: I plan to use punctuated equilibrium to turn this zit into a third eye.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's not a natural advantage. You'd better stay away from the fitter dinosaurs.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Ha ha! My only enemies are bullysaurs and they...

transcript.speaker: Bullysaur
transcript.text: Hey, Zit Eye!

setting: Prehistoric era, a dinosaur's den or cave with a couch
situation: A dinosaur boasts to Dogbert that he will use punctuated equilibrium to evolve a zit on his head into a third eye. Dogbert points out this is no real advantage and warns him to avoid fitter dinosaurs. The dinosaur laughs it off, saying only bullysaurs are his enemies, just as a bullysaur arrives and mocks him as 'Zit Eye'.
punchline: The dinosaur's plan to evolve a third eye from a zit backfires immediately, since the zit just gives bullies a new insulting nickname rather than any survival advantage.
summary: A boastful prehistoric lizard dreams of evolving a bonus eye from a pimple, only to be instantly taunted by a bully with a cruel new nickname.

file: 2002/2002-04-27_management decision_too distarcted_make informed decison_random_no answer.gif
title: Distracted Boss Gets Random Decision

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And that's why I need a management decision.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hi, Bill!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But you are too distracted to make an informed decision, so this will be random.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bob!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And here it comes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would "no" be an answer to anything you said?

situation: Dilbert walks down the hall explaining why he needs a management decision, but the Boss keeps greeting passing coworkers and barely listens. Dilbert announces that since the Boss is too distracted to decide properly, the answer will effectively be random. The Boss then asks whether 'no' would answer anything Dilbert said.
punchline: The Boss's decision is truly random and uninformed, since he never listened and just guesses that 'no' might fit whatever was asked.
summary: A manager who ignores a pitch while waving at colleagues ends up giving an uninformed decision that is basically a coin flip.

file: 2002/2002-12-26_bed hair_over slept_bad case_back to normal_unleash unhygenic.gif
title: Alice's Bed Hair Fist of Death

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Quit staring. I overslept and now I have a bad case of bed hair.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm confused. Surely it would have gone back to normal after your shower.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Please do not unleash the unhygienic fist of death!

situation: Alice sits at the meeting table with a towering, swept-up hairdo and snaps at her coworkers to stop staring, blaming oversleeping. Asok naively points out that a shower should have fixed her hair, which angers her. She clenches her fist and Asok's glasses fly off as he begs her not to punch him.
punchline: Asok's innocent, logical comment about showering insults Alice, who is known for her violent temper, and he cowers in fear of her signature punch, wrongly implying she skipped hygiene.
summary: A coworker's naive question about a coworker's wild morning hair provokes her famously violent temper.

file: 2002/2002-03-16_numbers down_reorganize dept_history for compariosn_fire people_save money.gif
title: Reorganize to Erase Bad Numbers

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Our numbers are way down. What should we do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Reorganize the department so there's no valid history for comparison.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then we'll fire a few people and give ourselves awards for saving money.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: El Diablo.

situation: Tina, holding a paper, tells the Boss that the department's numbers are way down and asks what to do. The Boss advises reorganizing the department so that no past data can be compared, then firing some people and handing out awards for the savings. Tina quietly mutters "El Diablo" in reaction.
punchline: Management's plan is to hide poor performance by destroying comparable data, lay people off, and reward themselves for the cost savings, which is so cynical that Tina calls the Boss the devil.
summary: A manager's scheme for dealing with falling results is to shuffle the org chart to hide the evidence, cut staff, and reward the executives.

file: 2002/2002-12-23_work out_company gym_jim the guard_exhausting_cow_milk_hamburgers.gif
title: Workout Through Security Guard Conversation

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Come work out with me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We don't have a company gym.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Try having a conversation with Jim the security guard; it's totally exhausting!

transcript.speaker: Jim the Security Guard
transcript.text: ...But a cow is not entirely full of milk; some of it is hamburgers!

setting: Office cubicle area and the lobby security desk
situation: Alice, dressed in workout clothes and a headband, invites a coworker to exercise with her. When told there is no company gym, she suggests chatting with Jim the security guard instead. In the last panel, Jim rambles at her with a bizarre non-sequitur about cows while she looks worn out and sweaty.
punchline: Talking to the security guard is so mentally draining and nonsensical that it counts as a full workout, and his absurd cow-and-hamburgers remark proves it.
summary: With no gym available at the office, Alice finds a substitute workout in enduring a tedious, rambling chat with the building's security guard.

file: 2002/2002-12-06_teds job_two jobs forever_verbal praise_down the road_future_manipulation_until hire.gif
title: Two Jobs, No Raise, Maybe Praise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to do Ted's job and your own job until we hire someone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I do well, you'll make me do two jobs forever. If I do poorly, I'll get no raise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't promise anything, but there might be some verbal praise down the road.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to cover Ted's job in addition to his own until a replacement is hired. Dilbert points out that he loses either way: success means permanent double duty, and failure means no raise. The Boss offers only a vague chance of verbal praise later.
punchline: The only reward management offers for doing double the work is an unpromised compliment, which confirms Dilbert's accurate assessment that he cannot win.
summary: A manager piles a departed coworker's duties onto an employee and dangles only the faint hope of future compliments as compensation.

file: 2002/2002-11-05_boss in jail_morale skyrocketed_profits soared_life had meaning_luck_two days.gif
title: Company Thrived While Boss Was Jailed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What happened while I was in jail?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Morale skyrocketed, profits soared, and for the first time, life had meaning.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's just my luck that I'd miss those two days.

situation: The Boss returns to the office after a stint in jail and asks Alice what he missed. She deadpans that morale and profits soared and life finally had meaning while he was gone. The Boss misses the insult entirely and complains that he was unlucky to miss those two good days.
punchline: The company flourished only because the Boss was absent, but he is too oblivious to realize he was the problem and just laments missing the good days.
summary: Returning from a jail term, a clueless manager hears that everything improved in his absence and takes it as bad timing rather than an insult.

file: 2002/2002-08-15_amorphous ad comapny_campaign_gaseous cloud_some music_ruin ad_politics.gif
title: Amorphous Ad Company Pitches Vague Campaign

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired the "Amorphous Ad Company" to do our campaign.

transcript.speaker: Ad Consultant
transcript.text: I see a gaseous cloud and some music...no, just a noise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Excellent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And then we say the name of our company?

transcript.speaker: Ad Consultant
transcript.text: Sure, if you want to ruin the ad.

situation: The Boss tells a meeting that he has hired the Amorphous Ad Company for the firm's campaign. The ad consultant describes his concept as a gaseous cloud and some music, then just a noise, and the Boss is delighted by it. When the Boss asks whether the ad will mention the company name, the consultant dismisses the idea as something that would spoil the ad.
punchline: The ad agency's idea is so vague and empty that it doesn't even advertise the client, and the Boss happily pays for it anyway.
summary: A boss gleefully buys an advertising pitch made of fog and noise, only to learn that naming his own company would wreck it.

file: 2002/2002-06-17_accounting gimmicks_accounting records_destroy records_illegal_make confusing_stockholders.gif
title: Boss Orders Records Destroyed, Then Confused

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stockholders are worried that our profits are nothing but accounting gimmicks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm putting you in charge of destroying all of our accounting records.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's illegal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh. Then just make them more confusing.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that stockholders suspect the company's profits are just accounting tricks. He then assigns Dilbert to destroy all the accounting records. When Dilbert points out that this is illegal, the Boss casually changes the order to making the records more confusing instead.
punchline: The Boss drops the plan only because it is illegal, then substitutes an equally deceptive but legally murkier way of hiding the accounting tricks, showing management cares about covering up fraud rather than avoiding it.
summary: Faced with investor suspicion of creative bookkeeping, a manager orders the evidence shredded and then, when told that's unlawful, simply asks for it to be obscured instead.

file: 2002/2002-07-24_bailout loan_excellent lobbyists_taxpayers give money_leagl.gif
title: Taxpayer-Funded Bailout Through Lobbying

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The government is giving us a bailout loan because we have excellent lobbyists!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha ha! Taxpayers will give us money so we can build overpriced products to sell to taxpayers!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Remind me again why any of this is legal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wuss.

situation: The Boss reads from a paper at a meeting table and gleefully announces the company is getting a government bailout loan thanks to its lobbyists. He explains that taxpayers will fund the company so it can build overpriced products to sell back to those same taxpayers. Dilbert asks why this is legal, and the Boss simply calls him a wuss.
punchline: The Boss dismisses Dilbert's reasonable ethical objection as weakness, highlighting how lobbying lets companies legally profit at taxpayers' expense with no accountability.
summary: A manager cheerfully describes a scheme in which public money bankrolls overpriced goods sold back to the public, and mocks the employee who questions its legality.

file: 2002/2002-12-19_early death_over working_grim reaper_love job_unlike you_don't look grim.gif
title: Grim Reaper Loves His Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm well on my way to an early death from overworking.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I expect a visit from the Grim Reaper any day now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't look grim.

transcript.speaker: Grim Reaper
transcript.text: Unlike you, I love my job.

situation: During a meeting, Dilbert complains to his boss and a coworker that overwork is going to kill him and that he expects the Grim Reaper any day. Later the Grim Reaper actually shows up in Dilbert's workspace. Dilbert remarks that he doesn't look grim, and the Reaper cheerfully replies that he loves his job.
punchline: Even Death, the bringer of doom, is happier at work than Dilbert, which shows how miserable Dilbert's job is.
summary: A burned-out engineer awaits death by overwork, only to meet a Grim Reaper who is far more content with his career than he is.

file: 2002/2002-02-16_trip cancelled_travel budget_contact centers_training_ignorance.gif
title: Travel Budget Spent on Renaming

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your trip is canceled.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We used up the travel budget renaming our call centers to "contact centers."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I need this training.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Isn't that another way of saying you're ignorant?

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert is walking past when the Boss tells him his trip is canceled. The Boss explains the travel budget was spent on renaming the company's call centers to contact centers. When Dilbert protests that he needs the training, the Boss responds by suggesting that needing training means he is ignorant.
punchline: The Boss wastes the budget on a meaningless rebranding and then turns Dilbert's reasonable request for training into an insult about his ignorance.
summary: A manager cancels an employee's training trip because the money went to a cosmetic name change, then insults him for wanting to learn.

file: 2002/2002-11-16_clear strategy_most profit_do more_less clear_illegal.gif
title: Strategy Must Be Less Clear

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need a clear strategy. Does anyone have a suggestion?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's figure out what makes us the most profit, and then do more of it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It needs to be less clear than that.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Can it be illegal?

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss asks his team for a clear strategy at a meeting. Dilbert offers the obvious suggestion of finding the most profitable activity and doing more of it. The Boss rejects it as too clear, and a bald coworker asks if the strategy can be illegal.
punchline: Management claims to want a clear strategy but rejects a sensible one for being too clear, and the coworker's suggestion of illegality implies that unethical practices are the only way the company would get more complicated or profitable.
summary: A boss begs for a clear plan, then dismisses the simplest sensible one as insufficiently vague, prompting a coworker to offer crime as an alternative.

file: 2002/2002-06-07_earned_enginner_life isn't fair_moving up_office space_private offcie_promotion_complaints.gif
title: Life Isn't Fair, Explain Individually

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The other engineers are complaining because you have a private office.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should explain to each of them that life isn't fair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah, I guess it IS easier to explain it to one person.

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, tells Dilbert that the other engineers are upset because he has a private office. He suggests Dilbert explain to each of them that life isn't fair. In the last panel Dilbert realizes the real implication of the advice.
punchline: Dilbert recognizes that it is easier to explain life's unfairness to one person (himself) than to a whole group, meaning that the person who actually has to accept the unfairness is the one being told to justify it, or that Catbert's advice is a hint that the office should go to someone else.
summary: A scheming HR cat suggests the engineer with a private office personally justify life's unfairness to his envious coworkers, and the engineer wryly sees the shortcut.

file: 2002/2002-04-12_online self assessment_survey_program_question blank_says you steal_bad advice.gif
title: Self-Assessment Survey: Check 'You Steal'

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't complete the online self-assessment survey. It asks where I need improvement and I don't need any.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The program won't let me leave that question blank.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Just check the box that says you steal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And people will understand that I don't mean it?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Sure.

situation: Dilbert complains that he cannot finish a mandatory online self-assessment because it requires him to name an area where he needs improvement, and he believes he needs none. Catbert, the evil HR director, cheerfully advises him to tick the box saying he steals. When Dilbert asks whether people will realize he doesn't mean it, Catbert grins and says sure.
punchline: Catbert's insincere 'Sure' reveals he is giving malicious advice that will get Dilbert in serious trouble, while Dilbert's arrogance about needing no improvement sets him up as the victim.
summary: Catbert tricks a self-satisfied Dilbert into admitting to theft on a compulsory HR evaluation form.

file: 2002/2002-06-22_cell phone_one ear_email_instant message_pager_messages_boss comes in_work stories_technology.gif
title: Dilbert's Work Stories Are Not Fascinating

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I had my cell phone at one ear and my regular phone at the other.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm reading e-mail, sending instant messages, my pager is vibrating, and my boss comes in!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You know what makes your work stories fascinating?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nothing.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on his couch and excitedly recounts a hectic moment at work, juggling two phones, e-mail, instant messages and a vibrating pager when his boss walked in. Dogbert listens patiently, then asks what makes Dilbert's work stories fascinating. When Dilbert eagerly asks what, Dogbert answers 'Nothing.'
punchline: Dogbert's setup flatters Dilbert into expecting a compliment, but the answer 'Nothing' reveals that his work stories are actually boring.
summary: After Dilbert breathlessly describes a frantic multitasking moment at the office, his dog deflates him by hinting that his tales are dull.

file: 2002/2002-02-09_evil hr dircetor_marketing department_bad news_good news_non dairy creamer_five cups a day.gif
title: Marketing Fired, Creamer Surplus

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The bad news is that I had to get rid of our marketing department.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The good news is that we have tons of nondairy creamer!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think those two things are related?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: If they are, I'm cutting back to five cups a day.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, announces at a meeting that he had to eliminate the marketing department, then cheerfully adds that the company now has a surplus of nondairy creamer. Dilbert wonders aloud whether the two facts are connected, and a coworker responds by worrying about his own coffee habit.
punchline: The implication is that the laid-off marketing staff were turned into nondairy creamer, and the coworker's only concern is moderating his own consumption rather than the horror of it.
summary: After a human resources chief blames a staffing cut for an unexpected stockpile of coffee whitener, the staff cheerfully ignore the grisly implication.

file: 2002/2002-08-13_females do hunting_alice stalks prey_razor sharp words_hyenas are laughing_tears her prey.gif
title: Dogbert Narrates Alice Like Wildlife

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The females of the group do all the hunting. The one I call Alice stalks her prey.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: She pounces. Her razor-sharp words tear the prey to shreds.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Grrrr

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The results are gruesome. Only the hyenas are laughing.

situation: Dogbert, wearing a pith helmet and taking notes, narrates the office like a nature documentary. He describes Alice as a hunting predator as she angrily types and growls at her computer. In the last panel a battered coworker lies slumped in his cubicle while two coworkers peer over the wall and laugh like hyenas.
punchline: Alice's verbal abuse of her coworkers is compared to a lioness killing prey, with the amused onlookers cast as scavenging hyenas.
summary: A pith-helmeted Dogbert treats the office as a wildlife documentary, casting Alice as a fearsome hunter whose sharp tongue leaves a coworker in ruins while others snicker.

file: 2002/2002-06-09_acquired benefits_adopt program_blend benefits progarm_blending_evil director_maternity leave_merger approved_smokers.gif
title: Evil HR Blends Merger Benefits

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The merger has been approved.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our evil Director of Human Resources will blend the acquired company's benefits program with our own.

transcript.speaker: Employees
transcript.text: Waaa! Waaa! Waaa!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Apparently they know what blending means.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Blending

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Let's see... My company offers six months of maternity leave for mothers.

transcript.speaker: Other HR Director
transcript.text: We treat 'em like smokers. They have to squat in the parking lot for ten minutes then go back to work.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's very evil.

transcript.speaker: Other HR Director
transcript.text: Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We'll adopt your program.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What is "draining"?

transcript.speaker: Other HR Director
transcript.text: Our company called it training.

setting: Corporate meeting room and HR conference table
situation: The Boss announces that a merger has been approved and that the evil HR director will blend the two companies' benefits programs, which makes employees wail in despair. The two HR directors, both cats, compare policies and each adopts the other's cruelest ideas, such as treating new mothers like smokers.
punchline: Blending two benefits programs means each evil HR department keeps the worst parts of the other's, so employees end up with the harshest combination.
summary: When two ruthless HR directors merge their benefits packages, each cheerfully steals the other's most cruel policies.

file: 2002/2002-11-01_dogcart attorney_too late_change_punish client_expect awkward silences_next break.gif
title: Dogbert Switches Sides Against Client

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Attorney

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your honor, is it too late to change sides?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: After hearing the evidence, I want to punish my client.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I expect some awkward silences during the next break.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a defense attorney, asks the judge whether he can switch sides mid-trial because he now wants to punish his own client after hearing the evidence. The judge, shown as a stern figure at the bench (the client sits beside him at the table), says no. Dogbert then notes that the next recess will be awkward.
punchline: Dogbert, having concluded his own client is guilty, is more bothered by the social awkwardness of continuing to represent him than by any ethical obligation.
summary: A defense lawyer who has decided his client deserves punishment is denied a switch to the other side and braces for uncomfortable breaks.

file: 2002/2002-05-28_downsized_no revenue_three months_fire billing_excellent performance.gif
title: Fired Billing Department, Now No Revenue

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, your performance is excellent but I have to downsize you.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Why?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our billing system is so defective that we haven't made any revenue in three months.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Why don't you fire the billing department?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I did... three months ago.

setting: The Boss's office, across his desk
situation: The Boss tells Ted that despite excellent performance he must be downsized because the company has earned no revenue in three months due to a defective billing system. Ted suggests firing the billing department, and the Boss reveals he already did exactly that three months ago.
punchline: The Boss fired the billing department, which is the very reason no bills went out and no revenue came in, yet he now blames a 'defective system' and punishes an innocent, high-performing employee.
summary: A manager lays off a top performer to cover for revenue lost after he himself eliminated the people who send out the invoices.

file: 2002/2002-08-23_bulk mail_first item_junk mail_morale skyrocketed_remained unopned_wm1_walls letter_only mail.gif
title: Wally Befriends His Junk Mail

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My morale skyrocketed when I received my first-ever item of bulk mail.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have designated it "WM1" for "Wally's Mail One" and it shall remain forever unopened.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bulk mail is the same as junk mail.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't listen to his lies, WM1.

situation: At a meeting table, Wally proudly holds up the first piece of bulk mail he has ever received and announces he has named it WM1 and will never open it. Dilbert points out that bulk mail is just junk mail. Wally covers the envelope's imaginary ears and tells it not to believe him.
punchline: Wally is so starved for attention that he treats an unsolicited junk mailing as a cherished friend and shields it from the truth.
summary: A lonely coworker adopts his first piece of advertising mail as a pet and refuses to hear that it is worthless.

file: 2002/2002-06-18_ethical_accounting records_massive shortsell_wrong one.gif
title: Dogbert's Unethical Short-Sell Advice

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss ordered me to make our accounting records more confusing. Is that ethical?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's as ethical as the massive short-sell order I'm going to place in the next ten seconds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you're the wrong one to ask.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now! Now!

setting: Dogbert's home, with Dilbert standing in front of the couch
situation: Dilbert, carrying his briefcase, asks Dogbert whether it is ethical that his boss ordered him to make the company's accounting records more confusing. Dogbert, holding a cell phone, replies that it is as ethical as the huge short-sell order he is about to place. Dilbert concludes Dogbert is the wrong one to ask, while Dogbert bounces on the couch urging his broker to act.
punchline: Dogbert's answer reveals that he is about to profit from the same kind of corporate wrongdoing, since he is shorting the stock of a company that is obviously cooking its books, so he is hardly an ethics authority.
summary: Dilbert seeks moral guidance about doctored books from Dogbert, who is busy betting against the very company that is committing the fraud.

file: 2002/2002-01-21_change your mind_sales + talk= stalk_sales guy_new position_not good_dilbert.gif
title: Sales Follow-Up Becomes Stalking

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert the Sales Guy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll talk to you every day to see if you change your mind.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Don't talk to me every day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You might change your mind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you know that if you cross "sales" with "talk" you get "stalk"?

setting: A sales meeting at a desk, then Dilbert's home or office
situation: Dilbert, working as a salesman, tells a female customer holding a brochure that he will contact her every day until she changes her mind. She objects to daily contact, but he insists she might yield. He then proudly points out to Dogbert that combining 'sales' and 'talk' makes 'stalk'.
punchline: Dilbert's relentless, persistent sales approach is indistinguishable from stalking, and he cheerfully acknowledges it with a wordplay.
summary: A pushy salesman vows daily pestering of a reluctant buyer and then gleefully notes his tactic amounts to stalking.

file: 2002/2002-07-23_bankruptcy_bring executives_money_shake at roof_sold stock_money falling.gif
title: Shaking Executives for Their Stock Money

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This is a list of our executives who sold their stock before announcing bankruptcy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My plan is to bring each executive to the roof, hold him by the ankles, and shake.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Ooh, a cat comb!

setting: Office meeting room and a street outside the building
situation: Alice shows Tina a list of executives who sold their stock just before the company announced bankruptcy. She proposes taking each one to the roof, holding him upside down by the ankles and shaking him until the money falls out. In the last panel Tina stands on the sidewalk holding a sack as bills rain down, and she is delighted to find a cat comb among the loot.
punchline: The executives' ill-gotten stock gains are shaken out of them like loose change, and Tina is more excited by a stray cat comb than by the falling money, which shows how little the shaken executives actually carried.
summary: An angry employee plans to dangle bankruptcy-dodging executives off a roof to shake their profits loose, and her coworker gleefully catches the haul below.

file: 2002/2002-05-18_the ceo visit_presentation_bloated department_eleiminate_budget meeting_marketing department.gif
title: Marketing Department Escapes the Layoffs

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The CEO visit

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Thanks for the presentation. Your department seems bloated.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I'll eliminate half of your group in the next budget meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you going to do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nothing. I told him we're the marketing department.

setting: Office, during a visit from the CEO
situation: The CEO tells the Pointy-Haired Boss that his department looks bloated and announces he will cut half the group at the next budget meeting. The Boss thanks him, then tells Dilbert he plans to do nothing because he told the CEO they are the marketing department.
punchline: The Boss believes that merely claiming to be the marketing department will protect his staff from cuts, and he thanks the CEO for threatening to eliminate half his people.
summary: A boss responds to a CEO's threat of heavy layoffs by misleading him about what his department does and then sitting back.

file: 2002/2002-11-14_short timer_refuse to leave_motorized wheel chair_lift me_drag to curb.gif
title: Retiring Without Using Muscles

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Short-Timer

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How will you leave if you refuse to use any major muscle groups until retirement?

transcript.speaker: Short-Timer
transcript.text: I'm hoping someone will buy me a motorized wheelchair and lift me into it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I would be willing to drag you to the curb.

transcript.speaker: Short-Timer
transcript.text: Face up?

setting: Office, in a cubicle or break area
situation: A coworker holding a coffee mug asks an older employee counting down to retirement how he plans to leave if he won't use any major muscle groups until then. The short-timer says he hopes someone will buy him a motorized wheelchair and lift him into it. The coworker offers to drag him to the curb, and the short-timer asks if it would be face up.
punchline: The short-timer is so committed to doing no work before retirement that he would accept being dragged out like cargo, only caring about the comfort of his orientation.
summary: An employee coasting toward retirement plans to exert no effort at all, even letting a colleague haul him out of the building.

file: 2002/2002-01-26_man without substance_use buzzwords_sell solutions_not products.gif
title: Empty Suit Joins Meeting, Wins Boss

transcript.speaker: M.T. Suit
transcript.text: Hi, I'm M.T. Suit. I'm a man without substance.

transcript.speaker: M.T. Suit
transcript.text: I compensate by using buzzwords and attending meetings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like his style.

transcript.speaker: M.T. Suit
transcript.text: We need to sell solutions, not products!

situation: At a meeting, an empty suit with no body introduces himself as M.T. Suit, a man without substance. He admits he makes up for it with buzzwords and meeting attendance. The Boss, thinking admiringly, approves of his style while the suit spouts a stock buzzword phrase.
punchline: The joke is that an empty suit literally embodies corporate emptiness, and management rewards exactly that: buzzwords and meeting attendance are mistaken for competence.
summary: A hollow suit with no one inside charms management by spouting jargon and showing up to meetings.

file: 2002/2002-05-23_demoted_one of the little people_buddy_anger_eyebrows_worked_years_snap out of it.gif
title: Demoted Boss Asks Dilbert for Lessons

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Demoted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey buddy, can you teach me to be one of the little people?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Buddy? My name is Dilbert. I worked for you for years.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, now I'll try. Am I doing the eyebrows right?

situation: The Boss has been demoted and approaches Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, to ask how to act like one of the lowly workers. He doesn't even know Dilbert's name despite years of managing him. Dilbert points this out, and the Boss responds by trying to imitate an angry expression, asking if he's doing the eyebrows correctly.
punchline: The formerly oblivious boss assumes that being a low-level employee means looking perpetually angry, and still shows no awareness of the people he used to manage.
summary: A newly demoted manager seeks coaching from the very employee whose name he never bothered to learn, then clumsily mimics an irritated scowl as his idea of subordinate behavior.

file: 2002/2002-12-05_motor noises_with lips_scorpion king_action figure_personal message with nose_trifecta_carol.gif
title: Carol's Noisy Personal Phone Calls

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: So I told him to stop making motor noises with his lips.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Get the Scorpion King action figure away from your sister's Barbie!!!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Now she's also typing a personal message with her nose!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a trifecta!

situation: Carol is on the phone at her desk, switching between a work-style conversation and shouting at her kids at home. She reports that one child is making motor noises, scolds him about the action figure and the Barbie, and then notes her daughter is typing a personal message with her nose. Wally and Dilbert eavesdrop over the cubicle wall.
punchline: Dilbert gleefully calls the pile-up of Carol's three household crises a 'trifecta,' treating her family chaos like a gambling win.
summary: Two coworkers listen in as a colleague juggles her kids' escalating misbehavior over the phone and treat it like a horse race payout.

file: 2002/2002-01-28_finish project_downsize_professionalism_delaying_timelines_passion for quality.gif
title: Wally Promises Slow Quality Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I have to downsize you as soon as you finish your project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I trust that your professionalism will prevent you from delaying unnecessarily.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I promise that my timeliness will be surpassed only by my passion for quality.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: The Boss tells Wally he will be laid off as soon as his current project is done, then appeals to Wally's professionalism not to stall. Wally calmly replies with a polished-sounding promise that is really a pledge to take as long as he likes.
punchline: Wally dresses up his intention to drag out the project in corporate buzzwords: his timeliness will be 'surpassed' by his passion for quality, meaning he will take forever.
summary: Told his job ends when his project does, a lazy engineer cheerfully vows that his dedication to quality will outrun any sense of urgency.

file: 2002/2002-08-03_dreaming about work_sleep at work_dreaming_sleeping_freaking out_considered work_pills.gif
title: Dreaming About Sleeping At Work

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't stop dreaming about work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I usually sleep at work, so I'm dreaming about sleeping and it's freaking me out.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Have you considered doing work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want pills, you quack.

situation: Dilbert lies on a couch and tells his therapist that he keeps dreaming about work, and since he usually sleeps at work he is really dreaming about sleeping, which disturbs him. The therapist suggests the obvious fix of actually doing work. Dilbert rejects this and demands medication instead.
punchline: Dilbert's real problem is solved by simply working, but he refuses the simple answer and insists on pills, insulting the therapist for suggesting it.
summary: A man who naps through his job complains to a psychiatrist about work dreams, then scorns the sensible cure in favor of medication.

file: 2002/2002-10-02_nitwit hates ogre_ogre ate nitwit_borrow nit iwt_requisition_work_coffee room_break room_ogre_nit wit_coworkers_new hires.gif
title: Borrowing a Nitwit for Stalled Project

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My project is stalled because my nitwit hates my ogre, and my #$%! won't do any work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My ogre ate my nitwit and my #$%! is trying to blame me for it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you want to borrow my nitwit?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I have a requisition in.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Alice, holding a coffee mug, complains to Dilbert that her project is stalled because of conflicts among the people working for her, culminating in her ogre eating her nitwit. She then offers to lend Dilbert her nitwit, and he declines because he already has a requisition in for new staff.
punchline: Alice's offer of a 'nitwit' who has supposedly been eaten shows how little she values her staff, and Dilbert declining because he is waiting on a hiring requisition suggests he would rather wait for a new hire than take on a useless employee.
summary: A frustrated Alice describes her dysfunctional team in fantasy terms and tries to loan out her leftover worker, but Dilbert prefers to wait for his own hire.

file: 2002/2002-09-08_cancel meetings_manage email_communicate_wants everything emailed_automated email.gif
title: Managing By E-mail Backfires Quickly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, cancel all of my meetings forever.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, I plan to stay in my office and manage by e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You still need to communicate some things in person.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I don't. I can do it all by e-mail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, e-mail me the budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And now, like magic...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ding. You have 1 message.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Auto-reply: Carol is out of the office.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have a situation here.

setting: Office cubicle area and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to cancel all his meetings forever because he will manage entirely by e-mail, and he dismisses her objection that some things need face-to-face communication. He then e-mails her a request for the budget and waits for a reply. He gets only an auto-reply saying she is out of the office, and in the last panel he sees her through the window, waving cheerfully from her desk.
punchline: The Boss's all-e-mail management scheme collapses at once because Carol's auto-reply shows she is away from the office, so he can't get the budget without an in-person conversation.
summary: A manager who swears off face-to-face contact in favor of e-mail is stymied when his assistant's automated out-of-office message is the only response to his first request.

file: 2002/2002-06-24_roboboss_good work_compliments employees_shallow compliment_feel good_high five.gif
title: Roboboss's Shallow Compliment Works Anyway

transcript.speaker: Roboboss
transcript.text: I am Roboboss. You are a valuable asset. Keep up the good work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That is the most shallow compliment I have ever heard. But it still made me feel good.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So... are you seeing anyone?

transcript.speaker: Roboboss
transcript.text: High five!

situation: A robotic boss delivers a stock line of praise to an employee carrying a briefcase. She admits the compliment is hollow but says it still lifted her mood, then starts flirting by asking if the robot is dating anyone. The robot responds only with a cheerful wave and a high five.
punchline: Even a canned, mechanical compliment from a robot boss is enough to make a starved-for-praise employee develop a crush, while the robot can only respond with another scripted gesture.
summary: A woman melts for a robot supervisor's generic praise and makes a pass at it, only to get a mechanical wave in return.

file: 2002/2002-06-23_interview_long story_bank story_argued_admit mistake_landmark court case_bank claims_dumb guy_fit in.gif
title: Three-Year Bank Error Obsession

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'd like you to interview Matt for our department.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a three-year gap in your work history. What were you doing?

transcript.speaker: Matt
transcript.text: One day I was balancing my checkbook and noticed a bank error.

transcript.speaker: Matt
transcript.text: So I embarked on a three-year mission to make the bank admit its mistake!

transcript.speaker: Matt
transcript.text: I worked the phones day and night, rarely eating or bathing.

transcript.speaker: Matt
transcript.text: Then came the sit-ins, the media frenzy and the landmark court case.

transcript.speaker: Matt
transcript.text: The bank claimed that seven minus four is three. And I'm like, "Since when?"

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would he fit in?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Unfortunately, yes.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to interview a job candidate named Matt. When Dilbert asks about a three-year gap in his work history, Matt describes an obsessive campaign against his bank over a supposed checkbook error, complete with sit-ins, media coverage and a court case. He is outraged that the bank claimed seven minus four is three, although that is correct arithmetic.
punchline: Matt's three-year crusade was based on his own bad math, since seven minus four really is three, and Dilbert admits he would fit in at the company because everyone there is equally irrational.
summary: A job applicant explains a three-year resume gap by recounting his epic battle against a bank over an error that was actually his own arithmetic mistake.

file: 2002/2002-12-10_cruel invention_disposible_evil_fossil fuel_lackey_life_no prupose_no purpose.gif
title: Dinosaur Becomes Dogbert's Disposable Lackey

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: My dream was to someday decompose and become fossil fuel.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: But Dilbert's cruel invention will make fuel unnecessary. Now my life has no purpose!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can be my disposable evil lackey.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: I-I-I can?

setting: Dogbert's lair, beside a spinning wheel-like device
situation: A green dinosaur laments that his lifelong dream of becoming fossil fuel has been ruined by an invention of Dilbert's that makes fuel unnecessary. Dogbert, seated at a wheel-like machine, seizes the moment to offer him a job as a disposable evil lackey. The dinosaur eagerly and nervously accepts the offer.
punchline: Dogbert exploits the dinosaur's despair by offering him a job that is explicitly disposable, and the grateful dinosaur hears only that he has a purpose again.
summary: A despondent dinosaur whose destiny as fuel has been cancelled gladly takes a degrading job offered by a scheming dog.

file: 2002/2002-09-18_elbonia_dress code_barrels_lack fashion_make up for.gif
title: Barrel Dress Code in Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, my company is so broke that our dress code is barrels...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But what we lack in fashion we make up for in...umm...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did I already say lack of fashion?

situation: Dilbert stands in a barrel in the mud of Elbonia, explaining to two onlooking locals that his company is so broke its dress code is barrels. He tries to say what the company makes up for its lack of fashion with, but can't think of any strength and ends up asking if he already mentioned the lack of fashion.
punchline: Dilbert tries to put a positive spin on his company's poverty but can't name a single thing it is good at, implying the company has no redeeming qualities.
summary: A barrel-clad Dilbert struggles to find any compensating virtue for his destitute company's dismal wardrobe.

file: 2002/2002-07-08_african vacation_natures wonders_shoot_window of suv_monkey brains_flared nostrils.gif
title: Boss's Safari Plans and Monkey Brains

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be taking my vacation in Africa so I can enjoy nature's wonders.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And shoot as much of it as possible from the window of an SUV.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you ever seen monkey brains?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Once, when you flared your nostrils.

situation: At a meeting table, the Pointy-Haired Boss announces his vacation plans in Africa, explaining that he wants to shoot as much nature as possible from an SUV window. He then asks a bald, bespectacled coworker whether he has ever seen monkey brains. The coworker replies that he saw them once when the boss flared his nostrils.
punchline: The coworker insults the boss by implying that his flared nostrils revealed that his brain is as small as a monkey's.
summary: A boss boasts about his safari getaway and asks a colleague about primate brains, only to get a pointed jab at his own expense.

file: 2002/2002-04-16_sentence finisher_money from orphans_sack and albi_uncanny accuracy.gif
title: The Sentence Finisher's Sinister Guesses

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Sentence Finisher

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I should take...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Money from orphans?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I mean I need...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: A large sack and an alibi?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're finishing my sentences with...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Uncanny accuracy?

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Dilbert sits across from a coworker who keeps finishing his sentences. Each completion is a sinister or criminal guess, like taking money from orphans and needing a large sack and an alibi. Dilbert, increasingly irritated, points out the habit, and the coworker cheerfully claims he is being accurate.
punchline: The sentence finisher's completions are absurdly villainous, yet he insists they show 'uncanny accuracy,' implying Dilbert's true intentions really are nefarious or that he is oblivious to his own wrongness.
summary: A talkative colleague keeps completing a man's thoughts with wildly criminal endings and then brags about how precisely he reads his mind.

file: 2002/2002-12-18_estate planning_probate costs_create living trust_lawyers_witty observation.gif
title: Lawyer Bills for Witty Remark

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Estate planning

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: You can avoid probate costs by creating a living trust.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So...I can use an inconvenient system created by lawyers to avoid a worse system created by lawyers?

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: According to my watch, that witty observation cost you four dollars.

situation: Dilbert meets with an estate planning lawyer, who explains that a living trust can avoid probate costs. Dilbert sarcastically points out that he would be using one lawyer-made system to escape another. The lawyer checks his watch and bills him four dollars for the remark.
punchline: The lawyer charges by the minute even for Dilbert's sarcastic comment criticizing lawyers, proving the point about lawyers profiting from every interaction.
summary: A client's sharp quip about legal systems gets turned into a billable expense by the lawyer he is quipping about.

file: 2002/2002-04-05_dogbert tech support._personal computer_defective_attractive package.gif
title: Tech Support Insults Selfish Caller

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It works fine on my machine.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, but this call is about my PC. May we talk about my problem now?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay. Your PC is defective and you're selfish. That's an attractive package you've got going there.

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center desk and the customer's computer desk
situation: Dogbert, working a tech support line with a headset, tells a caller that the software works fine on his own machine. The caller points out the call is about his PC and asks to focus on his problem. Dogbert responds by insulting both the caller's computer and his character.
punchline: Dogbert turns the customer's reasonable request into an insult, sarcastically calling his defective PC and selfishness an 'attractive package'.
summary: A support agent dismisses a caller's complaint, then answers his request for attention with a barbed put-down.

file: 2002/2002-06-12_new guy_no assignment_looking for project_ineffectual_good attendance_head nodding.gif
title: Ineffectual New Guy Seeks Project

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: I'm a new guy with no assignment. I'm looking for a project to horn into.

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: But don't be threatened by me. I'm exceptionally ineffectual.

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: I'm trying to build a career based on good attendance and head-nodding.

situation: A new employee in a green shirt and tie walks up to Dilbert's cubicle and announces that he has no assignment and wants to join a project. He reassures Dilbert that he is not a threat because he is exceptionally ineffectual. He then explains that his career strategy rests on showing up and nodding his head. Dilbert sits at his computer throughout.
punchline: The new guy cheerfully admits that his whole career plan is just attendance and head-nodding, which is sadly a workable strategy in many organizations.
summary: A newcomer with nothing to do volunteers himself for any project while openly confessing he contributes nothing but his presence and agreement.

file: 2002/2002-10-17_product launch party_day and night_working_five years_mime impression_party_add much.gif
title: Engineer Declines Launch Party, Threatens Mime

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you come to the product-launch party next week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. I'll be working day and night for five years to build the product you think you're launching.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Something tells me you don't add much to a party.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You haven't seen my mime impression.

situation: A coworker holding a notepad invites Dilbert to the launch party for a product. Dilbert refuses, explaining that the product being celebrated doesn't actually exist yet and will take him five years of nonstop work to build. When the coworker remarks that Dilbert wouldn't be much fun at a party anyway, Dilbert replies that he hasn't seen his mime impression.
punchline: The company is celebrating the launch of a product that engineering hasn't built yet, and Dilbert's deadpan reply about a mime impression offers a mock-threatening boast about his party skills.
summary: A premature celebration for a nonexistent product prompts a sarcastic refusal and an unexpectedly silent party trick.

file: 2002/2002-03-11_perfect world_eight months_incompetence multiplier_lying weasel factor.gif
title: Dilbert's Lying Weasel Factor Schedule

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In a perfect world the project would take eight months.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Schedule 8 months

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But based on past projects in this company, I applied a 1.5 incompetence multiplier.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: 1.5 x 8 = 12 months

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And then I applied an L.W.F. of 6.3.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: L.W.F.?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Lying weasel factor.

setting: Conference room during a project planning presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a project schedule to colleagues, starting with an ideal eight-month estimate. He multiplies it by 1.5 to account for the company's incompetence, then adds a further 'L.W.F.' of 6.3, which two coworkers ask about and one explains.
punchline: Dilbert's estimate pads the schedule not only for incompetence but for the deceitful behavior of the people he works with, implying everyone in the company lies about deadlines and progress.
summary: An engineer inflates a project timeline with successive fudge factors, ending with one that assumes his colleagues are dishonest.

file: 2002/2002-10-11_reducing inventory_sell to cutomers_feel free_tell board_idea.gif
title: Sell Inventory To Customers Idea

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does anyone have a suggestion for reducing our inventory?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's sell it to our customers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would that work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Feel free to tell the board that it's your idea.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss asks for ideas on reducing the company's inventory. Wally offers the obvious answer of selling the inventory to customers, and the Boss, unsure whether it would work, is happily told he can take credit for the idea in front of the board.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless that he doesn't recognize selling products as the normal purpose of inventory, and Wally lets him claim a trivial idea as his own brilliance.
summary: A manager seeking ways to shrink stock is handed the glaringly obvious answer of selling it, and is offered the glory of presenting it as his own.

file: 2002/2002-10-24_huge scam_upcoming merger_accretive earnings_stcockholders.gif
title: Merger Scam Worry Met With Laughter

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I worry that our upcoming merger is nothing but a huge scam on our stockholders.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Buwaha-hahaha!!

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I mean... it's accretive to earnings.

situation: At a meeting table, a nervous employee voices concern that the upcoming merger is a scam on stockholders. The Boss responds with an explosive fit of laughter while another employee looks on uneasily. The worried employee then hastily retracts the concern by claiming the merger is accretive to earnings.
punchline: The boss's gleeful laughter confirms the merger really is a scam, and the employee's panicked retreat into financial jargon shows he is too intimidated to press the point.
summary: A staffer's suspicion about a shady corporate deal is answered by his boss's wild cackling, prompting a quick backpedal into finance-speak.

file: 2002/2002-09-06_premature clickage_3 stooges_visualize_finger exercises_contort face.gif
title: Mouse Training: Avoiding Premature Clickage

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: Mouse Training

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: Today you will learn how to avoid premature click-age.

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: Contort your face and visualize what you look like with a contorted face.

transcript.speaker: Instructor
transcript.text: Now pair off and we'll do some finger exercises that I call "The Three Stooges."

setting: Corporate training room during a mouse training class
situation: A trainer leads a mouse training class and presents it as if teaching a delicate personal skill, starting with avoiding 'premature clickage'. He instructs the trainees to contort their faces and picture how they look, then to pair off for finger exercises he calls 'The Three Stooges'. A screen shows a man making a strained face.
punchline: The mouse training is worded like a sex-education class, with 'premature clickage' and pairing off for finger exercises, and the Three Stooges name hints at poking each other in the eyes.
summary: A computer class on using a mouse is taught in the unmistakable style of an awkward intimacy workshop, complete with innuendo and silly exercises.

file: 2002/2002-08-19_billion dollar idea_sweet mother_owns your ideas_fire you_then sue you_always hardest.gif
title: Company Claims Your Billion-Dollar Idea

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Sweet mother of potatoes! I just thought of a billion-dollar idea!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company owns all of your ideas. Cough it up or I'll fire you and then sue you.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Waaa!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Your first billion-dollar idea is always the hardest.

situation: At a meeting, an employee excitedly announces he has just thought of a billion-dollar idea. The boss immediately declares that the company owns all of his ideas and threatens to fire and then sue him if he doesn't hand it over. The employee breaks down crying while a coworker coldly consoles him.
punchline: The coworker's reassurance treats the company's seizure of his idea as a routine occurrence, implying that employees will keep having their valuable ideas taken from them.
summary: A worker's moment of inspiration is instantly confiscated by a threatening boss, leaving him sobbing while a colleague offers cold comfort.

file: 2002/2002-12-31_bio metric_security system_checks pulse_heat_fingerprints_wally_indentify.gif
title: Biometric System Says Wally Is Dead

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bob will demonstrate our new biometric security system.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: The system checks for pulse, heat and fingerprints to identify each employee.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It says I don't have any of those things.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Are you the one they call Wally?

situation: The Boss introduces Bob, who explains that the new biometric security system identifies employees by pulse, heat and fingerprints. Wally tries it and reports that the system says he has none of those things. Bob responds by asking whether he is the employee known as Wally.
punchline: The system's finding that Wally has no pulse, body heat or fingerprints suggests he is essentially lifeless, and Bob's remark implies Wally's famously idle, do-nothing reputation precedes him.
summary: A new security gadget concludes that a notoriously lazy employee shows no signs of life, and the demonstrator isn't surprised.

file: 2002/2002-04-11_flirting_non smoker_oil him up_ordering repair guy_shave back_tall_repair guy_copier.gif
title: Ordering a Hunky Copier Repairman

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: And I'd like the copier repair guy to be a tall non-smoker with well-defined abs.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Oh, you're not a dating service, eh? Well if I give you money and you send me a guy then it's just semantics.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: And could you shave his back and oil him up before you send him?

situation: Tina, sitting at her desk, phones the copier repair company and starts specifying the physical attributes she wants in the technician. When the company says it isn't a dating service, she argues that paying money for a man to be sent over makes it the same thing. She keeps escalating her requests while The Boss stands nearby in the final panel.
punchline: Tina treats a routine service call as a way to order a handsome man, dismissing the difference between hiring a repairman and a dating service as mere semantics.
summary: A woman at her desk orders a copier technician as if she were shopping for a date, adding ever more personal demands.

file: 2002/2002-01-31_man hating supervisor_justify pay_all day meeting_wrong one_meeting_this meeting_door open_business.gif
title: Wrong Meeting, Open Door

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Man-hating supervisor

transcript.speaker: Man-Hating Supervisor
transcript.text: Have any of you men done anything to justify your pay?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I attended an all-day meeting but later found out I was in the wrong one.

transcript.speaker: Man-Hating Supervisor
transcript.text: Actually, you're not supposed to be in this meeting either.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: The door was open.

situation: A stern female supervisor demands that the men at the table justify their pay. A bald coworker offers as his accomplishment that he sat through an all-day meeting before discovering it was the wrong one. The supervisor then tells him he is not supposed to be in this meeting either, and he explains he came in because the door was open.
punchline: The coworker keeps wandering into meetings he doesn't belong in, and his only defense is that the door was open, which shows he contributes nothing.
summary: A man who can't even attend the right meetings is caught crashing yet another one when his boss asks what he has done to earn his salary.

file: 2002/2002-09-22_full service broker_stick broker_brokers know stocks_earn trust_direct approach_garbage_biggest commission.gif
title: Honest Stockbroker Offers Two Options

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Full Service Broker

transcript.speaker: Bob Weaselton
transcript.text: I'm Bob Weaselton, your full-service stockbroker.

transcript.speaker: Bob Weaselton
transcript.text: There are two ways we can go here.

transcript.speaker: Bob Weaselton
transcript.text: Option one: I act as if brokers know which stocks are better than others.

transcript.speaker: Bob Weaselton
transcript.text: Then I'll earn your trust by comparing your portfolio to misleading benchmarks.

transcript.speaker: Bob Weaselton
transcript.text: But I prefer a more direct approach.

transcript.speaker: Bob Weaselton
transcript.text: Option two: I sell you whatever garbage earns me the biggest commission.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you do me a favor and lie to me?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nice haircut.

situation: Dilbert visits a full-service stockbroker, who cheerfully lays out two ways he can handle the relationship: pretend brokers can pick winning stocks and earn trust with misleading benchmarks, or simply sell whatever pays him the highest commission. Stunned by the candor, Dilbert asks to be lied to, and Dogbert, sitting nearby, obliges with a compliment.
