punchline: The broker's brutally honest admission that he sells whatever earns him the biggest commission is so disturbing that Dilbert begs for a comforting lie, and Dogbert's irrelevant compliment is the only lie on offer.
summary: A candid broker admits his advice is either an act or a commission grab, leaving his client pleading for a comforting falsehood.

file: 2002/2002-02-13_tribunal_admin. assistants_appeal_glass walled.gif
title: Admin Tribunal Judges Dilbert's Attractiveness

transcript.speaker: Admin Assistant
transcript.text: The tribunal of admin assistants has reached a decision.

transcript.speaker: Admin Assistant
transcript.text: Dilbert is not attractive enough to use the glass-walled conference room near the lobby.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I appeal?

transcript.speaker: Admin Assistant
transcript.text: Apparently not.

setting: Office, in front of a jury-style box of admin assistants
situation: A panel of administrative assistants sits like a jury while one of them announces their verdict. They have ruled that Dilbert is not good-looking enough to be allowed to use the glass-walled conference room near the lobby. Dilbert asks to appeal and is told that appeals are not permitted.
punchline: The admin assistants hold the real power over office resources and rule on room access by looks, and the decision is final with no appeal.
summary: A jury of secretaries bans Dilbert from a visible meeting room for being too plain, and his request to challenge the ruling is dismissed.

file: 2002/2002-02-17_voluntary layoff package_ted_retirement money_start a business_kites out of waffles_worlds largest_edible kites_value opinion_option._alice.gif
title: Ted Asks Wally About Waffle Kites

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Wally, may I ask you for advice?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Huh?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: My name is Ted. I'm planning to take the voluntary layoff package.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Then I plan to use my retirement money to start a business that makes kites out of waffles!

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: In five years I hope to be the world's largest maker of edible kites.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: So, what do you think? I value your opinion.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ted, who told you that I'd be a good person to ask for an opinion on your idea?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Alice said it reminded her of the quality of your... ideas.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Alice shoots for the double!!! She scores!!!

situation: Ted approaches Wally for advice about taking the voluntary layoff package and using his retirement money to start a company making kites out of waffles. Wally asks why Ted thought he was a good person to consult. Ted reveals Alice said the idea reminded her of the quality of Wally's own ideas, and in the last panel Alice is shown celebrating the double insult.
punchline: Alice managed to insult both Ted's absurd business idea and Wally's ideas at once, scoring a 'double' burn.
summary: A hopeful colleague seeks counsel on a ridiculous snack-based startup and unwittingly delivers a sly dig that Alice arranged against two people with one remark.

file: 2002/2002-06-04_vacant offices_layoffs_nice office_actual door.gif
title: Boss Grants Dilbert's Office Request

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We sure have a lot of vacant offices since the layoffs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wouldn't mind having a nice office with an actual door. Why don't you let me have one?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. Take one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop toying with me!

situation: Dilbert remarks to the Boss that there are many empty offices after the layoffs, then asks to be given a nice one with a real door instead of his cubicle. The Boss simply agrees and tells him to take one, which leaves Dilbert shaking and accusing him of toying with him.
punchline: Dilbert is so used to management refusing every request that an unexpected yes strikes him as a cruel trick.
summary: A cubicle worker asks for a vacant office and is so stunned when his manager agrees that he assumes it must be a prank.

file: 2002/2002-11-09_burned down_customer headquaters_employee screws up_performance reviews_demo unit.gif
title: Catbert's Advice: Pounce After Disaster

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Don't give performance reviews on time.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wait until an employee screws up something big, then pounce!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...I forgot to unplug the demo unit and it burned down our customer's headquarters.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have a minute?

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, advises The Boss to delay performance reviews until an employee makes a major mistake. In the last panel Dilbert, looking singed and rumpled, confesses that he forgot to unplug a demo unit and it burned down a customer's headquarters. The Boss immediately asks if Dilbert has a minute, ready to give the review.
punchline: Dilbert's catastrophic mistake arrives at exactly the moment the boss is primed to use it, so the delayed performance review becomes a punishment rather than an honest evaluation.
summary: Management is coached to hold off on evaluations until a worker's big blunder provides ammunition, and a disastrous fire right on cue proves the strategy.

file: 2002/2002-09-13_set up meeting_customer_technology_humiliating_poor_fgreat food.gif
title: Serving Pet Food to Customers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Set up a meeting with the customer so we can demonstrate our technology.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's humiliating because we're so poor now. What will I feed them?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you think the food is great, wait until you see our technology!

setting: Dilbert's company, after the staff have lost everything and wear barrels
situation: The Boss, standing in a barrel, orders Dilbert to arrange a customer meeting to demo their technology. Dilbert, also in a barrel, laments that the company is so broke he can't afford to feed the visitors. At the meeting he holds up a bag of pet food and serves it in dog bowls to two customers, boasting about the food and the technology.
punchline: The company is so broke it serves pet food to customers, and Dilbert implies the technology on show will be just as unimpressive as the meal.
summary: A bankrupt company still insists on wowing a client, so the host dishes up kibble in pet bowls and promises the tech will be equally impressive.

file: 2002/2002-03-29_20% pay cuts_downsize_sounds promising.gif
title: Wally Volunteers for Pay Cut

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can take 20% pay cuts or I'll have to downsize one of you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I know you're like a family but...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, Wally?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Tell us more about the pay cut. That sounds promising.

setting: Office meeting area, with the team gathered around the boss
situation: The Boss tells his team they must either accept 20% pay cuts or he will lay off one of them. Wally begins to object that the boss treats them like family, but the boss lets him speak. Wally then asks for more details about the pay cut, since he sees it as promising, while his coworkers look on.
punchline: Wally, who is notoriously lazy, treats a pay cut as a good deal because he'd happily earn less for doing even less, or sees it as a sign they'd pay him less to work less.
summary: Offered a choice between lower wages and a layoff, the office slacker is oddly enthusiastic about the reduced pay.

file: 2002/2002-11-04_pointy haired convict_bust joint_walking backward_little joke_fresh meat.gif
title: Boss Tries Escaping His Cubicle

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Pointy-Haired Convict

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've got to find a way to bust out of this joint.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Try walking backward.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, that didn't work...oh, I get it: This is a little joke you play on all the fresh meat.

situation: The Boss, dressed in an orange prison jumpsuit, announces that he must escape from this 'joint', treating the office like a prison. Wally, sitting calmly with his coffee, suggests walking backward. The Boss tries it, ends up trapped in a cubicle, and concludes it's a prank played on newcomers.
punchline: The office is so confining that the Boss, who thinks he's a convict, can't even find the way out of a cubicle maze, and he mistakes Wally's useless advice for a hazing ritual on new inmates.
summary: Dressed as an inmate, the boss seeks a prison break from his workplace and follows a coworker's nonsense tip straight into a dead end.

file: 2002/2002-03-08_compost drawer_secretary_urgent_carol_desk_office.gif
title: Urgent Papers Go to Compost Drawer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, this is urgent.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'll add it to the compost drawer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope that means the same thing as "urgent."

setting: Office cubicle area, at Carol's desk
situation: The Boss hands Carol a document and tells her it is urgent. Carol calmly says she will put it in her compost drawer, where papers presumably rot. The Boss, left standing there, hopes that this means the same thing as urgent.
punchline: Carol's 'compost drawer' implies urgent papers are left to decay, and the Boss's weak hope that it means 'urgent' shows he has no power over her and is too timid to challenge her.
summary: A boss insists a paper is urgent, but his assistant files it in a drawer where things go to rot, and he can only wishfully hope for the best.

file: 2002/2002-11-07_yemp_fear of commitment_one foot out door_swiped.gif
title: Temp Literally Keeps One Foot Out

transcript.speaker: Temp
transcript.text: I'm a temp with a fear of commitment. I keep one foot out the door.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whatever. Just take care of this for me. It'll take ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Zip

situation: A temp worker tells Dilbert he has a fear of commitment and keeps one foot out the door, standing with one leg raised. Dilbert ignores the warning and hands him a paper, saying it will only take ten minutes. The temp's leg flies out the door, knocking off Dilbert's tie and the paper.
punchline: The temp's claim that he keeps one foot out the door is taken literally, and his leg kicks out of the cubicle the moment he is given real work.
summary: A noncommittal temp turns out to be unable to resist bolting when handed a task, with his foot sweeping away Dilbert's tie.

file: 2002/2002-08-27_accounting irregularities_five year plan_five years ago_investigated_prophetic_5 year assessment.gif
title: Five-Year Plan Predicts Accounting Scandal

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I found our five-year plan from five years ago.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The last page says, "At the end of the fifth year, the entire management team will be..."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "...investigated for accounting irregularities."

situation: At a meeting, a manager reads aloud from a five-year plan he found that was written five years earlier. The last page turns out to say the entire management team will end up being investigated for accounting irregularities. The other attendees listen silently.
punchline: The old five-year plan accurately predicted, or perhaps deliberately planned, that management would be under investigation for accounting fraud, implying the scandal was the intended outcome all along.
summary: A reading of an old strategic plan reveals its final goal was a fraud investigation of the whole leadership team.

file: 2002/2002-01-30_alice in charge_drink coffee_insulting_man hating supervisor_hates men_picks on wally.gif
title: Man-Hating Supervisor Favors Alice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Man-hating supervisor

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: I'm putting Alice in charge of the project.

transcript.speaker: Supervisor
transcript.text: And Willy or Walter here can drink coffee until he grows into a fly.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't figure out why she's being so nice to me.

setting: Conference room, then a hallway or office
situation: A female supervisor in a meeting puts Alice in charge of the project and then insults Wally with a bizarre, mangled put-down about drinking coffee until he becomes a fly. Afterward Wally, holding his coffee mug and talking to Dilbert, says he can't understand why she is being so nice to him.
punchline: Wally is so oblivious, or so accustomed to being ignored and belittled, that he interprets a blatant insult as kindness because it lets him keep drinking coffee.
summary: A supervisor who clearly resents men hands the project to Alice and sneers at Wally, who somehow takes the slight as generosity.

file: 2002/2002-11-28_war on waste_wear shirt_honk_blow nose_program.gif
title: Free Shirt Becomes Nose Wipe

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Each of you will get a shirt as part of my war on waste program!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wouldn't wear that shirt at home or in the office, so what good is...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Honk!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh. Never mind.

situation: The Boss announces he will give everyone a free shirt as part of his war on waste program. Dilbert begins to object that nobody would wear such a shirt, but a bald coworker loudly blows his nose into his shirt. Dilbert then drops his objection.
punchline: The giveaway shirts are so useless that the best use anyone finds for them is as a handkerchief, which ironically proves the boss's 'waste reduction' program is itself wasteful.
summary: A boss hands out promotional shirts to cut waste, and the only person who finds a use for his gift is a coworker who blows his nose on it.

file: 2002/2002-06-25_falling for robot_human_robo boss_robot_shallow compliments_soulless machine.gif
title: Dating the Compliment-Spouting Roboboss

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Roboboss, can this relationship work? After all, I'm a human...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And you're a soulless machine designed to give shallow compliments to employees.

transcript.speaker: Roboboss
transcript.text: You're giving 110%.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop... Don't make me love you.

setting: A restaurant table with a flower, on a date
situation: Alice sits across from Roboboss, a robot manager, on what looks like a date. She asks whether a relationship between a human and a machine can work, acknowledging he is a soulless machine programmed to hand out shallow compliments to employees. Roboboss responds with a stock corporate compliment, and Alice is charmed anyway.
punchline: Alice knows the robot's praise is canned and meaningless, yet the cliché 'You're giving 110%' still makes her fall for him, showing how starved employees are for any recognition from management.
summary: A woman doubts her romance with a robot boss because his flattery is mechanical, but one hollow compliment melts her resolve.

file: 2002/2002-01-19_sales training_sell to customer_dare to be great_prove worthiness_beg.gif
title: Make Customers Beg For Product

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sales training

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Never sell to your customer. Make your customer sell to you.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Our products are only for those who dare to be great! Make the customer explain why he is worthy.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Please

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What did you just call me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You heard me, goober. Now beg for our product.

setting: Sales training seminar and a sales meeting at a conference table
situation: A sales trainer teaches that salespeople should never sell to customers but should make customers sell themselves and prove they are worthy of the product. A thumbnail shows a customer begging 'please' while being choked. Dilbert then applies the lesson literally, insulting a customer and demanding he beg.
punchline: Dilbert takes the absurd sales advice literally, insulting and humiliating the customer, showing how a bad sales philosophy would play out in practice.
summary: After a seminar preaches that buyers must earn the right to purchase, Dilbert tries the approach on a real customer by demanding he grovel.

file: 2002/2002-01-02_billion dollars_lose bid_winning less work_cost estimates.gif
title: Billion Dollar Overhead Estimate Wins Less Work

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need your cost estimates for my bid proposal.

transcript.speaker: Administrative Employee
transcript.text: A billion dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds high for administrative overhead.

transcript.speaker: Administrative Employee
transcript.text: If you already know the cost, why ask me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'll make us lose the bid.

transcript.speaker: Administrative Employee
transcript.text: I like to think of it as winning less work.

situation: Dilbert asks an administrative employee for cost estimates to include in a bid proposal. The employee gives an absurd figure of a billion dollars and refuses to justify it. When Dilbert warns that the inflated overhead will cost the company the bid, the employee cheerfully reframes losing as a benefit.
punchline: The lazy employee spins losing the bid as 'winning less work', revealing he sets inflated costs deliberately to avoid having to do more work.
summary: A support worker pads his budget to an absurd figure so the company will lose the contract and he'll have fewer tasks to handle.

file: 2002/2002-08-21_have mail_twelve years_glistens_envelope_happy_awed.gif
title: First Mail in Twelve Years

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have mail! I've never had mail in twelve years here.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's not addressed to me but it was in my box so I'm keeping it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No mail for twelve years?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I hold it just right it glistens.

situation: Wally excitedly announces that he has received mail for the first time in twelve years at the company. He admits it isn't addressed to him but keeps it anyway because it was in his mailbox. Dilbert is astonished that he has gone so long without mail, and Wally admires the envelope as it shimmers in the light.
punchline: Wally is so starved of mail after twelve years of being ignored that he gleefully keeps someone else's envelope and treats it like a treasure.
summary: After over a decade of an empty mailbox, a delighted Wally claims a misdelivered envelope as his own prize and admires its shine.

file: 2002/2002-05-27_bandwidth_budget_double click_engineer for week_interface_ping director_scope_batch mode.gif
title: Boss Misuses Engineering Jargon Constantly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's ping the Director of Marketing and double-click on the budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then we can interface in batch mode and put a scope on his bandwidth.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Please stop doing that!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have I mentioned that I was an engineer for a week?

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss strings together technical buzzwords, talking about pinging the Director of Marketing, double-clicking on the budget and putting a scope on his bandwidth. A frustrated coworker begs him to stop, and he responds by boasting that he was once an engineer for a week.
punchline: The Boss thinks a single week of engineering experience entitles him to misuse technical jargon, which he applies nonsensically to non-technical business matters.
summary: A manager peppers his meeting talk with misapplied tech terms and justifies it by citing his tiny stint in engineering.

file: 2002/2002-01-18_demo_good sale_sales training_see coming_selling_sucker_victim_wedgie_gullible.gif
title: Sales Training: The Wedgie Analogy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sales training

transcript.speaker: Sales Trainer
transcript.text: Don't act like you're selling something.

transcript.speaker: Sales Trainer
transcript.text: A good sale is like a good wedgie: your victim shouldn't see it coming.

transcript.speaker: Sales Trainer
transcript.text: For this next demonstration I need a volunteer who can't see what's coming.

situation: A sales trainer lectures a room of employees, telling them not to act like they're selling anything. He compares a good sale to a good wedgie, with a cartoon showing a man being given one. He then asks for a volunteer for his next demonstration, and one employee in the audience raises his hand.
punchline: The trainer's line about a victim not seeing it coming is a warning that he is about to give a wedgie to whoever volunteers, and the volunteer plainly doesn't see it coming, which proves the trainer's point.
summary: A sales instructor likens successful selling to giving an unsuspecting person a wedgie, then asks the audience for a volunteer who won't anticipate it.

file: 2002/2002-10-12_vacation_starts ten minutes_loose ends_reporter_designed computer_recycled paper.gif
title: Vacation Ruined By Boss's Lie

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My vacation starts in ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I tied up all of my loose ends. I only need to walk out the door.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told a reporter that we designed a computer made entirely of recycled paper.

situation: Dilbert sits at his desk checking his watch, thinking happily that his vacation begins in ten minutes and that he has finished all his work. Just as he is about to leave, the Boss appears and announces he told a reporter the company built a computer made entirely of recycled paper. This implies Dilbert will now be handed an absurd last-minute task.
punchline: Just as Dilbert is about to escape on vacation, the Boss dumps an impossible, self-created commitment on him, wrecking his plans.
summary: A worker counting down the minutes to his holiday is ambushed by a manager who has promised the press something ridiculous.

file: 2002/2002-05-19_annually_emotionally invested_math trick_save money_system_vendor_vendor tauntage.gif
title: Vendor's Cost Revealed by Math

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: If you buy our system it will pay for itself in three years.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Approximately how much does it cost?

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: It's hard to say. It depends on many factors.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine. Just tell me how much money it will save annually.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: You'll save $10,000 per year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well then, if it pays for itself in three years, it must cost about $30,000.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was a little trick I call "math."

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Oops. Now I'm not emotionally invested.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Your vendor tauntage is quite excellent today.

setting: Conference room during a sales meeting
situation: A vendor pitches a system that will pay for itself in three years but dodges every question about its price. Dilbert asks for the annual savings instead, then multiplies that figure by three to work out the cost himself. The vendor admits the trick has cost him his sales leverage, and Asok compliments Dilbert's taunting.
punchline: Dilbert defeats the vendor's evasiveness with simple arithmetic, and the vendor's sales tactic of getting buyers emotionally invested collapses.
summary: A salesman who refuses to name his product's price is outfoxed when a customer calculates it from the promised payback period.

file: 2002/2002-07-02_exclusive cable contarct_monkey_monkeys version_procurement manager_rope as electric_rope vendor_animals.gif
title: Monkey Procurement Manager Signs Rope Contract

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My technology test was a huge failure because I had to use rope as my electronic cable.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our procurement manager is a monkey who signed an exclusive cable contract with a rope vendor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd rather not take sides until I hear the monkey's version.

situation: Dilbert presents to management, explaining that his technology test failed because he was forced to use rope instead of an electronic cable. He points to a slide showing a monkey and blames it for being the procurement manager who signed an exclusive deal with a rope vendor. The Boss, seated at the table, declines to judge until he hears from the monkey.
punchline: The Boss treats the monkey as a legitimate party in a dispute, insisting on hearing 'both sides' even though a monkey obviously should never have been running procurement.
summary: A failed tech test is blamed on a monkey purchasing chief who bought rope in place of cable, and the boss solemnly wants to hear the monkey's side.

file: 2002/2002-05-02_celan desk award_winner_facilities people_appeared unused_higher tax bracket_asok_intern_desk_took desk.gif
title: Clean Desk Award Costs Asok

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok is the winner of the $25 "Clean Desk Award."

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Yesterday the facilities people took my desk because it appeared to be unused.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I hope this doesn't bump me into a higher tax bracket.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that Asok has won a $25 Clean Desk Award. Asok explains that the facilities department took his desk the day before because it looked unused. In the last panel he sits on the floor of his cubicle with no desk, worrying that the prize money will push him into a higher tax bracket.
punchline: Asok's spotless desk won him a trivial $25 prize but also got the desk confiscated, and his deadpan worry about taxes on the prize shows how little the reward is worth compared with what he lost.
summary: A tidy employee is rewarded with a small cash prize, only to reveal that his spotless desk was hauled away as abandoned furniture.

file: 2002/2002-01-16_best_hire back_not old job_sales_train you to lie_worst_desparate_take anything_need money_job_take advantage of_business.gif
title: Worst Salesperson Gets Sales Job

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We can hire you back but not at your old job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's okay. I'll do anything but sales. I would be the worst salesperson on earth.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's sales.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did I just say worst when I meant best?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We'll have to train you to lie better.

setting: Catbert's office, with Dilbert seated across the desk
situation: Dilbert, who has been laid off, asks Catbert for his job back and is told it can't be his old position. Dilbert says he'll take anything except sales because he'd be terrible at it, and Catbert replies that the opening is in sales. Dilbert tries to backpedal by claiming he meant best, and Catbert says he'll need training to lie more convincingly.
punchline: Dilbert's honest admission that he'd be a terrible salesperson is exactly why he's assigned to sales, and his clumsy attempt to take it back shows he needs to learn to lie, which is the core skill of the job.
summary: A rehired employee's refusal to take a sales role backfires when his cat boss assigns him there anyway and promises lessons in dishonesty.

file: 2002/2002-10-18_latest assignment_impossible_slow speed of light_perfect art_human cloing_eliminate garvity_stop the sun_reanimate dead_impossible tasks_change the world_nature.gif
title: Garbage Man Judges Impossible Assignment

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does my latest assignment look impossible?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Let's see... You'd need to slow the speed of light, and perfect the art of human cloning...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So there's hope?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Eliminate gravity, stop the sun, re-animate the dead...

setting: Outdoors by a trash bin on a street
situation: Dilbert hands his latest work assignment to a garbage man and asks whether it looks impossible. The garbage man reads it and lists the absurd feats of physics and science required to complete it. Dilbert hopefully asks if there's still a chance, and the garbage man just keeps listing more impossible requirements.
punchline: Dilbert's assignment is so absurdly unachievable that even a garbage man sees it requires violating the laws of nature, and Dilbert's optimism is met with ever more impossible demands.
summary: A worker shows his task list to a trash collector, who responds by itemizing the cosmic miracles it would take to finish it.

file: 2002/2002-10-25_assignment_blah blah_make holidays tense_stockholder_stop merger_suing us_dilberts mother.gif
title: Roughing Up Dilbert's Mother

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This stockholder is suing us to stop the merger. Go rough her up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This assignment disturbs me on many levels.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Name one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It will make the holidays tense.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Blah, blah, blah.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a file on a stockholder who is suing the company to stop a merger and orders him to intimidate her. Dilbert objects that the job disturbs him on many levels and is challenged to name one. He reveals the stockholder is his own mother, as shown by her photo, and the Boss dismisses his concern.
punchline: The stockholder Dilbert is told to rough up is his own mother, and his only worry is awkward holidays, which the Boss dismisses as irrelevant.
summary: Ordered to intimidate a litigious shareholder, Dilbert discovers the target is his mother and gets no sympathy from his unfeeling manager.

file: 2002/2002-04-10_copier repair guy_egg carton_fierce paper jam_flirting_good looking_joy.gif
title: Fake Copier Problem For Flirting

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Send a copier repair guy. And make sure he's good-looking.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Because I live in a big tin can and I work in an egg carton. Flirting is the only joy I have.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Nothing's wrong with the copier yet, but I feel a fierce paper jam coming on.

situation: Alice phones a service desk and requests a good-looking copier repair technician. She justifies it by saying her commute and cubicle are so dreary that flirting is her only pleasure. She admits the copier isn't actually broken, but predicts it soon will be.
punchline: Alice is planning to fake or cause a paper jam so she can get a handsome repairman to visit, since flirting is the only bright spot in her bleak work life.
summary: A bored cubicle worker orders up an attractive repairman for a machine that isn't even broken, just so she can have someone to flirt with.

file: 2002/2002-05-16_ceo visit_tour of cubicles_bunch of boxes_pretend to work.gif
title: CEO Declines Cubicle Tour

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The CEO visit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you like a tour of our cubicles?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Why would I want to see a bunch of boxes filled with people pretending to work?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Unless that's the only thing you planned for the first thirty minutes of my visit.

setting: Office, during a visit from the CEO
situation: The Boss eagerly offers the visiting CEO a tour of the cubicle area. The CEO dismisses it as a pointless look at people pretending to work. The CEO then guesses that the tour is the only thing the Boss has planned for the first half hour of the visit, and the Boss looks nervous.
punchline: The CEO sees through the Boss's lack of preparation, and the Boss's anxious grin confirms that a cubicle tour really is all he has planned.
summary: A manager who has nothing prepared for an executive's visit offers a walk past the workstations, and the executive immediately sees through it.

file: 2002/2002-03-21_elbonians_classified ad_nuclear war head_russian craftsmanship_third world countries_slingshot_hundred yards.gif
title: Dogbert Sells Warhead to Elbonians

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: We saw your classified ad for a nuclear warhead.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's genuine Russian craftsmanship, ideal for menacing other third-world countries.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Sweet.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Our slingshot can fling this a hundred yards. Is that enough?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's plenty.

setting: Dogbert's home doorway and living area
situation: Two hooded Elbonians answer Dogbert's classified ad and come to buy a nuclear warhead. Dogbert pitches it as Russian craftsmanship ideal for menacing neighboring countries, and the buyers explain that their only delivery system is a slingshot with a range of a hundred yards. Dogbert happily accepts their cash.
punchline: Dogbert will sell a nuclear weapon to anyone with money, even buyers whose primitive slingshot range means they would blow themselves up, and he doesn't care.
summary: A scheming dog sells an atomic bomb to a pair of impoverished foreigners who plan to launch it with a slingshot.

file: 2002/2002-01-01_winning bid contract_read the minds_competetors_bid lower_blocked by dense mass.gif
title: Mind-Reading the Competition's Bid

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I want you to put together the winning bid for this contract.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No problem. I'll just read the minds of our competitors and bid lower.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm picking up something now... but it's partly blocked by a dense mass.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to put together the winning bid for a contract. Dilbert sarcastically says he will simply read the competitors' minds and undercut them. He then pretends to be telepathically receiving something, while the Boss stands in front of him.
punchline: Dilbert implies his telepathy is being blocked by the Boss's dense head, insulting the Boss's intelligence while mocking the unrealistic expectation of knowing competitors' bids.
summary: Asked to guarantee a winning bid, Dilbert feigns psychic powers and blames his poor reception on his boss's thick skull.

file: 2002/2002-05-29_find calling_life and waste_metal detector_no to bottle cap_priceless treasure.gif
title: Wally's Metal Detector Calling

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, what do you expect to find here with a metal detector?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My first choice is some sort of priceless treasure. But I wouldn't say no to a bottle cap.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I finally find my calling in life and I waste all day explaining it.

situation: Alice asks Wally what he hopes to find while he sweeps the ground with a metal detector and headphones. Wally says he'd love a priceless treasure but would settle for a bottle cap. In the last panel he thinks to himself that he has finally found his calling but loses the whole day explaining it.
punchline: Wally has found a hobby he loves, but the only thing it produces is having to justify it to coworkers, which defeats the point of his day of leisure.
summary: Wally pursues his new passion for metal detecting but is frustrated that he must spend the day answering a coworker's questions about it.

file: 2002/2002-09-07_customer satisfaction_shows improvement_focus group_attacked researchers_two pencils_premeditated.gif
title: Violent Focus Group Counts as Improvement

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our survey of customer satisfaction shows improvement.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The focus group spontaneously attacked our researchers using number two pencils as shivs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's an improvement?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Last year the attack was premeditated.

situation: The Boss reads out the results of a customer satisfaction survey, claiming it shows improvement. He then describes a focus group that violently attacked researchers with pencils. When Dilbert questions how that is an improvement, the Boss explains that last year's attack was planned in advance.
punchline: Customers are so hostile that a spontaneous stabbing attack counts as progress over a premeditated one, showing how management spins terrible news as success.
summary: A manager cheerfully reports that angry test customers now lash out on impulse rather than by plan, and calls that better.

file: 2002/2002-10-05_strategy council_form a comittee_produce document_team_create council_ignores document_business.gif
title: A Team to Create a Council

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, put together a team to decide who'll be on the strategy council.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You want me to form a committee to create a committee that will produce a document that will be ignored?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, it's a team to create a council.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can I be on the team that ignores the document?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss tells Dilbert to assemble a team to choose the members of a strategy council. Dilbert sums it up as a chain of committees ending in a document nobody will read, and the Boss pedantically corrects the terminology. Wally then asks to join the team that ignores the document.
punchline: The layers of teams, committees and councils produce only a document that everyone will ignore, and Wally eagerly volunteers for the one role that involves no actual work.
summary: A manager's request for yet another layer of bureaucratic groups prompts a sarcastic summary and a lazy volunteer.

file: 2002/2002-05-01_dont email_cucbilce_manage and review_reveiwed_can't release.gif
title: Boss Micromanages Dilbert's Walk Route

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't e-mail your answer to my boss until I've reviewed it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um...okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I walk to my cubicle now or would you like to review the route first?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now that you mentioned it, I can't release.

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert not to email his answer to the Boss's own boss until the Boss has reviewed it. Dilbert sarcastically asks whether he should also have his walking route to his cubicle reviewed. The Boss takes the sarcasm seriously and says he can't let Dilbert leave yet.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic jab at micromanagement backfires because the Boss takes it as a genuinely good idea and extends his control even further.
summary: A manager insists on vetting an email, and when his employee mockingly offers up his walking route for approval, the manager decides he needs to approve that too.

file: 2002/2002-12-08_great vacation_beautiful sunsets_amazing food_descriptions_serve no purpose_selfish attempt_trigger memories.gif
title: Dilbert Dodges Vacation Photo Slideshow

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My vacation was great!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The sunsets were beautiful. The food was amazing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Descriptions of your vacation serve no purpose.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can neither see the sunsets nor taste the food.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It appears to be a selfish attempt to trigger happy memories for yourself at my expense.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Okay, buster! When my seven rolls of film get developed...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're out of the loop!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That worked out better than I hoped.

situation: A coworker returns from vacation and starts describing the sunsets and food. Dilbert coldly points out that her descriptions are pointless and only serve to make herself feel good. Offended, she threatens to show him her seven rolls of vacation film, then reverses herself and cuts him out of the loop, which is exactly what Dilbert wanted.
punchline: Dilbert's blunt rudeness was a deliberate ploy to escape being subjected to her vacation photos, and her angry retaliation of excluding him gave him the outcome he wanted.
summary: By picking apart a colleague's holiday small talk, Dilbert provokes her into withholding her vacation pictures, dodging a dreaded slideshow.

file: 2002/2002-04-06_safety tip_bend knees_bang head_art or science.gif
title: Boss Forgets Managing Art Versus Science

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Safety tip of the day:

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Always bend your knees when banging your head against a wall.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't remember if managing is an art or a science.

situation: The Boss sits at his desk typing at his computer while a voice delivers a 'safety tip of the day' about bending your knees when banging your head against a wall. In the final panel the Boss stands in a doorway, pointing, and wonders in a thought bubble whether managing is an art or a science.
punchline: The safety tip implies that working under this boss is so frustrating that employees habitually bang their heads against walls, while the Boss cluelessly muses about the nature of his own management.
summary: A sarcastic safety announcement about head-banging precedes the oblivious Boss pondering the philosophy of management.

file: 2002/2002-10-23_investment baker_hired wesel_media questions_stock holders_good for stcokholders_parking lot.gif
title: Weasel Teaches Boss Media Answers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Investment Banker

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I hired a weasel to teach you how to answer media questions.

transcript.speaker: Weasel
transcript.text: No matter what the reporters ask, always give the same answer: "It will be good for stockholders."

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Is it true that you ran over a stockholder in the parking lot?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It'll be good for him.

setting: Executive office conference table, then a press scrum
situation: Dogbert, working as an investment banker, hires a weasel to coach the Boss on handling media questions. The weasel instructs him to give the same answer to every question: that it will be good for stockholders. When reporters ask if he ran over a stockholder in the parking lot, the Boss robotically repeats the canned line.
punchline: The Boss applies the scripted corporate talking point so mindlessly that he implies running over a stockholder will be good for that stockholder.
summary: A coached executive parrots his one approved answer and ends up spinning a parking-lot hit-and-run as a benefit to the victim.

file: 2002/2002-04-19_done in 30days_faster than light_discover doorway_sounds iffy_being flexible.gif
title: Time Travel Through a Black Hole

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you get this done in thirty days?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes, absolutely.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We'll just travel faster than light to a black hole and discover a doorway in time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds iffy.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Excuse me for being flexible.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker whether a project can be finished within thirty days. The coworker confidently says yes, then explains the plan depends on faster-than-light travel to a black hole to find a doorway in time. When Dilbert calls this iffy, the coworker sarcastically claims to be merely flexible.
punchline: Agreeing to an impossible deadline requires a ridiculous plan, and the coworker mocks Dilbert's reasonable doubt by passing off absurdity as flexibility.
summary: Pressed to commit to a tight schedule, a coworker proposes bending the laws of physics and then bristles when his plan is questioned.

file: 2002/2002-02-11_glass walled conference room_main lobby_fish bowl_attractive employees_send opinion_convene tribunal.gif
title: Fish Bowl Reserved for Attractive Employees

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carol, I need to reserve the glass-walled conference room by the main lobby.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The "fish bowl" is only available to attractive employees. We don't want to scare visitors.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want a second opinion.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Very well. I'll convene the tribunal of admin assistants.

setting: Office cubicle area near Carol's desk
situation: Dilbert asks Carol, the administrative assistant, to book the glass-walled conference room by the main lobby. She tells him it is reserved for attractive employees so visitors aren't frightened, and when he asks for a second opinion she offers to convene a tribunal of admin assistants to judge his looks.
punchline: Carol bluntly implies Dilbert is too unattractive to use the visible conference room, and his request for a second opinion just invites a panel of admin assistants to confirm the insult.
summary: An office assistant gatekeeps a showcase meeting room by appearance, and the employee's appeal only subjects him to a panel of peers who will judge him.

file: 2002/2002-01-23_dilbert sales guy_card_no correct info_new ones_costs money_clout_company_buy something_business.gif
title: Dilbert's Incorrect Business Card

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert the Sales Guy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's my card. None of the information is correct.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Why don't you get new ones?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That costs money.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: You must have a lot of clout in your company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up and buy something.

setting: A business meeting between a salesperson and a customer
situation: Dilbert, acting as a salesman, hands a customer his business card and admits that none of the information on it is correct. The customer asks why he doesn't print new ones, and Dilbert says it costs money. When the customer sarcastically remarks that Dilbert must have a lot of clout in his company, Dilbert tells him to shut up and buy something.
punchline: Dilbert's company is so cheap that it won't reprint outdated business cards, and the customer's sarcastic remark about clout gets an abrasive sales pitch in return.
summary: A salesman shrugs off his useless business card with a cost-cutting excuse, then brusquely pushes the mocking customer to make a purchase.

file: 2002/2002-11-25_headphones in offcie_humming_wishing luck_inconsiderate_drumming fingers.gif
title: Headphones License to Be Annoying

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: From now on, I plan to wear headphones in the office.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll be drumming my fingers and humming all day. I might even whistle.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't hear you, but I assume you're wishing me luck.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Inconsiderate #%*!$

situation: Wally tells Dilbert he plans to wear headphones at work. He then announces he will drum his fingers, hum and maybe whistle all day. With the headphones on, Wally cheerfully says he can't hear Dilbert's reply and assumes it is good wishes, while Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, mutters an obscene insult.
punchline: Wally uses headphones as an excuse to be as noisy as he likes, while pretending Dilbert's angry reaction must be well-wishing, since he can't hear it.
summary: A coworker puts on headphones so he can annoy everyone around him with noise without having to hear their complaints.

file: 2002/2002-02-19_totally safe_nuclear power plant_elbonia_slacve labor_woo-hoo.gif
title: Safest Nuclear Plant Goes to Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our assignment is to design a totally safe nuclear power plant.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Let's put it in Elbonia. That seems safe to me.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Our offer of cheerful slave labor paid off!

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Woo-hoo!!

setting: Conference room, then a muddy Elbonian village
situation: At a meeting, Dilbert announces the team must design a totally safe nuclear power plant. A bald colleague suggests building it in Elbonia because that seems safe to him. In the final panel, mud-covered Elbonians celebrate that their offer of cheerful slave labor has won them the contract.
punchline: The team's idea of a 'safe' plant is simply to put it somewhere far away where any disaster would harm only someone else, and the Elbonians are delighted to supply cheap labor.
summary: Engineers asked to make a nuclear plant safe decide the simplest solution is to build it in a distant, impoverished country.

file: 2002/2002-02-12_efficient_glass walled room_name of case_too unattractive_tribunal of admin. assistants_verdict_humanity.gif
title: Tribunal Names Verdict in Case

transcript.speaker: Admin Assistant
transcript.text: The Tribunal of Admin Assistants will hear the case of...

transcript.speaker: Admin Assistant
transcript.text: The man who is too unattractive to use the glass-walled conference room versus humanity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You put the verdict in the name of the case!

transcript.speaker: Admin Assistant
transcript.text: We're efficient.

setting: Courtroom where a tribunal of administrative assistants sits as the jury
situation: Dilbert stands before a tribunal of admin assistants who announce the case they are about to hear. The case name turns out to be 'The man who is too unattractive to use the glass-walled conference room versus humanity.' Dilbert protests that the verdict is already built into the case title, and the admin assistant calmly replies that they are being efficient.
punchline: The admin assistants have already decided Dilbert is guilty of being too unattractive, so they cut the trial short by embedding the verdict in the case name and call it efficiency.
summary: Dilbert faces a jury of admin assistants whose case title gives away its own conclusion, which they shrug off as streamlined proceedings.

file: 2002/2002-05-07_successful fish market_inspirational book_characters_book_title characters_depressing.gif
title: Inspirational Book Characters Get Eaten

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm giving everyone on my staff this inspirational book about a successful fish market!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to be like the characters in the book.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The title characters get captured, tossed around and eaten.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Depressing.

situation: The Boss hands out a motivational book about a successful fish market and tells his staff to emulate its characters. Wally, reading it, points out that the title characters are fish who get captured, tossed around and eaten. Dilbert, also reading, remarks that it's depressing.
punchline: The boss's chosen role models in the inspirational book are fish that get caught and eaten, which mirrors how the employees are treated and makes the advice unintentionally grim.
summary: A manager passes out a feel-good business book, but his employees discover its heroes are fish destined for the dinner table.

file: 2002/2002-11-30_doctor is vet_military service_rubs belly.gif
title: Boss's Doctor Is Actually a Vet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is a guess, but I think your doctor is a vet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know about his military service. I just know he has great cookies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I like it when he rubs my belly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know something you don't know.

situation: The Boss is wearing a plastic cone around his head and has his arm in a sling. Dilbert guesses that the Boss's doctor is a veterinarian, and the Boss misunderstands, thinking Dilbert means a military veteran. The Boss cheerfully mentions the doctor's cookies and belly rubs, and Dilbert is left holding the secret that the Boss has been treated like a pet.
punchline: The Boss doesn't realize his doctor is a veterinarian who has been treating him like an animal, as shown by the cone, the cookies and the belly rubs.
summary: A cone-wearing boss proudly praises his doctor's treats and belly rubs without realizing he has been seeing a veterinarian.

file: 2002/2002-10-03_win- win scenarios_customer focused_solutions_actual prodcut_sell_partner_shovel.gif
title: Vendor Won't Say What They Sell

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: We provide win-win scenarios and customer-focused solutions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh... okay... But what is the actual product or service you sell?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: We don't sell; we partner.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't buy; I shovel.

situation: A salesman in a green jacket pitches Dilbert using vague buzzwords about win-win scenarios and customer-focused solutions. When Dilbert asks what product or service is actually being sold, the salesman replies that they don't sell, they partner. Dilbert answers that he doesn't buy, he shovels.
punchline: Dilbert mocks the salesman's evasive buzzword jargon by answering in kind with an equally meaningless but dismissive phrase, implying he is tossing the nonsense aside like manure.
summary: A vendor hides behind empty business slang rather than naming what he is selling, so Dilbert fires back with a sarcastic slogan of his own.

file: 2002/2002-11-11_need this afternoon_shirt timer_sit in this chaor_move arms_hesitate to ask_itch_awkward place.gif
title: Short-Timer's Awkward Itch Request

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And I need it this afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Forget it! I'm a short-timer.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I plan to sit in this chair and not move my arms or legs for a week. After that, I'll never work another day!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I hesitate to ask this, but I have an itch in an awkward place.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker, Phil, to do a task by this afternoon. Phil refuses because he is about to retire and announces he will sit motionless in his chair for a week until his last day. He then undercuts his plan by asking Dilbert to scratch an itch in an awkward place.
punchline: Phil's vow to do absolutely nothing for a week immediately backfires, since he is so committed to inactivity that he needs Dilbert to scratch his itch.
summary: A soon-to-retire coworker vows total immobility until his last day, then recruits the person he just refused to help with a very personal favor.

file: 2002/2002-09-10_new ceo_charisma_miracle worker_emptied wallte_gave back_classy.gif
title: Robbed by a Charismatic CEO

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like our new CEO. He has charisma.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The man sure knows how to rob. He's a miracle worker with duct tape.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He even gave me back my emptied wallet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Classy move.

situation: Dilbert and Wally stand with their hands bound and Wally wrapped in duct tape, having apparently been robbed by the new CEO. Dilbert praises the CEO's charisma while Wally admires his skill at robbing and taping people up. Wally notes that the CEO even returned his emptied wallet, and Dilbert calls it a classy move.
punchline: The new CEO is literally a robber, and the victims are praising his charisma and manners, mocking how employees admire executives who take everything from them as long as they do it with style.
summary: Two bound and robbed employees compliment their new chief executive's charm and good manners while he strips them of their money.

file: 2002/2002-08-29_evolving_sunlight_sensitive_attitude_zit_psychology.gif
title: Bob the Dinosaur Evolves an Eye

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, Bob. I haven't seen you lately.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I was doing some evolving.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I noticed I have a zit that's sensitive to sunlight. I'm hoping it becomes an eye.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like your attitude.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Try to sneak up on me.

setting: Office, with Dilbert and Bob sitting at a table holding coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert greets Bob the dinosaur, whom he hasn't seen in a while, and Bob explains he has been busy evolving. Bob says he has a zit sensitive to sunlight and hopes it will turn into an eye. Dilbert admires his attitude, and Bob confidently dares him to sneak up on him.
punchline: Bob's optimistic belief that a light-sensitive zit will become a working eye is a comically naive, wishful take on evolution, and his cocky challenge to sneak up on him is premature since the eye doesn't exist yet.
summary: A dinosaur coworker cheerfully claims he is evolving a new eye from a sunburned pimple and boasts that nobody could surprise him.

file: 2002/2002-09-29_be there minute_sniffing_cough_cooties_direct hot_unclean_bugs_sneezed_motivation_looks like.gif
title: Boss Coughs, Carol Flees Germs

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Tell everyone I'll be there in a minute.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sniff

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What's all that sniffing about? Do you have a cold?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Little one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mmph

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Cough

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I took a direct hit!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The cooties are burrowing into my skin.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm unclean!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope that's what motivation looks like.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Close enough.

setting: Office hallway outside a meeting room
situation: Carol tells the Boss she'll join the meeting shortly, then notices he is sniffling and asks if he has a cold. He suppresses a sneeze and then coughs directly at her, and she panics, convinced she is covered in germs, and runs off screaming. The Boss then hopes her reaction is what motivation looks like, and Catbert, lurking at the bottom, agrees.
punchline: The Boss mistakes Carol's germ-phobic panic for motivated enthusiasm, and Catbert sarcastically confirms it is close enough, as fear is the Boss's idea of motivation.
summary: A germ-fearing employee bolts in terror after her sick manager coughs on her, and he misreads her frantic dash as a sign of drive.

file: 2002/2002-11-22_turned into sheep_wear as sweater_advice not ridicule_pushy sheep_bright side_dilberts mother.gif
title: Dogbert Turned Into Sheep, Mocked

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...And the next thing I knew, I'd been turned into a sheep.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: On the bright side, I won't need to remind you to wear a sweater.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was hoping for advice, not ridicule.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: No one likes a pushy sheep.

setting: A kitchen, where Dilbert's mother is preparing food at the counter
situation: Dogbert, dressed in a sheep costume or transformed into a sheep, tells Dilbert's mother about his strange misfortune while she chops food in the kitchen. She responds with teasing jokes about wearing a sweater instead of offering sympathy. When Dogbert complains that he wanted advice, she retorts that nobody likes a pushy sheep.
punchline: Instead of giving sympathetic advice, Dilbert's mother heckles Dogbert's sheep predicament with sarcastic jokes, ending by calling him a pushy sheep, which turns his usual domineering personality into a woolly insult.
summary: A woolly Dogbert seeks guidance from a kitchen-bound motherly figure, who answers every complaint with a quip about his new fleece.

file: 2002/2002-03-01_demonstrate_life to have meaning_wrong place_can't do that_meeting_presentation_business.gif
title: Demonstrating What We Can't Do

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to demonstrate some things we can't do.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I don't care about things you can't do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know, but it makes a better demonstration this way.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I want my life to have meaning!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You came to the wrong place.

transcript.speaker: Sign on screen
transcript.text: Can't do that.

setting: Conference room during a product demonstration
situation: Dilbert sits at a laptop in a meeting and announces he will demonstrate things the product cannot do. The customer objects that he only cares about what it can do, but Dilbert says the negative demo works better. The customer then blurts out that he wants his life to have meaning, and Dilbert says he's in the wrong place.
punchline: The customer's desperate plea for life meaning is met with the same deadpan 'can't do that' as the product's limitations, implying the company offers nothing meaningful.
summary: A tech demo that showcases only failures ends with a despairing customer discovering that the vendor can't fix his existential emptiness either.

file: 2002/2002-06-30_meeting_boss requested_3 weeks_organized_wasting time_meeting about_brew coffeee_exaggerating accomplishments_business.gif
title: Coffee Duty Disguised as Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, can you come with me to a meeting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, no. I'm running this meeting and it took three weeks to get everyone together.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I leave now, sixteen people will be wasting their time.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll cover for you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You will?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sure. Just leave your notes and I'll take care of it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the meeting about?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not exactly a meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need someone to drink the crud on the bottom and then brew a fresh pot.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: All in favor of leaving before he gets back.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It looks like I'll be exaggerating my accomplishments again this year.

setting: Conference room and office coffee area
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to come to a meeting, but Dilbert declines because he is running a meeting that took three weeks to organize. Wally offers to cover, and the Boss reveals his 'meeting' is really a chore to finish the stale coffee and brew a new pot. When Dilbert leaves to do it, the attendees vote to leave before he returns.
punchline: Dilbert's three-week-organized meeting collapses the moment he steps out, so his only real accomplishment is making coffee, which he will have to exaggerate on his review.
summary: A mundane coffee errand for the Boss pulls Dilbert out of his own meeting, which promptly disbands and leaves him with nothing impressive to report.

file: 2002/2002-02-22_working model_test plant design_how big_real one_certificate.gif
title: Tiny Nuclear Plant Model, Tiny Praise

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I built a working model to test my nuclear power plant design.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How big will the real one be?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: About half this size. And it will cost $23 to build.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd give you an attaboy certificate but my printer is out of paper.

situation: Dilbert shows the Boss a small model he built to test his nuclear power plant design. The Boss asks how big the real plant will be, and Dilbert says it will be about half the size of the model and cost only $23 to build. The Boss responds by saying he would give him an attaboy certificate, but his printer is out of paper.
punchline: Dilbert delivers an absurdly cheap, impossibly small solution to a huge engineering problem, and the Boss still withholds even a free, printable bit of recognition with a lame excuse.
summary: An engineer presents a ridiculously cheap miniature reactor design and gets brushed off by a boss too stingy to print a congratulatory certificate.

file: 2002/2002-10-10_25 million dolalrs_rat hole_ride into space_russian rocket_poor_rocket.gif
title: Rich Man's Rat Hole Dilemma

transcript.speaker: Rich Man
transcript.text: I can't decide if I should throw 25 million dollars down a rat hole or...

transcript.speaker: Rich Man
transcript.text: ...buy a ride into space on a Russian rocket ship.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What about the poor?

transcript.speaker: Rich Man
transcript.text: Do they have a rocket?

situation: A wealthy man hugging a huge sack of money stands before Dogbert's 'Rat Hole' desk, weighing whether to waste 25 million dollars on the rat hole or on a ride into space on a Russian rocket. Dogbert suggests giving to the poor, and the rich man responds by asking whether the poor have a rocket.
punchline: Charity is dismissed entirely as a serious option; the rich man treats the poor as just another wasteful alternative and judges them only on whether they offer a rocket ride.
summary: A rich man agonizes over which frivolous way to squander a fortune, and brushes off the idea of helping the needy with a non sequitur about rockets.

file: 2002/2002-10-01_donuts_eat nit wit_nitwit_ogre_poor guy.gif
title: Eating the Nitwit Teammate

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our project team is composed of a nitwit, an ogre, and a #$%!

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Which one of them is the nitwit?

transcript.speaker: Ogre Coworker
transcript.text: You didn't bring donuts. May I eat the nitwit?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Poor guy.

setting: Conference room during a project team meeting
situation: Dilbert describes his project team as a nitwit, an ogre, and a censored insult. A bald coworker asks which one is the nitwit, apparently not realizing it is himself. The ogre coworker, annoyed that no donuts were brought, asks permission to eat the nitwit, and Dilbert agrees.
punchline: The nitwit's question proves he is the nitwit, and the hungry ogre, denied donuts, is granted permission to eat him, to which the victim finally reacts with self-pity.
summary: A clueless teammate fails to realize he has just been labeled the team's fool, and his hungry colleague gets the green light to devour him.

file: 2002/2002-05-08_interpersonal skills_propaganda cd_training cd_intern_looking for self imporvement.gif
title: Training CD Recruits Employee Against Humanity

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I would like to improve my interpersonal skills.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Take this training CD back to your cube and go wild.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Humans are weak. Computers are strong. Come, join our side.

setting: Catbert's office and the employee's cubicle
situation: An employee asks Catbert, the evil HR director, for help improving his interpersonal skills. Catbert hands him a training CD to take back to his cubicle. When the employee plays it, the computer delivers a message urging him to abandon humanity and side with the machines.
punchline: The 'interpersonal skills' CD is actually machine propaganda, so Catbert has tricked the employee into cutting himself off from people and joining the computers.
summary: A worker seeking to get along better with colleagues is handed a disc by the malicious HR cat that turns out to be a recruitment pitch from the machines.

file: 2002/2002-04-21_50 management_interpretor_jargin_languages_mumble_mumble mumble_pointy haired dialct.gif
title: Boss Mumbles, Interpreter Mistranslates Instructions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...And the most critical part of your objective is...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mumble mummble mumble.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mumble mummble mummble.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be right back. I need an interpreter who speaks mumble.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is Allen. He speaks fifty management languages including jargon, weaselese and mumble.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mumble mumble mumble mumble.

transcript.speaker: Allen
transcript.text: Mumble mumble mumble mumble.

transcript.speaker: Allen
transcript.text: I'm a bit rusty with the Pointy-Haired dialect but I think he wants you to line dance in a gazebo.

situation: The Boss tries to explain the most critical part of Dilbert's objective but only mumbles unintelligibly. When Dilbert can't understand him, the Boss fetches Allen, an interpreter fluent in fifty management languages. Allen mumbles back and offers a bizarre translation of the Boss's instructions.
punchline: Even a professional interpreter of management-speak can only guess at the Boss's meaning, and his guess, that Dilbert should line dance in a gazebo, is absurd, implying the Boss's directives are meaningless nonsense.
summary: A manager who can't communicate clearly brings in a specialist translator, who then deciphers his garbled speech as an utterly ridiculous task.

file: 2002/2002-12-14_rip out ego_put in box_rot_dead_envy dead_career day_afraid to work.gif
title: Career Day Horror Story

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then they rip out your ego and they put you in a box until you rot!!

transcript.speaker: Child
transcript.text: Gaaa!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll never know if you're dead or if you're simply envying the dead!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How was "Career Day"?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Kids these days are afraid of work.

setting: A classroom during career day, then the office break area
situation: The Boss speaks to a group of children at career day and terrifies them with a grim description of working life, including losing your ego and being boxed up until you rot. Afterward, Dilbert asks how it went, and the Boss complains that kids are afraid of work, oblivious to the fact that he caused it.
punchline: The Boss's horrifying and honest description of corporate life scared the kids, yet he blames them for being afraid of work instead of recognizing his own role.
summary: A manager traumatizes schoolchildren with a bleak account of office life and then wonders why the next generation dreads employment.

file: 2002/2002-10-27_epic year_unethical behavior_rebarnding_hired dogcart consulting_small improvements_rename company_stinking weasel_slogan_steal_rob_corruption_hiring pirate_diseased parrot.gif
title: Rebranding After Unethical Year

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks to an epic year of unethical behavior...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to do some rebranding so that no one knows who we are.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired the Dogbert Consulting Company to help.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can't fix your image all at once. I recommend starting with small improvements.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: First, rename the company to Stinkingweasels Inc.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The new slogan will be "We steal in ways you've never even heard of."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For your spokesperson, I recommend hiring a pirate with a diseased parrot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have standards.

transcript.speaker: Parrot
transcript.text: Cough

situation: After a year of unethical behavior, The Boss presents a declining chart and says the company needs rebranding so nobody recognizes it. Consultant Dogbert recommends a deliberately honest new name, slogan and spokesperson. The Boss rejects the pirate with a diseased parrot, claiming the company has standards, while holding a bag of money.
punchline: The Boss claims the company has standards while openly planning to hide its unethical behavior, holding a money bag next to the pirate he rejects.
summary: A disgraced company's consultant suggests rebranding that openly admits its thievery, and the boss draws the line only at a pirate mascot.

file: 2002/2002-07-20_accountants are weasels_defective_dilmom_make money_sell t shirts_selling defects_wesel soup.gif
title: Weasel Accountants and Weasel Soup

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our accountants are weasels. They let us go bankrupt so they could sell T-shirts that say, "I'm with Bankrupt."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Didn't your company make all of its money selling products you knew were defective?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Just stir your cauldron, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Ironically, we're having weasel soup.

situation: Dilbert complains to his mother, who is cooking at the stove, that his company's accountants let it go bankrupt just so they could sell T-shirts about it. His mom points out that the company made its money selling products it knew were defective. Dilbert tells her to just stir her cauldron, and she announces that they are having weasel soup.
punchline: Dilbert's mom deflates his complaint by noting the company was selling known-defective products, then caps it off by serving soup made from weasels, the very creatures Dilbert just called his accountants.
summary: A man grumbles about his scheming accountants while his mother, stirring a pot, points out his employer's own shady business and then reveals dinner is made of weasels.

file: 2002/2002-02-04_tech support_software is worn_typing too hard_decaf_paint walls_stop gym_holistic tec support_read more.gif
title: Dogbert's Holistic Tech Support Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your software is worn out. You must be typing too hard.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Switch to decaf, paint your walls pink and stop going to the gym.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've never heard of holistic tech support.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should read more.

setting: Tech support desk in an office
situation: Dogbert, wearing a headset at a tech support desk, tells a caller that their software is worn out from typing too hard. He then prescribes absurd lifestyle changes like switching to decaf, painting walls pink and quitting the gym. Dilbert stands by, puzzled, and says he has never heard of holistic tech support, and Dogbert replies that he should read more.
punchline: Dogbert gives nonsensical wellness advice as tech support and, when challenged, brushes off the criticism by implying Dilbert is simply uninformed.
summary: A tech support agent blames a user's broken software on bad habits and prescribes lifestyle changes, then dismisses a skeptical colleague by suggesting he's poorly read.

file: 2002/2002-08-31_evolving zit_third eye_cosmic reasons_dinosaur_topical antibiotics_tivo.gif
title: Dinosaur Evolves Zit Into Third Eye

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur 1
transcript.text: Hello, Bob. I hear you're evolving a zit into a third eye, trying to get an advantage.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Gaaa!! No, it's only for cosmetic reasons, I swear!!

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur 1
transcript.text: Hmm...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wanna watch a dinosaur be forced to use topical antibiotics?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Gaaa!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I have "TiVo".

setting: A prehistoric scene with dinosaurs, then Dilbert's living room couch watching TV
situation: One dinosaur confronts Bob, accusing him of evolving a zit into a third eye to gain a competitive advantage. Bob panics and insists it is purely cosmetic. The scene is revealed to be on Dilbert's TV, where Dogbert offers to watch the dinosaur suffer through topical antibiotics, and Dilbert declines because he has TiVo.
punchline: Dilbert turns down Dogbert's offer of watching a dinosaur suffer, because he has TiVo, implying he has something better to watch and skipping the show is easy.
summary: A scaly accuser calls out a nervous reptile for growing a bonus eye from a pimple, while two viewers on a couch decide they would rather use their video recorder than watch the cruelty.

file: 2002/2002-01-05_paper weight_mission statement_sun_fire_cubicle fire_mug_water_shards.gif
title: Mission Statement Paperweight Sets Cubicle Ablaze

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I left my mission statement paperweight in the sun and it set my cubicle on fire.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I tried to douse it using my "We Are Quality" mug but the handle broke and I got shards.

situation: A scorched, smoking, disheveled coworker arrives late to a meeting where Dilbert and Wally are already seated. He explains that a mission statement paperweight left in the sun started a fire in his cubicle. His attempt to put it out with a "We Are Quality" mug failed when the handle broke.
punchline: Corporate mission statement trinkets are not only useless but actively dangerous, and the "We Are Quality" mug is so poorly made that it breaks when needed.
