summary: A singed latecomer explains that his motivational desk gear caused a fire and then failed to put it out.

file: 2002/2002-04-08_good news_promoting work_pay and title_promotion_scaring me.gif
title: Promotion That Means More Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news, Dilbert. I'm promoting you to more work!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's the same pay and title. But it must be good because I called it a promotion and I'm smiling!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Still... smiling... good... news...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're scaring me.

situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert that he is being 'promoted', but it turns out to mean only more work with no change in pay or title. The Boss insists it must be good news because he used the word promotion and is smiling, then holds a strained grin while Dilbert watches uneasily.
punchline: The Boss tries to make a pay-free workload increase sound like good news by relabeling it a promotion and forcing a smile, which only frightens Dilbert.
summary: A manager rebrands extra duties as an advancement and keeps a rigid grin to convince his employee it's a reward.

file: 2002/2002-10-21_investment banker_deal sheet_company_defending_trillion doallr_asbestos_lawsuit_no earnings_stock analysts_business.gif
title: Dogbert Pitches Asbestos-Ridden Stock

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the investment banker

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's a deal sheet for a company you should buy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They're defending against a trillion-dollar asbestos lawsuit, and they have no earnings.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But that's okay, because stock analysts don't dig that far into the minutiae.

situation: Dogbert, working as an investment banker, hands a client a deal sheet for a company he should buy. He then reveals the company faces a trillion-dollar asbestos lawsuit and has no earnings. He reassures the client that this is fine because stock analysts never look into such details.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses a catastrophic liability and zero profits as irrelevant because Wall Street analysts only skim the surface, satirizing the superficial research and conflicts of interest behind stock recommendations.
summary: A cynical canine banker sells a client on a disastrous company by noting that the analysts who might expose its flaws never read the fine print.

file: 2002/2002-02-20_nuclear power plant_our process_gather customer requirements_free electricity_mutating_xray vision.gif
title: Nuclear Plant Requirements: Free Electricity, X-Ray Vision

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: None of us has designed a nuclear power plant before but we can figure it out by using our process.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In phase one we will gather customer requirements.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: So... you want free electricity, without mutating, unless the mutation gives you x-ray vision.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yep.

setting: Conference room during a project kickoff meeting
situation: Dilbert tells his team that although none of them has ever designed a nuclear power plant, they can figure it out by following their standard process. He moves on to phase one, gathering customer requirements, and a customer in a blue cap and overalls states his wishes. An engineer repeats them back, and they turn out to be absurd and self-contradictory.
punchline: The team's faith in a generic process despite having no expertise is mocked, as the customer's requirements, free power with no mutations except a useful superpower, prove that requirements gathering can't make up for ignorance or unrealistic expectations.
summary: A team with zero nuclear experience trusts its methodology to build a power plant, only to receive ridiculous wish-list demands from a layperson customer.

file: 2002/2002-05-03_alice performance_needs supervision_protest_evil_purr.gif
title: Catbert's Evil Review Trap

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Write on Alice's performance review, "Needs too much supervision."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: When she goes to your office to protest, say, "See what I mean?"

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ooh! That was so evil I need to purr with my lips!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: P-p-p-urrr p-p-p-urrr p-p-purr

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, advises the Boss to write on Alice's performance review that she needs too much supervision. He then tells the Boss to say 'See what I mean?' when she comes to protest the review. Catbert is so delighted by the trap that he purrs with his lips.
punchline: The criticism is designed so that any attempt by Alice to dispute it becomes proof of the criticism, a no-win catch-22 that Catbert finds deliciously evil.
summary: Catbert coaches the Boss on a rigged evaluation that turns the employee's own complaint into evidence against her, then purrs with glee at his own cruelty.

file: 2002/2002-07-09_boss on vacation_no chair sitting_vacation_in charge.gif
title: Wally Eyes Boss's Forbidden Chair

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, it's your turn to be in charge while I'm on vacation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But whatever you do, do NOT sit in my chair. It wouldn't be right.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ooh-baby! You want some of this. Yes, you do.

situation: The Boss tells Wally he will be in charge during the Boss's vacation, but warns him never to sit in the Boss's chair. As soon as the Boss is gone, Wally, coffee mug in hand, gleefully eyes the big leather chair and talks to it as if it were seducing him.
punchline: Telling Wally not to do something guarantees he will do it, and he is far more excited by the prospect of the boss's chair than by actually being in charge.
summary: A boss leaves a lazy employee in charge with one forbidden rule, and the employee immediately lusts after the off-limits chair.

file: 2002/2002-09-27_one project_finished one_measure worth_number of projects_track roi_losing_competition amongst mothers_dilberts mom.gif
title: Mom Compares Projects, Dilbert Counters

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Why have you only finished one project at work this year? Norma's son did three.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't measure someone's worth by counting the number of projects he does.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Maybe we should track ROI instead.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Why, because you're losing?

setting: Dilbert's mother's dining table at home, then a gathering of older women holding teacups
situation: Dilbert's mother scolds him at the table for finishing only one project this year while a neighbor's son finished three. Dilbert argues that project count is a poor measure of worth. His mom then tells her friends they should track ROI instead, and one of them guesses she is only saying so because her own son is losing the comparison.
punchline: The mother only abandons the project-count metric once it stops favoring her, which shows that the choice of metric depends on who is winning.
summary: A mother brags competitively about her son's achievements, then changes the scoring method the moment her friend's son pulls ahead.

file: 2002/2002-03-25_restructed_repurposed_reassigned_volunteered to quit.gif
title: Ten Seconds to Choose Layoff Euphemism

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, you have ten seconds to decide if you want to be restructured, repurposed or reassigned.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Repurposed! No, wait...restructured...no, reassigned! No, repurposed!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: How many people volunteered to quit and didn't know?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Two out of three!

situation: The Boss gives Ted ten seconds to pick one of three corporate euphemisms: restructured, repurposed or reassigned. Ted panics and flip-flops between the options. Catbert, the evil human resources director, then asks the Boss how many people volunteered to quit without realizing it.
punchline: All three options are disguised ways of getting Ted to quit, and the Boss cheerfully admits that two out of three employees fall for the trick and 'volunteer' to leave.
summary: A manager pressures an employee to pick a fancy-sounding fate, which turns out to be a sneaky way of tricking staff into resigning.

file: 2002/2002-06-27_book_choose good attitude_six months to live_depressed_bad advice_apathetic.gif
title: Boss Prescribes Attitude Book for Dying

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, guy, cheer up. You can choose to have a good attitude!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I just found out I have six months to live.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I'm saying it wrong. Try reading the book yourself.

situation: The Boss cheerfully tells a glum coworker to cheer up and choose a good attitude. The employee replies that he has just learned he has only six months to live. Undeterred, the Boss hands him a self-help book and suggests he read it himself.
punchline: The Boss is so wrapped up in his motivational platitudes that he responds to a terminal diagnosis by blaming his own delivery and pushing a self-help book, showing a total lack of empathy.
summary: A manager's glib advice to stay positive collides with a worker's grim medical news, and he answers by handing over a self-help book.

file: 2002/2002-07-29_face for wrinkles_face is killing me_inject deadly poison_botox_dermal fillers_botchulism.gif
title: Botox Question Gets Insulting Answer

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Do you think I should inject a deadly poison in my face to hide wrinkles?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's only fair that you poison your face, because your face is killing me. Hee hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: The correct answer is "You don't need to."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was your mother a Shar-Pei?

situation: A female coworker with a dark bob haircut and glasses asks Dilbert, who is seated at his computer, whether she should get Botox-style poison injections to hide her wrinkles. Dilbert answers with a cruel joke about her face being killing him. She tells him the polite answer he should have given, and he responds by asking if her mother was a Shar-Pei, a wrinkly dog breed.
punchline: Dilbert completely misses the social cue, doubling down on insulting her appearance by comparing her to a wrinkly dog breed instead of offering the expected reassurance.
summary: Asked for his opinion on cosmetic injections, a socially oblivious engineer responds with back-to-back insults about his coworker's face.

file: 2002/2002-03-30_email_employees_leave too early_menacing pose_more cars in lot_own email_parking lot_business.gif
title: Boss Won't Type His Own Threat

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Dorie, send an e-mail: Employees are leaving work too early.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I want to see more cars in the parking lot after 6 p.m. Otherwise, heads will roll!

transcript.speaker: Dorie
transcript.text: You type your own e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I can't do that and do this menacing pose at the same time.

setting: Office window overlooking the parking lot
situation: The Boss stands at a window looking at a mostly empty parking lot and tells his assistant Dorie to email employees about leaving work too early. He threatens that heads will roll unless more cars are in the lot after 6 p.m. When Dorie tells him to type his own email, he says he can't because he's busy holding his menacing pose.
punchline: The Boss refuses to do a trivial task himself because maintaining a threatening stance supposedly keeps him too occupied, exposing how hollow and theatrical his intimidation is.
summary: A manager demands staff stay later, but when his assistant balks at being his typist, he claims his intimidating posture prevents him from writing the message.

file: 2002/2002-08-22_junk mail_smiling list_letter of validation_existence_clean win.gif
title: Junk Mail Validates Wally's Existence

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've never seen anyone get this excited over a piece of junk mail.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've never been on a mailing list before. This letter is validation of my existence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not addressed to you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll grant you that it's not a clean win.

situation: Wally waves a piece of junk mail excitedly while Dilbert watches. Wally explains that being on a mailing list proves he exists, and Dilbert points out the letter is addressed to someone else. Wally concedes only that it isn't a perfect victory.
punchline: Wally is so desperate for proof that he matters that he treats misdirected junk mail as validation, and he only half-concedes when told it isn't even his.
summary: A man gleefully treats an advertising flyer as proof he is a real person, even though it was meant for somebody else.

file: 2002/2002-11-26_headphones_britney spears_slap him_singing_outloud.gif
title: Headphone Singer Channels Britney Spears

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Oops, I did it again...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: With headphones I sound exactly like Britney Spears.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Oops

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'd slap him but I don't want to touch him.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ooh ooh

situation: A coworker wearing headphones sits at his computer singing Britney Spears out loud, convinced that he sounds just like her. He gets carried away, dancing and singing so enthusiastically that his shirt rides up. Two coworkers watch over the cubicle wall, disgusted by the performance.
punchline: The singer is oblivious to how awful he looks and sounds, while his coworker's line shows she finds him so repellent she wouldn't even touch him to slap him.
summary: A headphone-wearing employee belts out pop hits, certain he's a dead ringer for a pop star, while appalled colleagues look on.

file: 2002/2002-05-06_minutes_meeting_read minutes_irrelevant things said_men are idiots_bad descions_implied_business.gif
title: Meeting Minutes: Men Are Idiots

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, would you read the minutes from our last meeting?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: People said irrelevant things. Bad decisions were made. Men are idiots.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't remember that last part.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It was implied.

situation: The Boss asks Alice to read the minutes from the previous meeting. Alice gives a blunt summary that includes irrelevant remarks, bad decisions, and the statement that men are idiots. The Boss says he doesn't recall that last part, and Alice says it was implied while Wally dozes off.
punchline: Alice's honest minutes record what really happens in meetings, and she justifies her insult by claiming it was implied by everything the men said and did.
summary: A secretary-style recap of a meeting turns into a candid verdict on the men in the room, defended as simply reading between the lines.

file: 2002/2002-10-06_compost_coot_landscaping_leadership skills_listening_long term potential_performance review_rating is feral_squirrely_thesaurus_words_ratings_new words.gif
title: Thesaurus Performance Review for Wally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, it's time for your annual performance review.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: None of my usual words fit your situation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I had to hit the thesaurus pretty hard.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your overall rating is "feral."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your leadership skills are rated "squirrelly."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And your teamwork is a solid "coot."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your long-term potential is to die in the landscaping and become compost.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How'd it go?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I wasn't really listening.

setting: Office cubicle and the boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss conducts Wally's annual performance review and, finding none of his usual words suitable, reads out bizarre thesaurus-derived ratings like "feral," "squirrelly" and "coot." He ends by predicting Wally will die in the landscaping and become compost. Afterward Dilbert asks how it went, and Wally admits he wasn't listening.
punchline: Wally is so disengaged that he tuned out an absurdly insulting review, which fits the review's low expectations and shows how meaningless the process is.
summary: A manager delivers a nonsensical, insult-laden annual review using odd synonyms, and the employee confesses he ignored all of it.

file: 2002/2002-09-05_mouse training_important_meeting_question_silly_pick me_answer_diagram_computer mouse_business.gif
title: Wally Eagerly Volunteers, Trainer Misses

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Who wants to share an opinion on why mouse training is important?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ooh-ooh! Pick me!

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Yes, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No one?

setting: Corporate training room during a mouse training session
situation: A trainer leading a session titled 'Mouse Training' asks the audience to share an opinion on why mouse training is important. Wally excitedly raises his hand and begs to be picked. When the trainer calls on him, Wally can't see anyone left to answer, or the answer is simply that no one cares.
punchline: Wally is so eager to be picked that he waves his hand wildly, but when finally called on he has nothing to say, showing no one in the room has a real opinion on why this pointless training matters.
summary: A trainer's call for opinions on mouse training draws one frantic volunteer who then has nothing to offer.

file: 2002/2002-05-21_demoting to engineer_job to crony_real work_pretend_working_one wally.gif
title: Demoted Boss Needs Wally's Slacking Lessons

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Boss
transcript.text: I'm demoting you to engineer so I can give your current job to one of my cronies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I won't survive. I don't know how to do real work!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, can you teach me how to pretend to be working?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Whoa! There can only be one Wally.

setting: Corporate office and the engineering area
situation: The Boss's own manager demotes him to engineer so a crony can take his management job. The panicked Boss admits he can't do real work, then asks Wally to teach him how to fake it. Wally, the office's master of looking busy, refuses to share his turf.
punchline: Wally's whole identity is pretending to work, so he guards that niche jealously and won't let another slacker compete for it.
summary: A manager stripped of his title begs the office's top idler for tips on faking productivity, only to be turned away as unwanted competition.

file: 2002/2002-06-08_mordac_information services_exceeded_server storage limit_double storage space_mystique_25 cents_preventer of info.gif
title: Mordac Bribed With Quarter

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I am Mordac the Preventer of Information Services. You have exceeded your server storage limit.

transcript.speaker: Woman at desk
transcript.text: Here's 25 cents so you can afford to double my storage space.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I think my mystique just took a hit.

situation: Mordac, the head of Information Services, confronts an employee at her desk and announces she has exceeded her server storage limit. She responds by handing him a quarter, suggesting that is enough to pay for doubling her storage. Mordac, left holding the coin, privately admits his intimidating reputation has been damaged.
punchline: The employee mocks the cost of storage by offering a quarter to double her space, deflating Mordac's usual air of menace and bureaucratic power.
summary: A feared IT gatekeeper's storage-limit threat is undercut when an employee flippantly tosses him pocket change to buy more space.

file: 2002/2002-09-16_reservation_computers are cardboard_props_furniture store_security prurposes_frisk me.gif
title: Cardboard Computers at Elbonia Air

transcript.speaker: Ticket Agent
transcript.text: I don't see your reservation.

transcript.speaker: Ticket Agent
transcript.text: Maybe it's because all of our computers are cardboard props that we stole from a furniture store.

transcript.speaker: Ticket Agent
transcript.text: For security purposes, would you care to frisk me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

setting: Elbonia Air ticket counter, in a muddy Elbonian airport
situation: Dilbert, standing in a barrel in Elbonian mud, tries to check in at the Elbonia Air counter. The veiled agent can't find his reservation and cheerfully admits that the computers are cardboard props stolen from a furniture store. He then offers to let Dilbert frisk him for security purposes, and Dilbert quickly accepts.
punchline: After revealing the airline's operations are completely fake, the agent makes the absurd offer of being frisked, and Dilbert eagerly agrees, treating the one dubious bit of 'security' as a bonus.
summary: An airline clerk in a fictional backwater admits the check-in computers are fake furniture-store props, then offers a pat-down that Dilbert gladly accepts.

file: 2002/2002-12-02_human resources_cubicle_grim reeper_layoffs_stranger_business.gif
title: Grim Reaper Does the Layoffs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Human Resources is sending a designated firer to do layoffs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If a stranger approaches your cubicle, it means you're toast!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

transcript.speaker: Grim Reaper
transcript.text: Hell-o-o-o, Carol.

transcript.speaker: Grim Reaper
transcript.text: Can you show me where Ted sits?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Gaaa!!

setting: Conference room meeting, then Carol's cubicle
situation: The Boss warns his staff in a meeting that Human Resources is sending a designated firer to carry out layoffs, and that a stranger approaching your cubicle means you are about to be fired. The employees panic, and then a hooded Grim Reaper with a scythe appears at Carol's cubicle asking where Ted sits.
punchline: The designated firer is literally the Grim Reaper, and the stranger's polite request for Ted's location shows that layoffs are as deadly as death itself, with Carol terrified in the meantime.
summary: A manager's warning about a layoff hit-man comes true when the angel of death shows up politely hunting for a coworker's desk.

file: 2002/2002-08-20_executive body guard class_pounce_kidnapper_sacrifice yourself_inside help_reimburse.gif
title: Carol Plans Inside Help Class

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I'm sending you to an executive bodyguard class.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll learn how to pounce on a kidnapper and sacrifice yourself to keep me safe.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm taking a class called "Inside Help."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't reimburse for that.

situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol he is sending her to an executive bodyguard class so she can throw herself at any kidnapper and sacrifice herself for him. Carol responds that she is instead taking a class called "Inside Help," implying she would assist a kidnapper. The Boss's only concern is that he can't reimburse the expense.
punchline: Carol hints she'd rather learn to help kidnap her boss than protect him, and the oblivious Boss responds only with a worry about expense reimbursement.
summary: A boss demands his assistant train to take a bullet for him, but she quietly signs up for a course in aiding his abductors, and he frets about the receipts.

file: 2002/2002-07-06_budget_spend it_can't tell budget_whats company strategy.gif
title: Boss Refuses to Reveal Anything

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't tell you how much your budget is, because if I did, you'd try to spend all of it.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Can you tell me when I'm over budget?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, because then you'd know what the budget is.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Can you tell me what our company strategy is?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure. It's... Ha ha ha! Just kidding.

situation: An employee sits across the desk from the Boss and asks about his budget. The Boss refuses to say how much it is, then refuses to say when it's exceeded, and finally pretends he might share the company strategy before laughing it off as a joke.
punchline: The Boss withholds all useful information from his staff, and the strategy question suggests he either has no strategy or would never share it.
summary: A manager stonewalls every question about money and direction, treating basic information as something employees can't be trusted with.

file: 2002/2002-11-12_short timer_chair_offcie_move arms_retirement_good example_piece of work.gif
title: Short-Timer Refuses To Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, go get the short-timer and push his chair to my office.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Is he injured?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, he refuses to move his arms or legs until retirement.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you a good example of what is called a "piece of work"?

transcript.speaker: Short-Timer
transcript.text: Except for the "work" part.

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss orders Asok to fetch an employee nearing retirement and wheel him in on his chair. Asok asks if the man is injured, and the Boss explains he simply refuses to move his arms or legs until he retires. Asok pushes the motionless employee in, and the Boss asks if he is a good example of a "piece of work."
punchline: The short-timer agrees he is a piece of work in the sense of being a character, but not in the sense of actually doing any work, since he has stopped working entirely before retirement.
summary: An employee counting down to retirement has stopped moving altogether, so a junior colleague has to wheel him to the boss, where he cheerfully admits to being all piece and no work.

file: 2002/2002-10-09_rat hole_business plan_pay huge investment fees_money losing_take your money_push in hole.gif
title: Dogbert Sells Rat Hole Investments

transcript.speaker: Investor
transcript.text: May I throw money down the rat hole?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Show me your business plan.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You plan to pay huge investment banking fees to buy a low-margin, money-losing business...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For an extra fee, I'll push you in the hole and take your money.

transcript.speaker: Investor
transcript.text: Oooh, sounds good.

setting: Outdoors at a booth labeled 'Rat Hole', then at Dogbert's desk
situation: An investor carrying a bag of money asks Dogbert, who is manning a booth labeled 'Rat Hole', if he can throw his money down it. Dogbert reviews the business plan and points out it involves paying huge banking fees to buy a money-losing business. He then offers to push the investor into the hole for an extra fee, and the investor eagerly agrees.
punchline: The investor is so determined to waste money on a bad deal that he happily pays extra to be fleeced even more, mocking foolish investors and the fee-hungry investment banking industry.
summary: A willing sucker hands over cash to a dog who cheerfully charges him more and more to squander it on a doomed venture.

file: 2002/2002-09-09_suspicious_new ceo_trailer park_burglar_mergers_acquisitions_accounting_wallet and watch.gif
title: New CEO Is Still a Burglar

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is our new CEO, Rufus T. Skwerrel. His first job was trailer park burglar.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But thanks to a series of mergers and acquisitions, not to mention suspicious accounting, here we are.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you like to say a few words?

transcript.speaker: Rufus T. Skwerrel
transcript.text: Wallet and watch.

setting: Conference room at a company meeting
situation: The Boss introduces the company's new CEO, a striped-shirt, beanie-wearing burglar with a sack, and cheerfully explains that mergers, acquisitions and dubious accounting took him from petty thief to the top job. When invited to say a few words, the CEO pulls a knife and demands wallets and watches from the people at the table.
punchline: The new CEO is literally still a burglar, implying that corporate leadership and mergers-and-acquisitions wealth-building are just robbery in a nicer suit.
summary: A grinning thief in a burglar's outfit gets introduced as the company's new chief executive and promptly mugs his audience.

file: 2002/2002-07-05_improve morale_want drinking enough_coffee meetings_never leave table.gif
title: Boss Needs Coffee Meetings Forever

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm having these coffee meetings to find out how I can improve morale.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My only problem was that I wasn't drinking enough coffee with you. So now I'm good, thanks.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Promise me you'll never leave this table. I can't go back to the way things were.

situation: A balding, bespectacled man sits across a table from The Boss, both holding coffee cups. He explains he's holding coffee meetings to find out how to improve morale, then declares that his only problem was not drinking enough coffee with The Boss. He then begs The Boss to never leave the table so things never return to how they were.
punchline: The man's own morale problem turns out to be a lack of coffee with the boss, and he pleads for the meeting to last forever because his normal workday is so miserable.
summary: A manager's morale-improvement coffee chat reveals that all he needed was a pleasant sit-down, and he dreads returning to his usual routine.

file: 2002/2002-01-04_name the restrooms_goddesses and morons_only one_entered contest.gif
title: Alice Wins Restroom Naming Contest

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The winner of our "Name the Restrooms" contest is Alice...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...for her suggestion of "Goddesses" and "Morons."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're right; I was the only one who would enter that ridiculous contest.

situation: The Boss announces that Alice has won the company's contest to name the restrooms, reading out her winning entries of "Goddesses" for the women's room and "Morons" for the men's. Alice hands over her entry and replies that she was the only person willing to enter such a ridiculous contest. Dilbert and Wally stand by holding coffee mugs.
punchline: Alice's "Goddesses" and "Morons" suggestion is a dig at the men (and perhaps management), and her reply is sarcastic confirmation that she won only because nobody else would take part in such a silly contest.
summary: A boss proudly crowns the winner of a bathroom-naming competition, and she dryly admits she won by default because the idea was too silly for anyone else to bother with.

file: 2002/2002-11-18_customers into sheep_device_buy whatever_free wool_marketing dept.gif
title: Marketing Wants Customers Turned Sheep

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: The marketing department wants you to build a device that turns customers into sheep.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why? So they'll buy whatever we tell them to buy?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: To be honest, we haven't given it much thought beyond free wool.

situation: A man from the marketing department asks Dilbert, the engineer, to build a device that turns customers into sheep. Dilbert guesses the goal is to make customers buy whatever they are told. The marketer admits the plan is not that well thought out and that the main appeal is getting free wool.
punchline: Marketing's absurd request has no strategic purpose at all, since the only benefit they have considered is free wool, which shows how little thought goes into their demands of engineering.
summary: A marketing rep asks an engineer to invent a customer-to-sheep converter and then confesses the only goal is harvesting free wool.

file: 2002/2002-03-27_least expensive vendor_requirements_change mid project_lowest bid_fired later_fired mid project_outplacement service_every sale.gif
title: Fired Now or Fired Later

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: We're the least expensive vendor unless your requirements change mid-project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So...I'll get fired if I don't select the lowest bid, or I'll be fired later when the bills for change orders pour in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I prefer to be fired mid-project.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: We offer outplacement service with every sale.

situation: A vendor salesman pitches his low price to Dilbert, then admits it only holds if the requirements never change. Dilbert realizes he is doomed either way: choosing a pricier bid gets him fired now, and choosing the lowest bid gets him fired when change-order costs balloon. He says he would rather be fired mid-project, and the vendor cheerfully offers outplacement services with every sale.
punchline: The vendor's low bid is a trap of inevitable change orders, and he even sells job-loss assistance as an upsell for the buyer he is setting up to be fired.
summary: A buyer weighing a lowball contractor bid sees that every option ends in his dismissal, and the salesman happily offers to help with the aftermath.

file: 2002/2002-02-25_added coffee_carpet_coffee stain_mans face_miracle_squirrel body.gif
title: Coffee Stain Miracle Gets Squirrel Body

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I found a coffee stain on my carpet that looks like a man's face.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It might be a miracle...or maybe a sign of the end of time.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hope not. I added coffee and gave him a squirrel body.

setting: Conference room table during a lunch break
situation: Dilbert, Alice and Wally sit around a table eating lunch. Wally announces that a coffee stain on his carpet looks like a man's face, and Alice suggests it could be a miracle or an omen of the apocalypse. Wally reveals he doctored the stain by adding more coffee and drawing a squirrel body on it.
punchline: Wally has tampered with a possibly miraculous image by turning it into a squirrel-bodied figure, hoping that his meddling means it is not an apocalyptic sign.
summary: A supposed holy image in a carpet stain turns out to have been casually altered by its owner into something silly.

file: 2002/2002-11-29_stretch first_sprained arm_tv remote control_wally_doctor_medical.gif
title: Wally's Remote Control Injury Explained

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I sprained my arm using the TV remote control.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I tried to change the channel and the volume at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's why you should always stretch first.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, who's your doctor?

situation: Wally, his arm in a sling and his head wrapped in a bulky bandage, tells Dilbert he sprained his arm trying to change the channel and adjust the volume on a TV remote simultaneously. Dilbert sits at his computer and jokes that Wally should have stretched first, then asks who Wally's doctor is.
punchline: Dilbert's question about Wally's doctor implies that the doctor will happily treat any absurd, self-inflicted injury and, more cynically, that Wally's claim is a questionable excuse for a sick day or a medical claim.
summary: A bandaged Wally blames a ridiculous remote-control accident for his injuries while Dilbert dryly asks for the name of the doctor who would believe it.

file: 2002/2002-08-12_study culture_in company_detailed recommendations_docile outcast_drinks brown water_staple tracking device.gif
title: Dogbert Anthropologist Studies Office Culture

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will study the culture in your company and make detailed recommendations.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "The one I call Wally is a docile outcast who eats bananas and drinks brown water."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I staple this tracking device to your ear?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not really.

setting: Corporate office, the Boss's desk and Wally's cubicle
situation: Dogbert, dressed like a field explorer with a pith helmet and backpack, tells the Boss he will study the company's culture as a consultant. He then observes Wally like a wildlife specimen, noting his banana and coffee habits in a notebook. Dogbert asks to staple a tracking device to Wally's ear, and Wally indifferently agrees.
punchline: Wally is so passive and apathetic that he lets himself be tagged like an animal with a stapled tracking device, confirming Dogbert's description of him as docile.
summary: A safari-clad Dogbert treats Wally as a specimen in a nature study and cheerfully tags him, and the lethargic employee barely objects.

file: 2002/2002-04-01_avoid finsihing_surplus employees_wrong about knowing.gif
title: Avoiding Layoffs By Never Finishing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Business is way down. You know what you need to do.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Avoid finishing anything so we never appear to be surplus employees?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe this would be a good time to admit that you were wrong about us knowing.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that business is down and implies the staff should know how to respond. Wally answers that they should avoid finishing any work so they never look like surplus employees. He then suggests the Boss admit he was wrong to assume they knew what to do.
punchline: The Boss expects employees to magically know the right response to a downturn, but Wally's cynical answer shows their instinct is job self-preservation by looking perpetually busy, and he jabs the Boss for his unfounded assumption.
summary: When told business is slumping, a lazy employee proposes keeping projects unfinished to dodge layoffs and then calls out his manager's baseless assumption.

file: 2002/2002-07-03_coffee with boss_one hour_quality time_rather staple skunk_snarky remarks_cutting insulting.gif
title: Coffee With the Boss Dreaded

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I call my idea "Coffee with the Boss." Each employee will get one hour of quality time with me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'd rather staple a skunk to my forehead and go to a trade show for banjo makers.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And yet, it's still better than working, so count me in.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the spirit!

situation: The Boss announces a new one-on-one program called "Coffee with the Boss" and describes it as quality time with each employee. Alice, seated at her desk, insults the idea by saying she would prefer a skunk stapled to her forehead and a banjo makers' trade show. She then reluctantly agrees because it beats working, and the Boss cheerfully takes this as enthusiasm.
punchline: Alice's backhanded acceptance is a thinly veiled insult, but the oblivious Boss mistakes her sarcasm for genuine team spirit.
summary: A manager's cheerful face-time initiative gets a scathing, grudging endorsement from an employee who just wants to avoid real work, and he takes it as praise.

file: 2002/2002-03-17_open door policy_ruining happiness_complain_morale inspiring_body language_protective bubble_stressed out scowl_stop by_insincere.gif
title: Faking an Open Door Policy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My open door policy is ruining my happiness.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People stop by all day long and complain.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can I maintain the morale-inspiring illusion of an open door policy without actually having one?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Use your body language to create a protective bubble of unwelcomeness.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Try this stressed-out scowl.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I poke in my head?

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: Sure. He has an open door policy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a pleasure to see you.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We value your input.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop by any time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ay-yi-yi-yi!!

setting: The Boss's office and the outer office area
situation: The Boss complains to Catbert that his open door policy means employees constantly stop by to complain. Catbert coaches him to scowl so people feel unwelcome while still appearing approachable. When Dilbert pokes his head in, the Boss and Catbert wear frightening scowls while cheerfully saying welcoming words, terrifying him.
punchline: The Boss keeps the appearance of an open door policy by speaking welcoming words while glaring so menacingly that nobody dares come in.
summary: A manager tired of employee complaints learns to look hostile while insisting everyone is welcome, and a visiting engineer flees in fright.

file: 2002/2002-03-07_hostile body language_not allowed_cross arams_stare_move eyebrows_nice day_female_controlling_unconscious emotions.gif
title: Banned From Hostile Body Language

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Someone accused me of having hostile body language.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm not allowed to cross my arms or stare or move my eyebrows or frown.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Have a nice day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too late.

situation: A coworker with big dark hair approaches Dilbert, who is holding a coffee mug, and complains that she was accused of having hostile body language. She lists the gestures she is now forbidden from making, then stiffly wishes him a nice day while still looking tense. Dilbert replies that it's too late.
punchline: Her forced, rigid cheerfulness still comes across as hostile, so Dilbert says his day is already ruined, showing that the HR-style restrictions can't change how she actually feels.
summary: After being reprimanded for unfriendly body language, a coworker rattles off her forbidden gestures and delivers a strained pleasantry that Dilbert deems too little, too late.

file: 2002/2002-11-10_red color_presentation_yellow_set standards_background colors_metero_pointy haired_managing nitwits_ear hole.gif
title: Managers Nitpick Slide Background Color

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And then I would end the presentation with this.

transcript.speaker: Manager 1
transcript.text: Whoa! I don't like the look of that background color.

transcript.speaker: Manager 1
transcript.text: Red says danger. We don't want to scare our customers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Okay. How about yellow?

transcript.speaker: Manager 2
transcript.text: Yellow? Are we saying we're cowards?

transcript.speaker: Manager 1
transcript.text: What we need is a committee to set some standards for background colors.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What we need is a meteor to pulverize you three pointy-haired, micro-managing nitwits.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If you didn't move your mouth, how did it get out?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It came out of my ear hole.

situation: Dilbert presents a slide with a red background and three pointy-haired managers object to the color, first saying red means danger, then that yellow makes them look like cowards. They propose forming a committee to set background color standards. Dilbert wishes aloud for a meteor to destroy them, though it turns out he only thought it, and he jokes that the words came out of his ear hole.
punchline: Dilbert's fantasy of the managers being obliterated by a meteor is only in his head, and he deadpans that the insult escaped through his ear to explain how his unspoken thought was heard.
summary: Meddling managers obsess over the color of a presentation slide until Dilbert's pent-up frustration erupts in a murderous wish he claims leaked out through his ear.

file: 2002/2002-11-08_drop by iq_measure of drop by visitor_stay in cubicle_one hour.gif
title: Drop-By IQ Measures Cubicle Visitors

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've developed a new theory of intelligence that I call "drop-by I.Q."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a measure of how long a drop-by visitor will stay in your cubicle when you're trying to work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: One hour and counting.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: ...and that's why I'm afraid of bananas.

setting: Dilbert's living room couch, then Alice's office cubicle
situation: Dogbert explains to Dilbert a new theory of intelligence he calls drop-by I.Q., based on how long a visitor lingers in your cubicle while you try to work. In the final panel, Alice sits at her desk checking a stopwatch while a coworker with a coffee mug rambles on about his fear of bananas.
punchline: Alice is timing how long a rambling coworker wastes her time, showing that the more oblivious the visitor, the longer he stays, so this 'intelligence' is really a measure of obliviousness.
summary: A dog's theory rating intelligence by how long visitors loiter in your workspace gets a real-world demonstration as a coworker chats pointlessly while his victim times him.

file: 2002/2002-11-17_indecion_intense pressure_impossible before deadline_layers of management._incompetence_odor of doom_scarce and sniff_3d glasses.gif
title: 3-D Schedule Reveals Management Incompetence

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The original schedule looked like this...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One month for a management decision and one year to do the project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The revised schedule is this...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One year of indecision followed by intense pressure to do the impossible before the deadline.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now if you'll each take a pair of 3-D glasses...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can see the layers of management incompetence practically jump out at you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now scratch one of these scented cards to sniff the unmistakable odor of doom.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't smell anything. Is mine broken?

setting: Conference room during a project schedule presentation
situation: Dilbert presents the original and revised project schedules to a group of managers, showing that a one-month decision turned into a year of indecision followed by an impossible deadline. He then hands out 3-D glasses and scented scratch cards so they can see and smell the management incompetence. The Boss, oblivious, only wonders if his scratch card is broken.
punchline: The managers are so incompetent that they fail to notice the insult and can't even smell the 'odor of doom' their own indecision created.
summary: Dilbert uses a gimmicky multimedia presentation to show managers how their delay doomed the project, and they completely miss the point.

file: 2002/2002-05-14_ceo visit_hide in restorrom_too soon_start dream assignment.gif
title: Hiding Wally Before CEO Visit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, our CEO is visiting next week. I want you to hide in the restroom.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's too soon.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's never too soon to start a dream assignment.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Wally that the CEO is visiting next week and orders him to hide in the restroom during the visit. Wally objects that it's too soon, then reveals that he sees the restroom hiding as a dream assignment he's happy to begin right away.
punchline: Wally is delighted to be ordered to hide in the restroom and eager to start immediately, since for a lazy employee that is the perfect job.
summary: A manager sends his slacker employee into hiding for a VIP visit, only to find the man treats the order as a coveted assignment to begin at once.

file: 2002/2002-06-11_new version_step backward_quality_reliability_irrational need_latest version software_home and office.gif
title: Selling Worse Software to Upgrade Addicts

transcript.speaker: Software Salesman
transcript.text: Our new version is a step backward in quality and reliability.

transcript.speaker: Software Salesman
transcript.text: We're counting on your irrational need to have the latest version of every software product.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate your weasel guts... but I'll take one for home and one for the office.

setting: Office desk during a sales pitch
situation: A software salesman across the desk from Dilbert openly admits that his company's new version is worse in quality and reliability than the old one. He says they are banking on customers' compulsion to own every latest release. Dilbert, holding the software box, grudgingly agrees to buy two copies anyway.
punchline: Dilbert knows he is being cynically exploited by a vendor that admits its product is worse, yet his compulsion to upgrade makes him buy two copies anyway.
summary: A candid vendor admits his product has gotten worse but bets on customers' upgrade compulsion, and Dilbert proves him right while insulting him.

file: 2002/2002-10-29_dogebrt attorney_best defense_ignorant_stock manipulation_convince judge_dumber than chocolate_outdoor las vegas_photo convention.gif
title: Dogbert's Dumber-Than-Chocolate-Pants Defense

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Attorney

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your best defense is to say you were ignorant of your company's stock manipulation.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We need to convince a judge that you're dumber than chocolate pants at an outdoor Las Vegas photography convention.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't get that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: E-e-excellent.

situation: Dogbert, acting as an attorney, advises his client, the Pointy-Haired Boss, that his best legal defense against stock manipulation charges is to claim ignorance. He says they must convince a judge the Boss is dumber than a bizarre, absurd comparison. The Boss doesn't understand the comparison.
punchline: The Boss's confusion at the nonsensical insult shows he is exactly as dim as Dogbert claims, which makes the ignorance defense look very convincing.
summary: A lawyer dog proposes pleading stupidity to a judge, and his client's bafflement at the weird insult proves the plan will work.

file: 2002/2002-02-23_elbonia_oversee construction_nuclear power plant_first order_uranium_director of security.gif
title: Pig Ate the Uranium Security

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm here to oversee construction of the nuclear power plant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The first order of business is security for the uranium.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: A pig ate it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?! I demand to see your director of security!

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: You'll have to wait; the pig ate him too.

setting: Muddy landscape in Elbonia with mud huts in the background
situation: Dilbert arrives in Elbonia to oversee construction of a nuclear power plant and asks about security for the uranium. The tall-hatted Elbonians casually tell him a pig ate the uranium. When he demands to see the director of security, he learns the pig ate him too.
punchline: Elbonia's security is so hopeless that a pig has consumed both the nuclear material and the person responsible for guarding it, which the locals report in a matter-of-fact way.
summary: An engineer sent to a backward country to build a reactor discovers that a hungry animal has swallowed the radioactive fuel and the official in charge of protecting it.

file: 2002/2002-02-28_non monetary rewards_program_self mentoring_talk to yourself.gif
title: Self-Mentoring: Management's Free Reward

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I'm putting you on our special self-mentoring program.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you have any questions whatsoever, feel free to talk to yourself.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm the master of non-monetary rewards.

situation: The Boss tells Asok he is being enrolled in a special self-mentoring program, standing over him at his computer. He explains that if Asok has any questions, he should simply talk to himself. In the last panel the Boss walks away and thinks proudly about how good he is at handing out rewards that cost nothing.
punchline: The 'self-mentoring program' is just a way for the Boss to avoid providing any real mentoring or money, and he smugly congratulates himself for giving employees worthless perks.
summary: A manager passes off an employee's lack of guidance as a special program, then privately boasts about how cheaply he rewards staff.

file: 2002/2002-09-21_dental floss_newly hored_peeved eve_peeved expression_public flossing!_piss off_annoyed_peeve_hate_get to hate_bug_provoke_tease_prop_objectify.gif
title: Public Flossing Annoys Peeved Eve

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Grab your dental floss and follow me. I'll explain on the way.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The newly hired mutant is named "Peeved Eve." Wait until you see her peeved expression.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Peeved Eve
transcript.text: Gaaa! Public flossing!

situation: Dilbert tells Wally to bring his dental floss and follow him, then explains that a newly hired mutant co-worker is called Peeved Eve and has a permanently peeved expression. When they reach her, Wally flosses his teeth in front of her and she recoils in disgust.
punchline: The mutant's special power is being easily annoyed, and Dilbert and Wally gleefully exploit it by provoking her with something as mundane as public flossing.
summary: Two co-workers set out to tease a newly hired colleague whose mutant trait is being perpetually irritated, and a bit of public tooth-cleaning does the trick.

file: 2002/2002-03-15_skills inventory_transfer jobs_check boxes_hazmat section.gif
title: Skills Inventory Leads to Hazmat Duty

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Have you completed your skills inventory?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm submitting it now.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: They use that information to transfer you to jobs you don't want.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You'll be okay as long as you didn't check any of the boxes in the hazmat section.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Stupid stupid stupid

situation: A coworker holding a coffee mug asks Asok whether he has completed his skills inventory, and Asok has just clicked submit. The coworker then explains that the company uses these inventories to transfer people into jobs they don't want, and warns him to hope he didn't check any hazmat boxes. Asok realizes he probably did and berates himself.
punchline: Employees who honestly list their skills get punished with undesirable reassignments, so the 'helpful' inventory is really a trap, and the warning comes too late to undo the click.
summary: A well-meaning warning about a company skills survey arrives only after the new hire has already submitted it, probably volunteering himself for dangerous work.

file: 2002/2002-07-10_filling in_pointy haired boss_carol is secretary_administrative assistant_name calling_arroagnt.gif
title: Carol Refuses To Be Secretary

transcript.speaker: Man with coffee mug
transcript.text: Carol, I'm filling in for the Pointy-Haired Boss, so that makes you my secretary.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I am an administrative assistant, you stinkin' baboon!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I will make you pay dearly for your arrogance!

transcript.speaker: Man with coffee mug
transcript.text: Could you put a head on this?

characters: Substitute manager (bald man with glasses and tie)
situation: A bald man in glasses, temporarily filling in for the Boss, tells Carol that this makes her his secretary. Carol angrily insists she is an administrative assistant and calls him a baboon, threatening that he will pay for his arrogance. Unfazed, he holds out his coffee mug and asks her to put a head on it, treating her as a servant.
punchline: Right after Carol angrily threatens revenge, the temporary boss keeps treating her like a secretary by asking her to fetch or fix his coffee, showing he learned nothing.
summary: A stand-in manager demotes Carol to his personal secretary, and she explodes at him, only for him to ask her to freshen up his mug.

file: 2002/2002-02-06_computer viruses_power cord_spinal adjustment_skeptical_anecdotal evidence.gif
title: Chiropractic Care for Power Cords

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What can I do to avoid getting computer viruses?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Give your power cord a spinal adjustment once a week to prevent disease.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I was skeptical until he said there's anecdotal evidence that it works!

situation: Alice phones a tech support line, which Dogbert answers, to ask how to avoid computer viruses. Dogbert tells her to give her power cord a weekly spinal adjustment, as if it were a patient. In the last panel Alice is on the floor manipulating the cord, persuaded because he mentioned anecdotal evidence.
punchline: Alice is won over by the phrase 'anecdotal evidence', which is no real evidence at all, so she follows absurd pseudo-medical advice for a computer virus problem.
summary: A gullible caller ends up on the floor adjusting a cable after a tech adviser invents a bogus cure and drops a scientific-sounding phrase.

file: 2002/2002-09-28_last kid picked_team sports_school_two people_super power_breakroom_coffee break_education.gif
title: Last Picked, Always Overlooked Power

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In school, I was always the last kid picked to be on a team.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I need two people right now. I'll take Asok and... I'll keep looking.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: So it's like a super power?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Pretty much.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Wally and Asok stand with coffee mugs while Wally remembers always being picked last for school teams. Alice then points at Asok to recruit him for a task, says she needs two people, and passes over Wally by saying she'll keep looking. Asok suggests Wally's being overlooked is like a super power, and Wally agrees.
punchline: Wally has turned being ignored and chosen last into a useful ability, since it lets him dodge work assignments, which he cheerfully admits.
summary: A coffee-sipping slacker shows that being passed over for teams as a child has grown into a handy talent for avoiding workplace tasks.

file: 2002/2002-10-31_defendant guilty_sentence tod eath_deliberated_heard evidence_lenos monlogues_not eveidence.gif
title: Jury Treats Leno Monologue as Evidence

transcript.speaker: Jury Foreman
transcript.text: We find the defendant guilty and we sentence him to death.

transcript.speaker: Juror
transcript.text: Umm...we haven't deliberated. We haven't even heard any evidence yet.

transcript.speaker: Jury Foreman
transcript.text: Okay, so, what I'm hearing is that Leno's monologue is NOT evidence?

situation: A juror stands in the jury box and announces a guilty verdict and death sentence before the trial has started. Another juror points out that they haven't deliberated or heard any evidence. The foreman then asks whether Leno's monologue doesn't count as evidence, revealing that he formed his opinion from late-night TV jokes.
punchline: The foreman has already decided the case based on Jay Leno's comedy monologue, assuming late-night jokes are legitimate evidence.
summary: A hasty juror delivers a death-sentence verdict before any trial evidence, having apparently relied on a talk show host's jokes.

file: 2002/2002-06-26_improve morale_evil director_disgruntled guy_fire guy_misunderstood_mixed signals.gif
title: Morale Survey Targets Disgruntled Employee

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This survey will help us improve morale.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I misjudged you. I thought you were an evil director of H.R., but you care about morale.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: When we fire this disgruntled guy, my morale will go way up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hee hee!

setting: Conference room and a boss's office
situation: Catbert, the H.R. director, hands out a survey in a meeting, saying it will help improve morale. Dilbert says he misjudged Catbert and thought he was evil. In the final panel, Catbert explains to the Boss that the survey is a way to identify a disgruntled employee to fire, which will boost his own morale.
punchline: Catbert really does care about morale, but only his own, which will rise when he gets to fire someone, confirming that he is indeed an evil H.R. director.
summary: A well-meaning compliment to the H.R. cat is shot down when he reveals the survey is really a hunt for someone to dismiss.

file: 2002/2002-03-22_elbonia_nuclear power_warhead_enemies_kneebonia_match.gif
title: Elbonia's Matchless Nuclear Warhead

transcript.speaker: Newscaster
transcript.text: The impoverished nation of Elbonia became a nuclear power today.

transcript.speaker: Newscaster
transcript.text: They plan to test their one and only warhead to frighten their enemies in Kneebonia.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: I'm not going to ask him for a match. You ask him!

setting: Dilbert's home watching TV, then a muddy Elbonian village
situation: Dilbert watches a TV news report announcing that impoverished Elbonia has become a nuclear power and plans to test its single warhead to scare enemies in neighboring Kneebonia. The final panel shows muddy, hooded Elbonians standing around the bomb, arguing about who has to ask a bearded man for a match to light it.
punchline: Elbonia's supposedly fearsome nuclear weapon is so primitive and poorly equipped that they need to borrow a match to set it off, and no one wants to ask.
summary: A poor, mud-bound country's grand atomic debut is undermined by the villagers squabbling over who must beg for a match to ignite their lone bomb.

file: 2002/2002-01-15_fired from restuarant_carried hot soup_spray doning room_soup_blame soup.gif
title: Blaming the Soup for Getting Fired

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got fired from my job at the restaurant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every time I carried hot soup my thumb would slip in and I'd scream and spray the whole dining room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I blame the soup.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Stupid soup.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the green couch
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he was fired from a restaurant job because he repeatedly stuck his thumb in hot soup while carrying it, then screamed and sprayed the dining room. Rather than accept responsibility, he declares that the soup is to blame, and Dogbert agrees.
punchline: Dilbert absurdly blames the soup for his own clumsiness, and Dogbert sycophantically validates the misplaced blame instead of pointing out the real cause.
summary: A man who lost his waiter job by repeatedly burning his thumb and splashing customers decides the soup is the real culprit, and his dog cheerfully agrees.

file: 2002/2002-05-09_training cd_gone bad_brainwashing_cyborg_brain washed.gif
title: Brainwashed Into Becoming a Cyborg

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My training CD has gone bad. It is brainwashing me to become a cyborg.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't worry. Smart people such as you can't be brainwashed to do stupid things.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Guess who doesn't know the first thing about brainwashing.

setting: Office break room or lunch table
situation: Asok tells his coworkers over lunch that a corporate training CD has malfunctioned and is brainwashing him into becoming a cyborg. Dilbert reassures him that smart people can't be brainwashed into doing stupid things. In the last panel Asok has been fully converted into a cyborg, with robotic parts attached to his face and body.
punchline: Dilbert's confident assumption that intelligence protects against brainwashing is proven wrong when Asok has already become a cyborg, and Asok's dry retort points out that Dilbert knows nothing about how brainwashing works.
summary: A malfunctioning software course turns a clever intern into a machine, despite a colleague's assurance that brains like his are immune.

file: 2002/2002-08-25_make box bluer_micromanaging_blood smaple_microscope_manage cellular level_erwin schrodinger_quantum level_free gifts_white blood cells_say hi.gif
title: Micromanaging Boss Gets Blood Sample

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make the box bluer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A little more... A little more... A little more...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's it!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When you get tired of micromanaging me...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Put this sample of my blood under a microscope so you can manage me on a cellular level.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And here's a book by Erwin Schrödinger in case you'd like to manage me on a quantum level!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you understand what I'm saying?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Free gifts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I want all of you white blood cells to spell "Hi."

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss stands over Alice's shoulder and nitpicks her work, repeatedly asking her to make a box on her screen bluer. Alice finally snaps and sarcastically hands him a sample of her blood and a book on quantum physics so he can micromanage her at the cellular and quantum levels. The Boss misses the point entirely and is just happy about the free gifts.
punchline: Alice's sarcastic offer is lost on the oblivious Boss, who treats it as free gifts and immediately tries to micromanage her white blood cells.
summary: A worker pushed past her limit hands her nitpicking supervisor a blood sample and a physics book, and he happily takes it as an invitation to direct her very cells.

file: 2002/2002-03-05_bad job_package_quit without notice_severance package.gif
title: Severance Package Double Entendre

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What's our current severance package?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I transfer you to a bad job and you quit without giving notice.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I hate your package.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hear that a lot.

situation: Carol, the Boss's assistant, asks him what the company's severance package is. The Boss explains that his approach is to transfer an employee to a bad job so they quit without notice, avoiding any payout. Carol replies that she hates his package, which he mistakes for an innuendo.
punchline: The Boss's cheap way of avoiding severance pay turns into an accidental crude double entendre when Carol says she hates his 'package', and he cheerfully admits he hears that a lot.
summary: A manager reveals his sneaky method for dodging severance costs, then unwittingly invites a rude joke about his own anatomy.

file: 2002/2002-03-14_medical mel_needle_four feet long_pencil_javelin champion_bob short_shiskabob.gif
title: Medical Mel's Shishkabob Hospital Story

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Medical Mel

transcript.speaker: Medical Mel
transcript.text: ...The needle was four feet long and thick as a pencil.

transcript.speaker: Medical Mel
transcript.text: I tried to run but the doctor had been an Olympic javelin champion.

transcript.speaker: Medical Mel
transcript.text: My new nickname at the hospital is Bob - short for shishkabob.

situation: Medical Mel, a coworker in a neighboring cubicle with an eye patch, chats on the phone and tells an exaggerated medical horror story about a giant needle. Dilbert sits stone-faced in his cubicle, overhearing the whole thing. In the last panel Dilbert flinches and clutches his papers as Mel finishes his tale.
punchline: Mel's hospital story escalates from an enormous needle to being speared by a former javelin champion, ending with the pun that his nickname 'Bob' is short for 'shishkabob'.
summary: A cubicle neighbor with a long history of medical misfortunes loudly recounts being skewered at the hospital while Dilbert is forced to listen.

file: 2002/2002-03-18_low morale_monkey at zoo_fling shit_survey_request for survey.gif
title: Ask a Monkey About Morale

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, put together a survey to find out why morale is so low.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Survey?!! You could ask any monkey at the zoo what the problem is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do not fling that. I repeat...

setting: Office cubicle, then a zoo monkey enclosure
situation: The Boss asks his assistant Carol to put together a survey to find out why morale is low. Carol scoffs that any zoo monkey could tell him the problem. In the last panel the Boss is at the zoo, standing at the monkey's cage, warning the monkey not to fling something.
punchline: Carol's sarcastic remark implies management is the problem, but the Boss takes it literally, goes to ask a monkey, and is promptly threatened with flung excrement, implying the monkey's answer is the same as hers.
summary: Told by his assistant that a monkey could explain the morale problem, the boss literally visits the zoo and nervously confronts the animal.

file: 2002/2002-04-26_walk and talk_not their names_boss waves_distarcted.gif
title: Boss Greets Everyone With Wrong Names

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a second?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Walk and talk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, the supplier won't...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hi, Pete. Hey, Tim. Hi, Barb. How are you? Not bad. Hi.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... those aren't their names.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My way is easier. Hi, Ted.

situation: Dilbert tries to raise a supplier problem with the Boss, who insists on a walk-and-talk. While Dilbert speaks, the Boss cheerfully waves at passing coworkers and greets them with names. Dilbert points out that the names are wrong, and the Boss admits he makes up names because it's easier.
punchline: The Boss doesn't bother learning his employees' names and just invents greetings, showing he is both inattentive to Dilbert's problem and indifferent to the people who work for him.
summary: A manager who won't stop to listen breezily hails passing staff with invented names and defends the habit as simpler.

file: 2002/2002-06-16_the master_overworked_carefree_powerful secret_volunteer_many tasks_complaints later_gandhi that eats_dont recall_agree.gif
title: Wally's Secret to Looking Busy

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally, I need advice from the master.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Huh?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How do you remain so carefree while everyone else seems overworked?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Asok, you are ready to learn my most powerful secret.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Always volunteer to do lots of tasks. That will make you appear very busy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Later, when someone complains that you didn't do a task...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Say you remember the topic but you don't recall agreeing to do anything.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Offer a glimmer of hope that you might yet do the task if no one yells at you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then repeat.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wow.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: He is like a Gandhi that eats.

situation: Asok wakes the dozing Wally and asks how he stays so relaxed while everyone else is overworked. Wally shares his supposed secret: volunteer for lots of tasks to look busy, then deny ever agreeing to do them when people complain, while hinting you might still do them if nobody yells. Asok is awed by the technique.
punchline: Wally's 'powerful secret' is a cynical system of fake commitment and plausible deniability, which Asok admiringly compares to a Gandhi that eats, a passive-resistance master who doesn't starve.
summary: A junior engineer begs the office slacker for his secret and learns it is a cycle of volunteering, forgetting, and stalling that Asok treats as enlightenment.

file: 2002/2002-12-16_health_life expectency_current workload_two peoples jobs_six months_five months_shop_card.gif
title: Workload Gives Dilbert Six Months

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I calculated the impact of work on my health and life expectancy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At my current workload, doing two people's jobs, I have...six months to live.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Remind me in five and a half months so I can shop for a card.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer and announces he has calculated how his workload affects his health. Doing two people's jobs, he concludes he has only six months to live. Dogbert, sitting beside him, responds by asking to be reminded in five and a half months so he can buy a card.
punchline: Dogbert reacts to Dilbert's looming death with callous indifference, treating it as a card-buying occasion rather than a tragedy.
summary: After figuring out that overwork will kill him within half a year, Dilbert gets nothing but a cheerfully heartless scheduling request from Dogbert.

file: 2002/2002-07-25_feng shui_office_trerrible_energy being drained_computer fan.gif
title: Feng Shui Consultant Scares The Boss

transcript.speaker: Feng Shui Consultant
transcript.text: The feng shui in your office is terrible.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It is?

transcript.speaker: Feng Shui Consultant
transcript.text: That hum... it's the sound of your energy being drained into the Internet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who told him that his computer fan is killing him?

situation: A feng shui consultant visits the Boss's office and tells him the arrangement is terrible. She then claims the hum of his computer is his energy draining into the Internet, and the Boss looks alarmed. Dilbert, passing by, asks who told the Boss his computer fan is killing him, while the consultant smiles.
punchline: The consultant has scared the gullible Boss with nonsense about his computer fan draining his life force, and Dilbert recognizes the scam.
summary: A self-assured decorating expert persuades a credulous manager that his machine's ordinary noise is sucking away his vitality.

file: 2002/2002-07-14_be charming_more important_project thwarted_seriously hound her_unhelpful_woman_application_boss advice.gif
title: Boss Advises Hounding Unhelpful Coworker

transcript.speaker: Woman on phone
transcript.text: I'll get to your application as soon as I have nothing more important to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay... Thank you very much.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just thanked someone for doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Beep

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My project is being thwarted by a woman who gets satisfaction from being unhelpful.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you tried using your charm?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess I can try.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha ha ha! Just kidding.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But seriously, try hounding her until she recoils in pain at the sound of your voice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will that work?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes the best you can do is make other people feel bad.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert phones a coworker about his application and she says she will get to it only when she has nothing more important to do. He complains to the Boss that his project is being blocked by someone who enjoys being unhelpful. The Boss jokes that he should try charm, then advises him to harass her until she dreads hearing his voice.
punchline: The Boss's management wisdom is that when you can't get results, the best you can do is make other people miserable.
summary: After a stonewalling coworker brushes off his request, Dilbert gets his manager's cynical advice to pester her into misery.

file: 2002/2002-06-15_roboboss_trivial task_insulted_mange with machine_plywoodboss_handle it.gif
title: Roboboss Delegates to Plywoodboss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is Roboboss. He'll handle all of my trivial tasks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm totally insulted that you think you can manage us with a machine!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Handle that.

transcript.speaker: Roboboss
transcript.text: I'll delegate it to my assistant, Plywoodboss.

situation: The Boss introduces Roboboss, a robot he plans to use to handle all of his trivial tasks. Dilbert is offended that management thinks a machine can manage the staff. The Boss orders Roboboss to handle Dilbert's complaint, and the robot immediately passes it down to its own assistant, Plywoodboss.
