punchline: Even the robot manager copies the boss's habit of passing everything on, so a complaint about being managed by a machine gets delegated to an even dumber stand-in, a plywood boss.
summary: A manager hands his petty duties to a robot double that promptly offloads them onto an even more useless helper.

file: 2002/2002-10-04_vendor_integrates_resources_optimize_performance_technology_integrated.gif
title: Vendor Can't Say What Product Does

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The vendor that couldn't describe his company's product

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: It integrates the resources...

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: To optimize the performance of technology.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah, but what is it?

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Hey, if you don't want your resources to be integrated, just say so.

setting: Conference room during a sales presentation
situation: A vendor pitches his company's product to Dilbert using nothing but vague buzzwords about integrating resources and optimizing technology. When Dilbert asks what the product actually is, the vendor still gives no answer and instead acts offended, implying Dilbert is rejecting integration itself.
punchline: Faced with a direct question about what his product is, the vendor deflects by treating the buzzwords as if they were self-evidently desirable, so questioning them looks unreasonable.
summary: A salesman who cannot explain his product hides behind jargon and turns a simple question into an accusation.

file: 2002/2002-04-14_little people allowed_strategy decisions_project opal_executive intuition_budget cut_opal project_named after daughter_increase budget_secret meetings_decision makers.gif
title: Executives Decide Budget by Intuition

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All the important decision-makers in the company are in this room.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No little people are allowed because we'll be making important strategy decisions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: First, let's make decisions about Project Opal.

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Opal

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does anyone know what the project is or what we need to decide?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: My executive intuition tells me we should cut the budget by 10%.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I think Opal is one of your projects. It's named after your daughter.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Wait...a new intuition is coming in now... It says to increase the budget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why are those meetings secret?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't want to know.

setting: Executive conference room, then a hallway
situation: The Boss gathers the company's top decision-makers, excludes lower-level staff, and opens a strategy meeting about Project Opal. Nobody knows what the project is or what needs deciding, so an executive announces a budget cut based on intuition, then reverses to a budget increase when told the project is named after the Boss's daughter. Afterward Dilbert asks why the meetings are secret.
punchline: Executive strategy meetings are secret because the high-level decisions are really just clueless guesses and whims, which would embarrass everyone if exposed.
summary: Top managers make budget calls on gut feelings alone, flip-flopping with no idea what the project even is, which explains the secrecy.

file: 2002/2002-12-22_how to be annoying_nasal sounds_rainstorm_sugar donught_oil on fingers_leaky coffee mug.gif
title: Paul Ooshen's Guide to Annoying Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Adventures of Paul Ooshen* (*Say it fast)

transcript.speaker: Paul Ooshen
transcript.text: Aaah... the scent of a hog farm in a rainstorm.

transcript.speaker: Paul Ooshen
transcript.text: Oil for fingers.

transcript.speaker: Paul Ooshen
transcript.text: Onion sandwich.

transcript.speaker: Paul Ooshen
transcript.text: Annoying nasal sounds.

transcript.speaker: Paul Ooshen
transcript.text: Sniff snort

transcript.speaker: Paul Ooshen
transcript.text: Leaky coffee mug.

transcript.speaker: Paul Ooshen
transcript.text: I'm ready for my meeting.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes! Yes! I agree to everything! Please leave!!

transcript.speaker: Paul Ooshen
transcript.text: I didn't even need to lean over her keyboard with my sugar doughnut.

situation: Paul Ooshen, a man whose name sounds like 'pollution' when said fast, prepares for a meeting by deliberately making himself as unpleasant as possible: spraying a foul scent, oiling his fingers, eating an onion sandwich, making nasal noises, and carrying a leaky coffee mug. A female coworker is so repelled that she immediately agrees to everything and begs him to leave.
punchline: Paul wins the negotiation purely through offensiveness, and he still has an even worse tactic, leaning over her keyboard with a sugar doughnut, left in reserve.
summary: A man named for pollution sabotages the senses of everyone around him to get his way in a meeting.

file: 2002/2002-08-16_shape no text_all good ideas used_green_creative person_meeting_print ads_brain storming_limited ideas_business.gif
title: Ad Agency's Blank Shape Concept

transcript.speaker: Ad Agency Guy
transcript.text: Your print ads would look like this. It's a shape with no text.

transcript.speaker: Ad Agency Guy
transcript.text: I did some checking and found out that all the good ideas have been used. This is all that's left.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can it be green?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whoa! Who's the creative person here?

setting: Conference room meeting with an advertising agency
situation: An ad agency creative presents a blank splotchy shape with no text as the concept for the company's print ads, claiming all the good ideas have already been used. The Boss, evaluating the pitch, asks only whether the shape can be green. Dilbert is stunned by the Boss's contribution.
punchline: The Boss's trivial request to change the color is sarcastically treated by Dilbert as a burst of creative genius in response to an absurdly empty ad concept.
summary: A marketing firm pitches a meaningless blob as the ultimate remaining ad idea, and the boss's only input is a color preference that Dilbert mockingly praises.

file: 2002/2002-10-28_get fired_mother_drop lawsuit_despicable wesels_enjoy challenge_demand dna test_family.gif
title: Mom Sues Dilbert's Weasel Employer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mom, I'll get fired unless you drop your lawsuit against my company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Why do you work for a company that's managed by despicable weasels?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They tell me it's because I enjoy the challenge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I demand a DNA test.

setting: A dining table at home during a meal
situation: Dilbert sits down to dinner with his mother and asks her to drop her lawsuit against his employer, or he will lose his job. She asks why he works for a company run by despicable weasels. He says he's told it's because he enjoys the challenge, and she responds by demanding a DNA test.
punchline: Dilbert's mother is so appalled that her son would claim to enjoy working for a terrible company that she suspects he can't really be her child.
summary: A son pleads with his mother to stop suing his employer, and she is so horrified by his excuse for staying that she questions whether he is truly hers.

file: 2002/2002-08-01_stretch goals_signaling surrender_no to doughnut.gif
title: Stretch Goals Mean Giving Up

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Starting today, our goals will be replaced by stretch goals.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Stretch goals?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stretch goals are like stretch pants. It's a way of signaling surrender.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Speaking of which, I wouldn't say no to a doughnut.

situation: The Boss announces to the team that regular goals will now be replaced by stretch goals. Alice explains that stretch goals are like stretch pants, a polite way of admitting defeat, and then segues into asking for a doughnut.
punchline: Alice equates stretch goals with stretch pants as a sign of giving up, then underscores the point by casually asking for a doughnut, as if surrendering to indulgence too.
summary: A meeting announcement about lofty new targets gets deflated by a colleague's wry comparison to comfy elastic clothing and a request for a pastry.

file: 2002/2002-02-15_on time_hourly fee_specified_wag.gif
title: Dogbert Wags Tail at Scope Creep

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow! You finished the project below your estimate and on time.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: (thought) Hold... hold...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All I need are a few changes at your hourly fee, which was never specified in our contract.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: (thought) Hold... hold... hold.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: WAG!

situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, sits across the desk from The Boss, who praises him for finishing the project under budget and on time. The Boss then asks for a few more changes, noting that the hourly fee for extra work was never written into the contract. Dogbert silently tells himself to hold back, then wildly wags his tail in delight at the chance to bill freely.
punchline: Dogbert hides his excitement until the boss hands him unlimited billable extra work, then his tail gives away his glee, showing the contract loophole is a goldmine for consultants.
summary: A consultant barely contains his joy when a client offers open-ended extra work with no agreed rate.

file: 2002/2002-07-17_selling stock options_made fortune_now bankrupt_401k worthless_stolen savings_bad time_make quote marks_in effect.gif
title: Air Quotes During Retirement Theft Accusation

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You made a fortune selling your stock options last month, and now we're bankrupt.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My 401k is worthless. So, in effect, you've stolen my life savings.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This would be a bad time to make quote marks in the air while saying, "in effect."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh.

situation: Alice confronts the Boss, accusing him of cashing out his stock options for a fortune just before the company went bankrupt, leaving her 401k worthless. She says that effectively he has stolen her life savings. The Boss starts to raise his hands to make air quotes, and Alice warns him that it would be a very bad moment for that gesture.
punchline: Alice anticipates the Boss's habit of doing annoying air quotes and threatens him with it, while the Boss's disappointed 'Ooh' shows he was about to do exactly that, even as he's being accused of ruining her retirement.
summary: An angry employee blames her boss for cashing out his shares before the company collapsed, then pre-emptively warns him against a smug hand gesture.

file: 2002/2002-12-09_magnetic cancelation wheel_create free energy_rule the world_technology.gif
title: Dilbert's Free Energy Wheel Stolen

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My magnetic-cancellation wheel will create unlimited free energy.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Buwahaha!!! I will use this technology to rule the world!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... It's not yours.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: What time are you going to bed?

situation: Dilbert is tinkering at his desk with a wheel he claims will generate unlimited free energy. Ratbert, watching, declares he will use this technology to rule the world and laughs maniacally. Dilbert points out the invention isn't his, and Ratbert responds by asking when Dilbert goes to bed, implying he will steal it.
punchline: Ratbert's evil-genius plan to seize Dilbert's invention is revealed to be as simple as waiting until Dilbert falls asleep and taking it.
summary: A small white pet gleefully plots world domination with his owner's invention, then casually plans to swipe it once the inventor is asleep.

file: 2002/2002-07-18_broke_bankrupt comapny_401k worthless_diversifying your investments_37% retrurn_burn in hell.gif
title: Dogbert's Unethical Investment Portfolio

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm broke. The company declared bankruptcy and my 401k savings are worthless.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, I've been impersonating you and diversifying your investments into tobacco, sweat shops, and diamond mines.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really?! How am I doing?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's mixed. You have a 37% return but your soul will burn for eternity.

situation: Dilbert comes home with a briefcase and announces that his company went bankrupt and his 401k is worthless. Dogbert, sitting on the couch, reveals he secretly impersonated Dilbert and moved his retirement money into morally questionable industries. Dilbert eagerly asks how he is doing.
punchline: Dogbert's unethical investments earned a great financial return, but at the cost of Dilbert's soul, and Dilbert only cares about the return.
summary: A broke Dilbert learns his dog secretly invested his retirement savings in vice industries that paid off handsomely but damned him morally.

file: 2002/2002-05-30_treasure hunt_loot_thrill of hunt_seed the carpet_nickles_can't find.gif
title: Metal Detecting the Office Carpet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's the treasure hunt going? Have you found any loot?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's not about the "loot," as you say. We detectors are motivated by the thrill of the hunt.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could seed the carpet with nickels.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I tried that but I can't find them.

setting: Office cubicle area with carpeted floor
situation: Wally, wearing headphones, sweeps a metal detector across the office carpet while Dilbert watches over the cubicle wall and asks if he has found any loot. Wally claims detectorists care only about the thrill of the hunt, so Dilbert offers to plant nickels in the carpet for him to find.
punchline: Wally has already tried seeding the carpet with nickels himself, but he is so incompetent or lazy that he can't find them, which undercuts his claim that he only cares about the thrill of the hunt.
summary: A coworker sweeping the carpet with a metal detector insists he's in it for the adventure, then admits his own planted coins have defeated him.

file: 2002/2002-11-15_emergency meeting_five minutes_warm and cozy_cubicle paradise_sound of not caring.gif
title: Dilbert Doesn't Care About Emergency Meeting

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's an emergency strategy meeting in five minutes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was all warm and cozy in my cubicle paradise. Why must you ruin it?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can you hear the sound of me not caring?

situation: Alice stops by Dilbert's cubicle to tell him an emergency strategy meeting starts in five minutes. Dilbert complains that she is disturbing his comfortable time at his desk. Alice responds by cupping her ear and asking if he can hear the sound of her not caring.
punchline: Alice turns Dilbert's complaint around, sarcastically telling him she has no sympathy for his reluctance to attend the meeting.
summary: A coworker's summons to a last-minute meeting is met with a gripe about lost comfort, and she answers with deadpan indifference.

file: 2002/2002-08-09_telecommunting_fired four years_get email_stopped coming.gif
title: Telecommuter Fired Four Years Ago

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who are you?

transcript.speaker: Allen
transcript.text: I'm Allen. I've been telecommuting for four years.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Allen? I fired you four years ago. Didn't you get my e-mail?

transcript.speaker: Allen
transcript.text: This is exactly why I stopped coming to the office.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss doesn't recognize a man who says he has been telecommuting for four years. The Boss replies that he fired him four years ago and sent an e-mail about it. Afterward, the man tells Dilbert, who is holding a coffee mug, that this kind of communication failure is exactly why he stopped coming to the office.
punchline: The telecommuter was fired four years ago, but the notice only went by e-mail, so he kept working remotely without knowing; the Boss's reliance on e-mail illustrates the very problem that made him stay away from the office.
summary: A remote worker turns up at a meeting and learns he was dismissed years earlier, a message that never reached him.

file: 2002/2002-09-01_feedback meeting_ball rolling_long tern strategy_leak to competition_crushing_cubicle dwelling_optimists life_never easy.gif
title: Feedback Meeting Ends in Rage

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Welcome to my quarterly employee feedback meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who wants to get the ball rolling?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It would be helpful if you told us our company's long term strategy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, would it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why? So you can leak it to our competitors?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's your stupid suggestion in my hand! I'm crushing it! Crush, crush, crush!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I'll chew it up so I can spit it in your cubicle-dwelling face!!!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You fell in that trap last quarter too.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: An optimist's life is never easy.

setting: Conference room during a quarterly employee feedback meeting
situation: The Boss invites employees to give feedback, and one employee politely asks for the company's long-term strategy. The Boss accuses him of wanting to leak it to competitors, then crushes the imaginary suggestion in his fist and threatens to chew it up and spit it at him. Afterward, two employees note that the same employee fell for the same trap last quarter.
punchline: The feedback meeting is a trap: any honest suggestion gets met with paranoid rage, yet the optimistic employee keeps believing it will work this time.
summary: A manager who solicits employee suggestions responds to a reasonable request with paranoid, theatrical fury, while a hopeful coworker repeats his mistake from last time.

file: 2002/2002-07-16_chapter 11_profits are fake_sold all stock_diversifying investments_bankruptcy_files for bankruptcy.gif
title: Boss Dumps Stock Before Bankruptcy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha ha! We're filing for Chapter 11 because all of our so-called profits are fake.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm laughing because I sold all of my stock the same day I heard that our CFO did.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You said he was just diversifying his investments!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It sounds funny now.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss cheerfully announces the company is filing for Chapter 11 because its profits were fake. He then explains that he laughs because he sold all his stock on the same day he learned the CFO had sold his. Alice angrily reminds him that he had claimed the CFO was merely diversifying his investments.
punchline: The Boss dismissed the CFO's stock sale as harmless diversification, yet he quietly dumped his own shares right after hearing about it, showing management's insider-trading hypocrisy in a collapsing company.
summary: A manager chuckles over his company's imminent bankruptcy and admits he cashed out his shares the moment he learned the finance chief had done the same.

file: 2002/2002-09-14_elbonia_meeting_no limo servoce_cheapest way_brownies barrel service_business.gif
title: Cheapest Way to Elbonia: Barrel Service

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sending you to Elbonia for a meeting, but we're on a tight budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So there will be no limo service to the airport. Go there in the cheapest possible way.

transcript.speaker: Brownie
transcript.text: And then I started Brownie's Barrel Service.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's a talker.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being sent to Elbonia on a tight budget, with no limo to the airport and orders to travel the cheapest way possible. Dilbert ends up wearing a barrel, rolling along the road on top of a talkative bear who runs 'Brownie's Barrel Service', while cars pass by.
punchline: Taking the cheapest possible transport literally means rolling to the airport in a barrel pushed by a chatty bear, and Dilbert's only complaint is that the driver won't stop talking.
summary: On a shoestring travel budget, an employee is shipped to the airport by a talkative bear who runs a barrel-rolling service.

file: 2002/2002-01-06_best practices_classified budget_consultanats_layoffs_merger_new ceo_office relocation_reorganized_savings_startegy_whole industry_budget freeze.gif
title: Best Practices: A Failed Project Timeline

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The project got off to a slow start.

transcript.speaker: Chart
transcript.text: Year 1

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: First we had the reorganization.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then the merger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And the layoffs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Budget freeze.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Office relocation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: New CEO.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: New consultants.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: New strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eventually the whole industry changed and the opportunity evaporated.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So we classified our unused budget as "savings" and gave everyone a shirt.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: You said you'd show us your "best practices."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you implying?

setting: Conference room during a project review presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a project post-mortem to three executives, walking through a long series of disruptions such as a reorganization, merger, layoffs, budget freeze, relocation and new leadership. The project ultimately produced nothing, so the unused budget was relabeled as savings and the team got shirts. The executives ask to see his best practices and he indignantly asks what they are implying.
punchline: Dilbert claims his project's failure-ridden history is a model of best practices, and he takes offense when management seems to doubt it, even though the only result was a rebranded budget and free shirts.
summary: A project presenter recounts a chain of corporate upheavals that doomed his effort, then bristles when asked to showcase what he did right.

file: 2002/2002-01-22_dilebrt the sales guy_mother_overpirced_hard to use_spit_packaging_mom_surprised_mother and son_family.gif
title: Dilbert's Mother Trashes His Product

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert the Sales Guy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy this @#!%!!$ with YOUR money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: It's overpriced, hard to use, full of bugs and it solves no problem.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mother
transcript.text: I spit on your packaging!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Mom...

situation: Dilbert, working as a sales guy, tries to sell a boxed product to his elderly mother as a practice sales call. She sits in her armchair and savagely criticizes the product, listing its flaws and finally spitting on its packaging. Dilbert looks on and timidly says 'Um... Mom...'
punchline: Dilbert's own mother is the harshest, most honest customer, brutally describing everything wrong with the product he is supposed to sell while he realizes she's gone too far.
summary: A salesman's elderly mother delivers a scathing, brutally honest review of the product he is pitching to her.

file: 2002/2002-07-04_coffee with the boss_meeting_feel free_don't hold back_squeaky chair_ungrateful wretch_name calling_business.gif
title: Boss Invites Feedback, Explodes Over Squeak

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're the first employee for my "Coffee with the Boss" program.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Feel free to say whatever is on your mind. Don't hold back. Give it to me straight.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My chair has a squeak.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You ungrateful whiny wretch!!!

setting: Office, at a table over coffee
situation: The Boss announces his new "Coffee with the Boss" program and urges Dilbert, its first participant, to speak freely and candidly. Dilbert offers a tiny complaint that his chair squeaks, and the Boss immediately loses his temper and insults him.
punchline: The Boss claims to want brutally honest feedback but cannot handle even the most trivial complaint, showing that open-door programs are only for praise.
summary: A manager begging for candid criticism over coffee flies into a rage when his employee mentions a squeaky chair.

file: 2002/2002-01-25_michael t. suit_core competencies_platforms_did we shake.gif
title: Empty Suit Spouts Buzzwords

transcript.speaker: Michael T. Suit
transcript.text: Hi. My name is Michael T. Suit. All my friends call me M.T.

transcript.speaker: Michael T. Suit
transcript.text: I enhance core competencies by leveraging platforms.

transcript.speaker: Michael T. Suit
transcript.text: Did we shake yet? Sometimes I can't tell.

setting: Office hallway or break area, with Dilbert holding a coffee mug
situation: Dilbert meets a visitor who is literally an empty green suit with a tie but no body, who introduces himself as Michael T. Suit. The suit spouts meaningless business jargon while Dilbert stands silently holding his coffee. At the end the suit asks whether a handshake has happened, since he can't tell.
punchline: The name 'M.T. Suit' is a pun on 'empty suit', and the jargon-spewing, invisible-handed visitor embodies a manager who is all appearance and buzzwords with no substance.
summary: A hollow suit with no occupant introduces himself with corporate jargon and cannot even tell whether he has shaken hands.

file: 2002/2002-03-03_away from home more_career advice_good advice_hearing it_hideous commute_longer hours_no growth potential_self loathing_unhappiness.gif
title: Dogbert's Brutally Honest Career Advice

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need career advice.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You came to the right place.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I keep my comfortable job that has no growth potential?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or should I take a better job with longer hours and a hideous commute?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The first choice is a sure path to self-loathing and unhappiness.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The second choice will squeeze the life out of you like a vise on a peach.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can't win. So I recommend the choice that keeps you away from home more.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because frankly - and I'll try to say this delicately - a little bit of you goes a long way.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's the problem with good advice: no one wants to hear it.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dilbert in a bathrobe in an armchair and Dogbert on a couch like a therapist
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert for career advice, laying out a choice between a comfortable dead-end job and a better job with long hours and a terrible commute. Dogbert explains that both options are bad, then recommends the one that keeps Dilbert away from home more, bluntly saying people can only tolerate a little of him.
punchline: Dogbert's 'good advice' is really an insult, that Dilbert is annoying to be around, and he points out that nobody wants to hear honest advice.
summary: Dogbert, playing therapist, tells a conflicted Dilbert to pick whichever job gets him out of the house more because others can only stand so much of him.

file: 2002/2002-01-11_job as waiter_job as engineer_qualified_manager_slapping drunk.gif
title: Waiter Job Harder Than Engineering

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'll take a job as a waiter until I can get a job as an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're not qualified to wait on tables.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How hard could it be?

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: The manager is over there slapping a drunk.

setting: A restaurant table, with a busy restaurant floor in the last panel
situation: Dilbert, between engineering jobs, suggests working as a waiter in the meantime. Dogbert tells him he is not qualified, and Dilbert asks how hard it could be. A harried waiter balancing a huge pile of dishes and drinks then explains that the manager is off slapping a drunk, showing the job's hidden difficulties.
punchline: Dilbert's assumption that waiting tables is easy is undercut by a frazzled waiter who casually reveals the job involves chaos and managers physically dealing with unruly drunks.
summary: A jobless engineer assumes serving tables is a breeze until a overloaded waiter reveals the chaotic reality of the job.

file: 2002/2002-05-24_demoted_spread rumors_new boss_fired_clueless human_doesn't work_denial.gif
title: Rumors About the Clueless Boss

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Demoted

transcript.speaker: Demoted Boss
transcript.text: I plan to spread rumors about our new boss until I get him fired.

transcript.speaker: Demoted Boss
transcript.text: I'll tell everyone that he's the most clueless human that ever lived. Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Believe me, that doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have no idea what you're talking about.

setting: Office break area, with coworkers holding coffee mugs
situation: The Boss, who has been demoted, tells Wally he plans to spread rumors that the new boss is the most clueless human ever until he gets fired. Wally replies from experience that this tactic doesn't work. The Boss, oblivious that he is the clueless one being described, says he has no idea what Wally means.
punchline: Wally's remark that the rumor strategy doesn't work is a jab at the Boss himself, who is famously clueless yet never got fired, and he fails to grasp the insult.
summary: A demoted manager schemes to oust his replacement by calling him clueless, not realizing the failed tactic is a dig at his own obliviousness.

file: 2002/2002-04-29_committee across hall_west side story_dance fight_teach.gif
title: Committee Resolves Duplication With West Side Story

transcript.speaker: Committee Member
transcript.text: I just found out that the committee across the hall is doing the same thing we are.

transcript.speaker: Committee Member
transcript.text: All we can do now is hum "West Side Story" and have a dance-fight.

transcript.speaker: Bald Committee Member
transcript.text: Can you teach me how to hum?

setting: Conference room during a committee meeting
situation: A committee member announces that another committee across the hall is doing exactly the same work as theirs. Rather than propose a practical response, he suggests they hum "West Side Story" and have a dance-fight, and in the last panel he is shown mid-dance-move. A bald colleague, ignoring the absurdity, only asks to be taught how to hum.
punchline: Faced with wasted duplicate effort, the committee chooses a ridiculous musical rivalry over any sensible action, and one member is more concerned with learning to hum than with the actual problem.
summary: Learning that a rival committee is duplicating their work, a meeting attendee proposes settling it with a musical gang-style dance battle, and a colleague just wants humming lessons.

file: 2002/2002-05-25_gained empathy_im not a loser_promoted_noble little people.gif
title: Demoted Boss Celebrates Promotion Immediately

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe it's a good thing that I was demoted to work among you noble little people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have gained a valuable empathy that will serve me well if I ever become a manager again.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You've been promoted.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yee-ha!! I'm not a loser!!

situation: The demoted Pointy-Haired Boss tells Dilbert he has benefited from working among ordinary employees and claims to have gained empathy. A coworker then arrives with a paper and announces he has been promoted. He instantly drops the humble act and cheers that he is not a loser.
punchline: His supposed newfound empathy for ordinary workers was just a coping story, and it vanishes the instant he gets his management status back.
summary: A humbled former manager praises the lessons of being a lowly worker, then abandons the speech the moment he learns he is a boss again.

file: 2002/2002-02-07_bugs_database_not to learn_put bugs back in_strong desire_apathetic.gif
title: Put Back the Bugs

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I worked all weekend to get the bugs out of the database.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But now the data make us look bad. Put back the bugs.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Can you teach me to be apathetic like you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Only if you have a strong desire not to learn.

setting: Boss's office, then a hallway or break area with coffee mugs
situation: Asok proudly tells the boss he spent his weekend removing bugs from the database. The boss objects because the corrected data makes the department look bad and orders him to put the bugs back. Discouraged, Asok asks Wally to teach him apathy, and Wally says it only works if he has a strong desire not to learn.
punchline: Wally's reply is a joke about apathy: being apathetic means not wanting to learn, so it can't be taught to someone who is eager, which mocks Asok's enthusiasm and Wally's own laziness.
summary: After being punished for doing good work, an eager young employee seeks lessons in indifference from the office's most committed slacker.

file: 2002/2002-06-13_appear smarter_less is more_sound more wise_agreements.gif
title: Agreeing Your Way to Wisdom

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I've learned to appear smarter than I am.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I agree with whatever people say then I reword it to sound more wise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please leave my cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Because sometimes less is more!

situation: A coworker stands in Dilbert's cubicle and explains his trick for seeming intelligent: he agrees with whatever others say and then rewords it to sound wiser. Dilbert, seated at his computer, finally asks him to leave. The coworker responds with a pseudo-profound slogan, demonstrating the very technique he described.
punchline: Dilbert's blunt request is immediately repackaged by the coworker as a wise-sounding aphorism, proving his technique of rewording what others say to seem profound.
summary: A cubicle visitor brags about faking wisdom by echoing others, then does exactly that when Dilbert tells him to go away.

file: 2002/2002-12-13_bankrupt_company_sing along_weasel dance_business.gif
title: Dogbert's Bankruptcy Weasel Dance

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I sold my stock and made billions before driving my company into bankruptcy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now I do the weasel dance. Hoo-ah! Yee-ha! Woo-woo-woo!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would it kill you to clap and sing along?

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert on the couch
situation: Dogbert, standing next to Dilbert's couch, boasts that he cashed out his stock and made billions before running his company into bankruptcy. He then performs a celebratory 'weasel dance' while Dilbert sits in a bathrobe reading a book and ignores him. Dogbert finally complains that Dilbert won't clap or sing along.
punchline: Dogbert gleefully celebrates profiting from his own corporate collapse, and Dilbert's stony silence in the face of this unethical gloating is what annoys him.
summary: A gloating Dogbert dances after enriching himself by wrecking his own firm, while an unimpressed Dilbert keeps reading.

file: 2002/2002-02-24_god of management time_insatiable appetite_kronos_manipulate perception_month_plenty of time_states reprts_upgrade servers_side effects.gif
title: Kronos Hypnotizes the Boss's Deadline

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Upgrade all of our network servers by Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's impossible. I need at least a month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, it's impossible, is it? Watch this.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I summon Kronos, the God of Management Time!!

transcript.speaker: Kronos
transcript.text: I, Kronos, will manipulate your perception of time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't see how that helps...

transcript.speaker: Kronos
transcript.text: When he wakes up he will believe there is plenty of time and that you are a weasel.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Any side effects?

transcript.speaker: Kronos
transcript.text: Just an insatiable appetite for status reports.

situation: The Boss demands that Dilbert upgrade all the network servers by Tuesday, and when Dilbert says it needs a month, the Boss summons Kronos, the god of management time. Kronos hypnotizes the Boss so he believes there is plenty of time and that Dilbert is a weasel. Dilbert asks about side effects.
punchline: The cure for the Boss's unreasonable deadline comes with a side effect that is just as bad: he becomes obsessed with demanding status reports, which would eat up the time Dilbert just gained.
summary: A magical time god tweaks the Boss's sense of urgency, but the fix leaves him hungry for paperwork.

file: 2002/2002-03-06_hostile bahavior_unacceptable body language_cold_eyebrows.gif
title: Catbert Polices Tina's Body Language

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Tina, we've gotten some complaints about your hostile behavior.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: At a recent meeting you crossed your arms. That is unacceptable body language.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Maybe I was cold.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Eyebrows! Eyebrows!

situation: Catbert, acting as the HR director, reprimands Tina for hostile behavior after complaints. His evidence is that she crossed her arms in a meeting, which he deems unacceptable body language. When Tina offers an innocent explanation, Catbert simply points at her scowling face and shouts about her eyebrows.
punchline: HR treats ordinary gestures and facial expressions as evidence of misconduct, so any excuse just yields another accusation, and Tina's angry eyebrows ironically confirm his complaint.
summary: An HR cat disciplines a coworker over her folded arms and then moves on to criticizing her furrowed brow when she tries to explain herself.

file: 2002/2002-03-09_empowered button_life in one package_refusal_enforced_empowered to wear button.gif
title: Mandatory Empowerment Buttons For Employees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every employee will wear a button that says "I'm empowered."

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I don't want to.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have to.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That was everything you need to know about life in one package.

setting: Office break area, with employees holding coffee mugs
situation: The Boss announces that every employee must wear a button declaring "I'm empowered." One employee says he doesn't want to, and the Boss simply replies that he has to. Afterwards the employees wear the buttons and one remarks that the exchange sums up life.
punchline: Being 'empowered' is compulsory and refusing is not allowed, so the empowerment is meaningless, and this contradiction is presented as a lesson about how life works.
summary: A manager orders staff to wear buttons proclaiming their empowerment, brushes off an objection with a flat command, and a coworker calls the whole thing a lesson in life.

file: 2002/2002-02-03_budget contraints_free soda_no free soda_near had free soda_soda stolen_daily_boss steals intern.gif
title: Free Soda Was Never Free

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Due to budget constraints, the company will no longer provide free soda.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What free soda? We never had free soda.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure we did. It was in the refrigerator in the break room.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every day I'd go in there and get a refreshing beverage.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The next morning, as if by magic, the soda would be replenished.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I brought a soda to work every day for five years only to have it stolen from the refrigerator every time.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Why didn't you just drink the free ones?

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces to his staff that free soda is being cut because of budget constraints. Dilbert says there never was any free soda, and the Boss explains that he used to take drinks from the break room fridge that were mysteriously replenished each day. An employee reveals he had been bringing his own soda that was stolen daily, and in the last panel an employee, possibly Dilbert, is pictured lying on the table in a rage while another coworker asks why he didn't just drink the free ones.
punchline: The Boss has been unknowingly stealing employees' own sodas for years, believing they were a free company perk, and now the budget cut is really just his loss of a stolen drink supply.
summary: A manager mourns the loss of a perk that was actually coworkers' private drinks he had been helping himself to for years.

file: 2002/2002-06-01_defective copy_employees still low_low morale_motivational book_thinking.gif
title: Boss Blames Defective Motivational Book

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I read this motivational book and yet the employees still have low morale.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Maybe you have a defective copy. You should compare it to another one and see what's different.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if the second one is defective too?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Sheesh... It's like I'm doing all of your thinking here.

situation: The Boss sits in his armchair holding a motivational book and complains that employee morale is still low even though he read it. Catbert, his advisor, suggests the book copy might be defective and that he should compare it with another one. The Boss then asks what if the second copy is defective too, and Catbert grumbles that he is doing all the thinking.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless that he blames a defective book rather than himself, and he can't even follow Catbert's simple advice without needing it spelled out.
summary: A manager who thinks a faulty book is the reason his staff are still miserable has to be walked through basic reasoning by his exasperated advisor.

file: 2002/2002-09-25_poisoned_bad user interface design_crowd out ugly_staggering beauty_drink in_garbageman advice.gif
title: Garbage Man's Cure for Ugly Interface

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I have one week to live. I've been poisoned by looking at a bad user interface design.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: I see a lot of this. The only cure is to crowd out the ugly memory with images of staggering beauty.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Where would I...

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Drink it in, baby. And don't forget it.

setting: A city street curb beside a trash can and a parked blue car
situation: A woman in a pink suit tells a garbage man she has a week to live because she was poisoned by seeing a terrible user interface design. The garbage man calmly says he sees this often and prescribes images of staggering beauty as the only cure. When she asks where she could find such beauty, he gestures at the trash and street around them.
punchline: The garbage man's idea of 'staggering beauty' is the garbage-strewn street around him, which is a bleak joke about how ugly software interfaces are and how little beauty is on offer in everyday life.
summary: A woman claims bad software design has doomed her, and a sanitation worker's cure is to soak in the nearby heap of trash as if it were scenic splendor.

file: 2002/2002-04-17_camouflage suit_cubicle wall_make tie_don't be afraid.gif
title: Cubicle Camouflage Suit Startles Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't be afraid.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I made a camouflage suit out of cubicle-wall fabric. Heh, heh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You need a mask too.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I ran out of material. It was a mistake to make a tie.

situation: Dilbert walks along and jumps in fright, dropping his coffee, when Wally's head appears to float beside a cubicle wall. Wally explains he made a camouflage suit from cubicle-wall fabric so he blends in. Dilbert points out that he needs a mask too, and Wally admits he ran out of material because he wasted some on a tie.
punchline: Wally's cubicle-fabric camouflage is so complete it leaves only his face visible, and his plan failed because he wasted fabric on a tie nobody would ever see.
summary: A lazy coworker hides in plain sight inside a suit sewn from office partition material, but poor planning leaves his face exposed.

file: 2002/2002-01-27_email_engineer_huge_huge buzz_huge success_sales increase_six emails_track numbers_engineering.gif
title: Six Emails Prove Huge Success

transcript.speaker: Marketing Exec
transcript.text: The ad campaign was a huge, huge success!

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: Wow!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Define "huge, huge success." How much did sales increase?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Exec
transcript.text: We don't track those numbers.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Exec
transcript.text: But I know the ad created a huge buzz because of all the e-mail I got the next day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many messages did you get?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Exec
transcript.text: Six. But that's a lot for one topic.

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: Wow! Six!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many of the six were from your own employees?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Exec
transcript.text: Who invited the engineer?

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: I thought he was with you.

setting: Conference room during a marketing meeting
situation: A marketing executive boasts that an ad campaign was a huge success, and an easily impressed colleague agrees. Dilbert, the engineer, asks for actual sales figures and then probes the executive's only evidence, six emails, until it is clear the claim is baseless. The marketers respond by wondering who let him into the meeting.
punchline: When an engineer exposes the lack of real data behind a claimed success, the marketers do not defend their claim but instead try to figure out why he was allowed in the room.
summary: A marketer's boast about a triumphant ad campaign collapses under an engineer's basic questions about evidence, so the marketers blame his presence rather than their lack of numbers.

file: 2002/2002-01-17_sales training_sell anything_roadkill_thousand dollars_class_got hat_seminar_prop.gif
title: Salesman Sells Roadkill for Hat

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sales training

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: A trained salesperson can sell anything to anyone.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: I will prove it by selling this roadkill to one of you for a thousand dollars.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Um... How was your class?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got a hat!

situation: A sales trainer tells his class that a trained salesperson can sell anything to anyone, then holds up a dead animal from a bag and promises to sell it to someone in the audience for a thousand dollars. Afterward, Dogbert asks Dilbert how the class went, and Dilbert is seen wearing the roadkill on his head.
punchline: The trainer's demonstration worked so well that Dilbert paid a thousand dollars for roadkill and is proudly calling it a hat.
summary: A sales instructor's bold claim about selling anything is proven when a student ends up buying a dead animal and wearing it as headgear.

file: 2002/2002-11-02_defrauding stockholders_serve time_rommie_burp_wally and boss_arrested_jail.gif
title: Prison Sentence: Sharing Wally's Cubicle

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: The court finds you guilty of defrauding stockholders.

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: You will serve your time in a place so horrible that it has no name.

transcript.speaker: Guard
transcript.text: Here's your roomie.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Burp.

setting: A courtroom, then an office cubicle
situation: A judge convicts the Pointy-Haired Boss of defrauding stockholders and sentences him to a place so horrible it has no name. A guard then escorts the shaken Boss, who is wearing a prison jumpsuit, into a cubicle and introduces his new roommate, Wally, who burps while drinking coffee.
punchline: The horrific unnamed prison is simply a cubicle shared with the lazy, slovenly Wally, implying that ordinary office life is a punishment worse than jail.
summary: A corrupt executive is sentenced to a terrifying fate that turns out to be sharing a cubicle with a coworker.

file: 2002/2002-12-21_technically dead_wasn't afraid_life in cubicle.gif
title: Dead for Eight Minutes, Unafraid

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Technically, I was dead for eight minutes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know why I wasn't afraid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh.

setting: Office lunch table, then Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Dilbert tells his coworkers over lunch that he was clinically dead for eight minutes, and says he doesn't know why he wasn't afraid. In the last panel he sits alone and motionless in his cubicle, with a thought bubble reading 'Oh.'
punchline: Dilbert suddenly realizes that his lack of fear of death is because his dull, lifeless cubicle existence already feels like being dead.
summary: After a near-death experience, a puzzled engineer finally grasps why dying didn't scare him when he sits back down in his drab cubicle.

file: 2002/2002-09-19_business attire_changing dress code_clothing style_sartorial alchemy lab_might spark.gif
title: Boss Seeks Profit-Boosting Dress Code

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our dress code policy will go back to business attire.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I will keep changing the dress code until I find the clothing style that makes our profits go up!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later, at the sartorial alchemy lab

transcript.speaker: Lab Scientist
transcript.text: Watch out. This might spark.

situation: The Boss announces that the dress code is returning to business attire and vows to keep changing it until he finds the clothing style that raises profits. A caption then shows a lab where a scientist in goggles experiments on a yellow shirt with a small machine nearby, warning that it might spark.
punchline: The Boss treats clothing policy like a scientific experiment, randomly changing the dress code in the belief that the right outfit will magically boost profits.
summary: A manager keeps flip-flopping the dress code in hopes of stumbling on the wardrobe that makes money, as if clothes could be turned to gold in a lab.

file: 2002/2002-11-23_change happens_kickboxing_reverse sheep effect_reverse sheep effecte_wear pants.gif
title: Sheep Effect Reversal Misinterpreted Advice

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: You can reverse the sheep effect by signing up for a kickboxing class.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: The change will happen quickly, so be prepared.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Umm...okay.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Suddenly I realize he meant "wear pants."

setting: Outdoors beside a trash can, then a kickboxing ring
situation: Dogbert, dressed as a sheep, is told by a garbage man that he can reverse the 'sheep effect' by signing up for a kickboxing class and that the change will happen quickly. Dogbert follows the advice literally and ends up in a boxing ring, half-shaved and kicking his wool off as an opponent looks on nervously. Only then does he realize the man probably said 'wear pants' rather than 'kickboxing class.'
punchline: Dogbert misheard the vague, mumbled advice and has now put himself through a ridiculous kickboxing fight over a misunderstanding of 'wear pants.'
summary: After taking an odd tip too literally, a woolly dog finds himself shedding fleece in a boxing match and realizes he misunderstood the advice.

file: 2002/2002-06-29_act as boss_imitates her boss_alice_funny faces_makes hair pointy.gif
title: Alice Acts As Her Own Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you should act as if you're your own boss.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My hair is pointy and I'm confused. Suddenly I have no respect for myself.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Must... golf... now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That is so-o-o not funny.

situation: The Boss tells Alice to act as if she were her own boss. Alice complies literally by pulling her hair into two pointy horns, adopting a vacant expression, and mimicking his confusion and love of golf. The Boss, watching her impression, is offended.
punchline: Alice mocks the Boss by perfectly imitating his incompetence, and the only thing that bothers him is that her impression is unflattering.
summary: Told to behave like her own manager, a worker responds by lampooning her manager to his face.

file: 2002/2002-05-26_competitor_better job_employment agreement_knowledge or skills_crazy_clamp_suck_took away_verbal skills_golf ball head.gif
title: Catbert Sucks Out Departing Employee's Skills

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I quit. I got a better job with our competitor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, but remember the employment agreement you signed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You agreed to not take away knowledge or skills you acquired at this job.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That's crazy. How can I stop knowing what I learned?!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Come with me.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Will this hurt?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I hope so.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Clamp

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Suck suck suck suck suck suck suck suck suck

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ha ha!! I got your technical knowledge! And there go your verbal skills!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Great. Now what do I do?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'd stay away from the golf course.

situation: An employee tells his boss he is quitting for a competitor, and the boss reminds him of an employment agreement forbidding him from taking knowledge or skills away. Catbert takes the employee to a machine that clamps onto his head and sucks out his technical knowledge and verbal skills, leaving him with a hollow head.
punchline: Catbert interprets the non-compete clause literally by physically removing the employee's brain contents, then cruelly suggests his only remaining use is as a golf ball tee.
summary: A quitting worker is held to his contract's letter when Catbert drains his mind with a head-sucking machine and leaves him an empty shell.

file: 2002/2002-04-07_tech support_document_free paper_quality of paper_lousy regular_silkier_accept the things can't change.gif
title: Dogbert Gaslights Customer About Blank Pages

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Dogbert's tech support. How may I abuse you?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: My printer prints a blank page after every document.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why would you complain about getting free paper?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Free? Isn't it just giving me my own paper?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Egad, man! Look at the quality of the free paper compared to your lousy regular paper!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Only a fool or a liar would say they look the same!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Now that you mention it, it does seem silkier.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you doing?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm helping people accept the things they can't change.

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center desk and the customer's office
situation: Dogbert runs a tech support line and takes a call from a customer whose printer outputs a blank page after every document. Rather than fix it, Dogbert bullies the customer into believing the blank pages are a free bonus of superior quality. Dilbert asks what he's doing, and Dogbert explains his philosophy.
punchline: Instead of fixing the defect, Dogbert manipulates customers into accepting the problem as a feature, calling it helping people accept what they can't change.
summary: A tech support dog browbeats a caller into thinking his printer's wasted blank sheets are a luxurious freebie rather than a malfunction.

file: 2002/2002-04-04_3 year anniversary_first meeting_project requirements_probelm.gif
title: Three Years of Requirements Meetings

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today is the three-year anniversary of our first meeting to discuss project requirements.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And we're still discussing requirements. Does anyone else see a problem here?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: When you're done, can we talk about requirements?

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: Dilbert points out to the meeting attendees that it has been three years since their first meeting about project requirements, and they are still only discussing requirements. He asks if anyone sees a problem. A coworker misses the point entirely and asks to discuss requirements once Dilbert finishes.
punchline: The group is so stuck in endless requirements discussions that even when the absurdity is pointed out, a colleague just wants to continue talking about requirements.
summary: A project team marks three years of meetings that have produced nothing but more talk, and nobody grasps the obvious problem.

file: 2002/2002-08-28_quitting_work for myslef_deal with morons_freelance webdesigner.gif
title: Quitting, Then Asking for Freelance Work

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Ha ha! I quit, you stinkin' pile of rubbish!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm going to work for myself. I won't need to deal with morons like you again!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: On an unrelated note, if you need a freelance web designer, please call me.

situation: An employee stands before the seated Boss and gleefully quits, insulting him and boasting that he will now work for himself and never deal with morons again. In the final panel his tone shifts and he asks the Boss to hire him as a freelance web designer.
punchline: The employee's triumphant resignation tirade collapses into a plea for contract work from the very boss he just insulted, showing he still depends on the company for income.
summary: A worker storms out with insults and then immediately tries to drum up business from the man he just berated.

file: 2002/2002-10-22_investment banker_merger success_corrupt auditors_corrupt cfo_stock analysts_greedy bankers_clueless board memebers.gif
title: Merger Needs Corrupt Everyone Except You

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Investment Banker

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have all of the elements to make the merger a success.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...Corrupt auditors, corrupt CFO, corrupt stock analysts, greedy bankers and clueless board members.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What are you implying?

setting: Investment banking office, at a desk
situation: Dogbert, working as an investment banker, meets with the Boss, who says everything needed for a successful merger is in place. Dogbert lists a series of corrupt and incompetent players that make up those elements. When the Boss asks whether Dogbert is also part of the list, Dogbert acts offended.
punchline: Dogbert lists every corrupt party in the merger machinery but takes offense at the suggestion that he, the investment banker, might be one of them.
summary: An investment banker cheerfully catalogs the rot behind a deal's success, then bristles when asked if he belongs on the list.

file: 2002/2002-04-22_training budget slashed_cancel class_already paid_appear smart_while secretly stupid.gif
title: Skipping Paid Class to Look Smart

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The training budget got slashed. You have to cancel your class.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We already paid for the class.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll look bad if you go.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, our plan is to appear smart while secretly being stupid?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can make anything sound bad.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to cancel his training class because the training budget was cut. Dilbert points out the class has already been paid for, but the Boss insists the company will look bad if he attends. Dilbert summarizes the logic as appearing smart while secretly being stupid, and the Boss accuses him of making everything sound bad.
punchline: Dilbert's blunt restatement exposes the absurd logic of the Boss's decision, and the Boss deflects by blaming Dilbert's framing rather than the decision itself.
summary: A manager forces an employee to skip a prepaid course for the sake of appearances, then dismisses the employee's accurate summary of the plan as mere negativity.

file: 2002/2002-09-17_bad hotel_bubonic inn_elbonia_fleas_mattress_what kind of fleas.gif
title: Dilbert Seeks Cheap Elbonian Hotel

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excuse me. My boss is cheap; can you direct me to a bad hotel?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: I recommend the Bubonic Inn. It is so bad they will pay you to stay there.

transcript.speaker: Hotel Clerk
transcript.text: What kind of fleas do you want in your mattress?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lazy ones.

setting: Muddy street and hotel front desk in Elbonia
situation: Dilbert, standing in a barrel in Elbonia's mud, asks a local to direct him to a bad hotel because his boss is cheap. The local recommends the Bubonic Inn, which is so awful it would pay guests to stay. At the front desk the clerk offers him a choice of fleas in his mattress, and Dilbert asks for lazy ones.
punchline: Dilbert's resigned request for lazy fleas shows he accepts infested bedding as a given, simply hoping for the least bothersome pests, all because his boss won't pay for anything decent.
summary: Forced by a tightfisted employer to find the worst lodging possible, a traveler ends up in a flea-ridden inn and politely requests the most sluggish insects available.

file: 2002/2002-07-07_ideas for boosting morale_employee pot luck_schedule conflcits_brings small meal_pviep.gif
title: Permanent Virtual Individual Employee Potluck

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does anyone have any ideas for boosting morale?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Oooh! Oooh! Oooh!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The employee potluck lunch that we had last year was almost perfect.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But we only did it once and some people had schedule conflicts.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I call my idea the "Permanent Virtual Individual Employee Potluck" or P.V.I.E.P. for short.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Every day, each employee brings a small meal in a bag and eats it whenever he gets hungry.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You already do that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And look how happy I am!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. Who is going to organize the P.V.I.E.P.?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Alice hasn't helped yet.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss asks for morale-boosting ideas at a meeting. Wally eagerly proposes a 'permanent virtual individual employee potluck', which turns out to be just everyone bringing their own lunch in a bag, something employees already do. The Boss accepts it and asks who will organize it, and Wally volunteers Alice.
punchline: Wally's brilliant morale idea is just people eating their own packed lunches, and he still manages to dump the organizing work on Alice.
summary: A colleague dresses up the everyday habit of brown-bagging lunch as a bold morale initiative and then volunteers a coworker to run it.

file: 2002/2002-06-05_vacant private offcie_last one_ill-will_coworkers_diltopia_take off shoes_reverence.gif
title: Dilbert Claims Private Office, Demands Reverence

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm moving into a vacant private office. I got the last one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope this doesn't cause ill-will in the cubicle-bound co-workers I'm leaving behind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I ask is that when you enter Diltopia, you bow in reverence and take off your shoes.

situation: Dilbert carries a cardboard box and tells Alice he is moving into the last vacant private office. He pretends to worry about ill-will from the co-workers he is leaving in cubicles, then demands that visitors bow and remove their shoes when entering his new office, which he calls Diltopia. Alice grows increasingly annoyed and angry.
punchline: Dilbert's feigned concern for his colleagues' feelings is just a setup for smug, self-aggrandizing demands that they treat his new private office like a sacred place.
summary: After winning the final private office, a gloating Dilbert insists that his envious colleague show him ceremonial worship upon visiting his new domain.

file: 2002/2002-01-13_engineer of the year_fly to ny_receive trophy_winners_other companies_critical time_name someone lese_sick day_sleep_bathe_carol_marketing_upside awards_on head_health_business.gif
title: Marketing Posing As Engineer Winners

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I'm naming you our company's "Engineer of the Year."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll fly to New York and receive a trophy with the winners from other companies.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm too busy. Name someone else.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a critical time for my project.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm flattered but I already have no time for sleeping or bathing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have a sick day scheduled for that Friday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I need you to go to New York and pretend to be an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Award Winner
transcript.text: Why yes, most of us are really from marketing. How can you tell?

setting: Office cubicles, then an awards event in New York
situation: The Boss tries to give the Engineer of the Year award to Alice, Dilbert, Asok and Wally in turn, but each one refuses with an excuse. He then sends Carol from marketing to New York to pretend to be an engineer. At the ceremony, the other winners holding trophies and wearing trophy-topped hats turn out to be marketing people too.
punchline: Engineers avoid the award so thoroughly that every company sends marketing people to pose as engineers, making the whole contest meaningless.
summary: Nobody technical wants the trophy trip, so the company sends a marketing employee in disguise and discovers that every other winner did the same.

file: 2002/2002-03-26_water company_pipe water_toothpaste_turn faucet_pudding_meteor.gif
title: Toothpaste Piped Through Every Faucet

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If the water company can pipe water to my house, why can't the toothpaste company do the same?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The toothpaste factory should have a pipe to every home so you can turn a faucet...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And don't even get me started about pudding.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Meteor meteor meteor meteor

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk and rambles about why toothpaste isn't piped into homes like water, then adds that pudding should be too. Dilbert sits at his computer, growing visibly more aggravated, and in the last panel his thought bubble reveals he is wishing for a meteor to strike.
punchline: Dilbert is so exasperated by the Boss's absurd ideas that he silently fantasizes about a meteor wiping everything out.
summary: Dilbert endures his boss's ridiculous utility-pipe schemes while mentally praying for a catastrophic space rock.
